Index             This is a convenient cross-reference to all the concepts, commands,
                  and functions discussed in your dBASE III PLUS manuals . The
                  index references all the manuals in both Volumes One and Two . A
                  duplicate index is also in Volume Two .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                              UI-3
Introduction
                  Using dBASE III PLUS is an encyclopedia of information on key-
                  words, commands and functions, and how to do basic data manage-
                  ment tasks in dBASE III PLUS . If you have completed Learning
                  dBASE III PLUS or are otherwise familiar with dBASE, program-
                  ming, or database management, this section is for you .
                  If you are an intermediate-to-advanced user, you may also wish to
                  refer to Programming with dBASE III PLUS .
                  This section is organized into seven chapters :

Chapter 1 :       This contains the technical specifications of dBASE III PLUS and
                  discussions of the basics : file types, field types, memory variables,
Overview          and the like .

Chapter 2 :       This chapter provides another path for learning the program . It
                  gives you more detail on the information you learned in Chapter 9,
Using             "dBASE III PLUS Commands," in Learning dBASE III PLUS . You'll
Commands          find out more about command syntax, operators, handling multiple
                  databases via work areas, relations, or catalogs, and how to organize
                  and search your data to get the facts and results you need . The
                  chapter is divided into task-oriented sections which describe the
                  commands you need to complete basic operations in
                  dBASE III PLUS .

Chapter 3 :       This chapter takes up where Chapter 10 in Learning dBASE III PLUS
                  left off. You learn about running dBASE III PLUS by means of pro-
About             gram files. With program files you gain more control over your data
Program Files     than you have by using commands only at the dot prompt . This
                  chapter tells you about programming commands and how to create,
                  execute, close, and debug program files .

Chapter 4 :       This chapter describes two configuration files that you need to run
                  dBASE III PLUS properly: Config.sys and Config .db . You'll also
dBASE 111 PLUS    learn about the SET menu and the different options you have to
Configuration     customize dBASE III PLUS or the programs you create .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                   UI-1
                                                                   INTRODUCTION


Chapter 5 :   This chapter is the bulk of the manual, as commands are the bulk of
              dBASE III PLUS . Chapter 5 along with Chapter 6, "Functions,"
Commands      make up the reference section of your manuals . Chapter 5 has a
              Classes of Commands section in which the commands are divided
              according to how they're used . The commands are then listed in
              alphabetical order and thoroughly described . The description
              includes a definition of the command, its syntax, usage, examples,
              and any tips that may make it easier for you to use . The files used in
              the examples are on the Sample Programs and Utilities disk .

Chapter b :   This chapter along with Chapter 5, "Commands," make up the ref-
              erence section of your manual . Chapter 6 contains the same type of
Functions     information for each function as Chapter 5 . The functions are
              divided into classes according to how they're used . Each function is
              also listed in alphabetical order and thoroughly described . The
              description includes a definition, syntax, usage, examples, and any
              tips that make it easier for you to use . The files used in the exam-
              ples are on the Sample Programs and Utilities disk .

Chapter 7:    Each error message that can appear in dBASE III PLUS is listed
              here, along with an explanation of possible causes of the message
Error         and applicable code numbers .
Messages
Appendices    These contain :
               • A table of control characters and their meanings
               • A table of end-of-file and beginning-of-file conditions for indexed
                 and nonindexed files
               • The structure of a database ( .dbf) file
               • A table of printable ASCII character codes

Glossary      This contains special words used in dBASE III PLUS with their defi-
              nitions . A separate glossary for network systems can be found in
              Networking with dBASE 111 PLUS .

Chapter 1
OVERVIEW


                  This chapter describes the technical specifications of
                  dBASE III PLUS . As an overview, it also describes the different file
                  types and field types, and discusses memory variables, which give
                  you more flexibility in handling your data .

dBASE 111 PLUS
                  The following values may be limited by the amount of RAM in your
                  computer .
Technical
Specifications
                  Database File
                       Number of records             1 billion maximum
                       Number of bytes               2 billion maximum
                       Record size                   4,000 bytes in .dbf file
                                                     512 kilobytes in .dbt file
                       Fields                        128 maximum
                  Field Sizes
                       Character fields              254 bytes maximum
                       Date fields                   8 bytes
                       Logical fields                1 byte
                       Memo fields                   5,000 bytes maximum or the capacity
                                                     of the word processor used
                       Numeric fields                19 bytes maximum
                  File Operations
                      15 open files of all types .
                       10 open database files . A database file counts as two files if
                       memo fields are used .
                       Seven open index files per active database file .
                       One open format file per active database file .




USING dBASE III PLUS
                                                            CHAPTER 1


Numeric Accuracy
   15 .9 digits . Note that the decimal point does not count as a digit
   in determining accuracy . Accuracy is 13 digits when comparing
   numbers, except zero .

Memory Variables
    Number of active memory variables : 256 maximum .
    Number of bytes available for memory variables : 6,000 default .
    The size of a memory variable depends on its type :

    Character                 assigned string + 2 bytes
    Numeric                   9 bytes
    Date                      9 bytes
    Logical                   2 bytes
Command Line
   Maximum length            254 characters

File Types   dBASE III PLUS saves information as disk files in several special-
             ized formats . Each serves a specific dBASE III PLUS processing
             need.
             Each disk file has a filename of not more than eight characters and
             a file extension consisting of a period and three characters maxi-
             mum. A filename can contain letters, numbers, and the underscore
             (_) character, but not special characters or spaces . It cannot begin
             with a number.
             You assign a filename at the time the file is created . The filename
             extension must be assigned at the same time . Normally,
             dBASE III PLUS assigns a default filename extension according to
             the type of file being created . However, you can override the
             dBASE III PLUS assignment by simply typing in an extension when
             you enter the filename . The default extensions, as well as the kinds
             of files, are defined in the following table :

                        Kind of File                       File Type
                        Binary                             .bin
                        Catalog                            .cat
                        Command and Procedure              .prg
                        Database                           .dbf
                        Database Backup                    .bak*
                        Database Memo                      .dbt
                        Database Memo Backup               .tbk
                        Format                             .fmt
                        Index                              .ndx
                        Label                              .lbl
                        Memory                             .mem
                        Query                              .qry
                        Report Form                        .frm
                        Screen                             .scr
                        Text Output                        .txt
                        View                               .vue
                        * Command and procedure backup files also have a
                          .bak extension .


                                 Table 1-1 File types and extensions




U1-4                                                              USING dBASE III PLUS
OVERVIEW


                  If you do not use the default extension, you must include the exten-
                  sion whenever the file is selected for use .

Binary ( .bin)    Binary files are assembly language programs that are assembled,
                  linked, and converted to a binary form so they can be LOADed
Files             directly into memory and executed with the CALL command .
                  Binary files are created when an assembled and linked program is
                  converted from the .EXE format to the .COM format with the DOS
                  EXE2BIN command .

Catalog ( .cat)   A catalog ( .cat) file (or catalog, for short) is like a register to help
                  you keep track of all your files . For example, if you have a database
Files             file that you use regularly with an index file, a custom screen for-
                  mat, a report form, a view file, and a query file, you can store the
                  names of all these files in a catalog . When you activate the catalog,
                  only these files can be opened . A catalog file is created and
                  activated with the SET CATALOG TO command .

Command           Command files contain sets of dBASE III PLUS commands that
                  have been stored as programs. They are ASCII files and may be cre-
and               ated with either MODIFY COMMAND or any word processing pro-
Procedure         gram that creates ASCII text files .
( .prg) Files     Procedure files also contain dBASE III PLUS instructions, but they
                  are stored in memory . A procedure file is like a programming tool
                  kit. It contains utility programs (called procedures) which complete
                  simple tasks that you do often in dBASE III PLUS . Having a proce-
                  dure file in memory reduces disk access time and enables an appli-
                  cations program to run faster . You can only have one procedure file
                  in memory at a time .

Database          Database ( .dbf) files store data in records and fields . Viewing a
                  database file as a table, each record represents a row in the table
( .dbf) Files     and each field a column . Each record is intended to contain a set of
                  unique information. The structure of records in a database file is
                  created with CREATE and changed with MODIFY STRUCTURE .

Database File     Each time you modify the structure of a database file,
                  dBASE III PLUS creates a backup of the file, and a new file contain-
Backups           ing the new structure . The data in the backup file is added to the
(.bak)            new file in fields with the same name .



USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                   U1-5
                                                                              CHAPTER 1


                  Back-up files with a .bak extension are also created when you alter
                  a file that was created with MODIFY COMMAND .

Database          Database memo ( .dbt) files are text files which contain the contents
                  of memo fields . All memo fields in a database ( .dbf) file are stored
Memo ( .dbt)      in the same database memo file . The .dbt file is created at the same
Files             time as the .dbf file .
                  Because the contents of memo fields are stored in a separate file, a
                  memo field only occupies ten spaces per record in the database file .

Database          If a database file has memo fields, they are stored in a memo ( .dbt)
                  file . When you modify the structure of the database file, a new
Memo File         database file with the new structure as well as a backup of the
Backups ( .tbk)   memo file is created and saved . The data in the back-up file is
                  added to the new file in memo fields with the same name .

Format ( .fmt)    You use format files to create custom screen forms for use in data
                  entry and printed output . They are generated from screen ( .scr) files
Files             set up by the CREATE SCREEN command . You can also write for-
                  mat files directly using MODIFY COMMAND or any word processor
                  that creates ASCII text files .

Index (.ndx)      Index files enable you to use a database file in a logical order rather
                  than the physical order . The physical order is the order in which
Files             you enter records in a database file . A logical order is an alphabeti-
                  cal, chronological, or numerical order based on the contents of one
                  or more selected fields . The selected field is called a key field .
                  Index files are created with the INDEX command .
                  Index files store the database record numbers according to the
                  selected field(s) . When using a database with an index file, the
                  database appears to be in the order of the key item . For example, if
                  the key field is a name field, the records appear in alphabetical
                  order according to the names .
                  The key, which can be one or more fields, may also be used to pro-
                  vide direct access to a particular record .

Label (.lbl)      Label files contain the information needed by the LABEL command
                  to print labels . They are created and altered by the CREATE/
Form              MODIFY LABEL command .

Memory            Memory files are used to save the contents of memory variables for
                  later use . Memory files may contain up to 256 memory variables or
(.mem) Files      6,000 bytes (default value) . These files are created by the command
                  SAVE and are read back into memory by the command RESTORE .

Files             be in USE. Query files are created with the CREATE/MODIFY

( .frm) Files     the CREATE/MODIFY REPORT command .

Files             able ASCII characters .
                  You read text files from other software into dBASE III PLUS with a
                  special form of the APPEND FROM command . You create text files
                  from dBASE III PLUS files for use with other software via a special
                  form of the COPY command . A text file is also created when you
                  use the SET ALTERNATE command to store screen output such as
                  the commands you type at the dot prompt and their results or the
                  output from a program file .

A view file contains a list of selected field names from one or more
specified database ( .dbf) files . You set up a view file so only the
selected fields are seen when using the database files . View files can
also store associated index files and relationships between the
database files . You can create a format file and filter conditions
which reference the selected field names . You use CREATE/
MODIFY VIEW to set up the view file . A view file can also be stored
in a catalog .

The structure of a database file is established by defining fields to
store data . You use the CREATE and MODIFY STRUCTURE com-
mands to define a field which consists of the name, type, and width .
Field names may be up to ten characters long . They must begin
with a letter and cannot contain embedded blank spaces . Letters,
numbers, and underscores are permitted .
There are five field types in dBASE III PLUS . They are Character
(C), Date (D), Logical (L), Memo (M), and Numeric (N) . Each one is
discussed below .
The field width is the maximum number of characters or digits that
are to be contained in the field. You define the field width for char-
acter and numeric fields . Date, logical, and memo fields have fixed
lengths . In the case of numeric fields, you need to include the sign
(if any), the decimal point, and the number of decimal places (digits
to the right of the decimal point) in the total number of characters .
See Appendix C for further information .




                                                USING dBASE III PLUS
OVERVIEW


Character         Character fields may be used to store any printable ASCII character
                  (letters, numbers, special symbols, and blank spaces) . The
Fields            maximum field width of a character field is 254 .

Date Fields       Date fields are used to store dates . Dates may be entered and dis-
                  played in different ways by using the SET DATE command or the
                  PICTURE option of the       command. The default date entry and dis-
                  play format is mm/dd/yy . The field width of a date field is always
                  eight.
                  Dates may be used in calculations with other dates and numbers .
                  For example, a number may be added to a date to calculate a date
                  in the future ; a date may be subtracted from a date ; and a number
                  may be subtracted from a date .

Numeric           Numeric fields are of two types : integer and decimal . An integer is a
                  number that does not have decimal places (for example, the num-
Fields            ber of students in a class) . The width of a numeric field is the num-
                  ber of digits the field can hold . The decimal point and negative sign
                  each count as one digit .
                  Accuracy of numeric fields extends to 15 .9 digits, not including the
                  decimal point itself . This means that the most significant 15 digits of
                  any number will be reliable .

Logical Fields    Logical fields accept only single characters representing True/ False
                  values . Logical True (.T.) is entered as T, t, Y, or y . Logical False
                  ( .F.) is entered as F, f, N, or n .

Memo Fields       Memo fields are designed to accommodate large blocks of textual
                  information . All memo fields in a database file are stored in a
                  database memo ( .dbt) file which is created when you set up the
                  database file . Memo fields are indicated in the database ( .dbf) file by
                  the word memo.
                  Memo fields may contain the same kind of information as character
                  fields, but can have 5,000 characters or more, depending on the
                  word processor you use . Each memo field requires a minimum of
                  512 bytes per record if any data is specified . Each memo field occu-
                  pies only ten spaces per record in the database file, because the text
                  is stored in a separate file on your disk .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                  U1-9
                                                            CHAPTER 1


Memory variables enable you to store data outside of the database
file structure . For example, the contents of a field in several records
can all be summed, and the result stored as a memory variable . The
content of the memory variable could then be directly used in fur-
ther calculations. Memory variables are often used in programming
applications where they provide a means for controlling the pro-
gram . Memory variables ordinarily provide temporary storage,
and their values are kept only during a current session in
dBASE III PLUS . However, you can SAVE memory variables to a
memory ( .mem) file, and RESTORE them to reuse their values .
Here are the specifications for memory variables :
Memvar Names
Memory variable names can be up to ten characters long. They can
contain letters, numbers, and underscores . They must begin with a
letter and cannot contain embedded blank spaces .
The only restricted names for memory variables are those created
with the syntax < memory variable > _ < expression > . In this
case, the memory variable name cannot be the same as a
dBASE III PLUS command .
Memvar Types
There are four types of memory variables : character, date, numeric,
and logical .
Memvar Sizes
In memory, the size of a memory variable depends on its type .
Character type variables are the length of the assigned string plus
two bytes . Date variables are nine bytes . Numeric variables are also
nine bytes . Logical variables take up two bytes .
There can be as many as 256 active memory variables with a com-
bined size of up to 6,000 bytes . This 6,000-byte capacity can be
increased by using the MVARSIZ option in Config .db, provided
that you have more memory than the recommended 384K . (See
Chapter 4 in this manual for more information on Config .db .)

Re-entering   The dBASE III PLUS dot prompt has a memory buffer called
              history that automatically stores the last 20 commands you enter .
Commands      This allows you to go back and edit or run a previously entered
              command . You can use the SET HISTORY TO command to change
              the default number of stored commands from 20 to any number
              you prefer .
              Press T at the dot prompt to display commands previously stored in
              the history buffer . The commands appear one at a time in reverse
              order ; that is, the last command you entered appears first, the next-
              to-last command appears second, and so on . y moves the cursor
              back down the list of commands . Use DISPLAY HISTORY and LIST
              HISTORY to view more than one command at a time .
              To run a command stored in the history buffer, display the com-
              mand at the dot prompt as just described and then press + . To edit
              a command in the buffer, display the command at the dot prompt,
              then use the editing keys listed in the table above to make any nec-
              essary changes . Press    to run the new command .

Structure of a    The structure of a command is called its syntax . Each command
                  line begins with a verb, which is the basic command . Many com-
dBASE             mand lines also have one or more clauses that tailor the command
Command           to meet a particular need . The general syntax of a command is illus-
(Syntax)          trated by :
                  VERB [ < scope > ] [ < expression li st > ] [FOR < condition > ]
                  [WHILE < condition >
                  The verb is the name of the dBASE command .
                  The [] (square brackets) indicate that the item is optional .
                  The < > means that you enter the enclosed item .
                   • scope > defines how many records the command applies to . The
                  keywords for scope are: RECORD <n> to specify a single record
                  by its number ; NEXT <n> means n records beginning with the
                  current record; ALL for all the records in the database ; and REST
                  for records from the current record to the end of the file .
                   • expression list > is one or more expressions, separated by a
                  comma . They do not have to be the same data type (see Expressions
                  below) .
                  FOR < condition >  is known as a clause or condition statement . It
                  tells dBASE III PLUS that the command applies only to records
                  which meet the condition . WHILE < condition > tells
                  dBASE III PLUS to repeat the command as long as long as the con-
                  dition is true .
                   • condition > is a comparison between two items like
                  Name = 'Smith' or a logical statement like .NOT . EOFQ .
                  Do not type the square brackets ([ ]) or angle brackets (< > )
                  when entering a command .

                                                                                CHAPTER 2


              To illustrate the syntax of a typical command :

                     DISPLAY NEXT 25 Name,Address FOR Name ='Jones'

              The specific syntax of each command is shown in Chapter 5 .

                            Expression Type             Abbreviation

                           Numeric                       expN

              When you combine fields or memory variables or both in one

              functions to convert them . Note, however, that an expression list
              does not have to be one data type .

Precedence          Each type of operator has a set of rules that governs the order
                    in which operations are performed . These are referred to as the
of Operators        order o f precedence for the operator .


                    The relational and string operators have only one level of prece-
                    dence and are performed in order from left to right .
                    The precedence levels for mathematical operators are :
                    1 . Unary + and - signs
                    2. Exponentiation
                    3 . Multiplication and division
                    4. Addition and subtraction
                    The precedence levels for the logical operators are :
                    1 . .NOT.
                    2.     .AND.
                    3.      OR.




U2-6                                                                 USING dBASE III PLUS
USING COMMANDS

                  When several of the four types of operators are used in the same
                  expression, the precedence levels for the types are :
                   1 . Mathematical and string
                  2 . Relational
                  3 . Logical
                  All operations at the same precedence level are performed in order
                  from left to right. Parentheses are used to override the order in
                  which operations are performed. Operations within the innermost
                  nested parentheses are performed first .

Basic Rules       When using the dBASE III PLUS command language, there are cer-
                  tain rules that must be followed to ensure that commands are prop-
                  erly written :
                  1 . Each command must begin with a command verb taken from
                      Chapter 5 in this manual .
                  2 . Each command must conform to the syntax for that command
                      as described in Chapter 5 .
                  3 . A command consists of a verb and, optionally, one or more
                      clauses and keywords that qualify the verb . Optional clauses
                      (beginning with WHILE or FOR) and keywords such as
                      NEXT may occur in any order . For example, the following are
                      equivalent :
                         DISPLAY NEXT 25 FOR Name   = 'Johnson'
                         DISPLAY FOR Name   = 'Johnson' NEXT 25

                  4. The maximum command line length is 254 characters .
                  5 . Words within a command may be separated by any number of
                      blank spaces . Blank spaces, however, count in the 254-character
                      limit .
                  6. Commands and certain keywords may be abbreviated to the first
                       four characters, for example, DISPLAY MEMORY can be abbre-
                       viated as DISP MEMO .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                 U2-7
                                                                     CHAPTER 2


            7.   Command verbs, keywords, field names, memory variable
                 names, and filenames may be in upper case, lower case, or any
                 mixture .
            8 . Do not use the letters A through J and M by themselves as
                database filenames because they are reserved for ALIAS names .
                For example, "AA" is a valid database filename, whereas "A" is
                 not. Also, do not use DOS device names as filenames because
                these are reserved by the operating system . See your DOS man-
                ual for details .
            9. Although dBASE III PLUS has no prohibited words, try to avoid
               using keywords and commands for filenames, field names, or
               memory variable names, as this may cause some confusion . For
               example, a field named Status could not be displayed by the
               command DISPLAY STATUS because the command would dis-
               play the current processing status rather than the content of the
               field Status.

            You use these values to perform calculations, comparisons, and

            WAIT .
            You assign each memory variable a name of up to ten characters
            long, including letters, numbers, and underscores . The name must
            begin with a letter and cannot contain embedded blank spaces . The
            only restricted names for variables are those created with
            the syntax < memvar name > _ < expression > . In this case, the
            memory variable name cannot be the same as a dBASE III PLUS

                       When fields and memory variables have the same name, fields

Memory       There are four data types for memory variables : character, numeric,
             date, and logical . These are discussed below .
Variable
Data Types

Character    Character type memory variables are normally used to store charac-
             ter strings . However, a binary sequence may be stored to a charac-
             ter string by means of the CHR() function . Character variables may
             contain as many as 254 characters . The total memory space used by
             a character variable is its length in bytes plus two bytes .

Date         Date type memory variables are used to store dates . The size of a
             date variable is always eight bytes . The total memory requirement is
             nine bytes . Date variables are validated whenever they are entered
             or changed. They are normally presented in the mm/dd/yy (Ameri-
             can) format. They may be presented in other formats by use of the
             SET DATE and SET CENTURY commands .
             Date variables may be created from other date variables or fields .
             The CTOD() function must be used when you enter a date directly
             from the keyboard .
             A date may be subtracted from another date . The result is a number
             (the number of days between the dates) . A number (representing a
             number of days) may be added to or subtracted from a date . The
             result will also be a date .

Numeric      Numeric type memory variables are used to store numbers that may
             be used in calculations . Numeric variables use up to nine bytes in
             memory . The accuracy of numeric variables extends to 15 .9 digits .
             This means that the most significant 15 digits are reliable (not
             counting the decimal point) . This is reduced to 13 digits for com-
             parisons of non-zero numbers.
Logical      Logical variables are stored as True ( .T .) or False ( .F .) . The size of a
             logical variable is always one byte . It requires a total of two bytes of
             memory. Logical variables will accept T, t, Y, or y for True and F, f,
             N, or n for False . When created from the keyboard, a logical value
             must be delimited by periods, for example, STORE .T. TO Mlogic .

USING COMMANDS

Menu Bar           The menu bar is located at the top of the screen and contains sev-
                   eral menus and a clock . Some commands are menu-driven, mean-
                   ing that the command is operated using the menu bar . Other com-
                   mands are menu-assisted, meaning that the menu bar is optional . In
                   these commands, you will not see a menu bar unless you ask for it
                   by pressing Ctrl-Home or F10 .

Main Menu          Each menu on the menu bar has a main pull-down menu associated
                   with it.

Selection Bar      The selection bar or highlight is a reverse video bar that indicates
(Highlight)        the current menu option . Several selection bars may be on the
                   screen at one time . For example, when using The Assistant, select-
                   ing the Database file option under Set Up presents a submenu of
                   drive letters . You can see that Database file is still in reverse video .
                   Using the T and y keys moves the selection bar in the drive letter
                   submenu until you make a selection by pressing 4-'.


USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                    U2-13
                                                                             CHAPTER 2

Submenu           Some main menu options activate a submenu of further options
                  from which you make selections . A submenu is similar to a main
                  menu in that it offers a set of options . An option can, in turn, call
                  another submenu . A submenu can be a list of things such as fields,
                  files, or drive letters, from which one, or sometimes more than one,
                  option can be selected .

Dialogue Box      This box displays long prompts and allows you to enter multiple
                  parameters to perform an operation . For example, when creating an
                  index, you are prompted to enter the key expression in the dialogue
                  box .

Action Line       As you build a command in The Assistant, the syntax is written on
                  the action line . This helps you learn the dBASE III PLUS syntax of
                  individual commands so you can build them from the dot prompt
                  or in a program . Other menu-driven commands, such as CREATE/
                  MODIFY VIEW, use this line to provide useful information .

Status Bar        The status bar provides pertinent information about the current
                  operation : the name of the operation, the active filename, the cur-
                  rent drive, the number of options in a menu and which option is
                  highlighted, the number of records in a file, and the record at
                  which you're positioned . The status bar also indicates whether you

Using Screen   A number of commands are referred to as full-screen commands
               because of the way they use the screen display . These are APPEND,
Forms          CREATE, EDIT, MODIFY STRUCTURE, and READ .
               When you use these commands, data is presented to you as a form
               to be filled in or changed . CREATE and MODIFY STRUCTURE dis-
               play standard forms . APPEND and EDIT also have standard forms,
               but you can design your own via The Assistant or the
               CREATE/MODIFY SCREEN command . You can also create forms
               using the @a command with GET and SAY options . In this case, you
               are building a format ( .fmt) file (see Creating Screen Forms below) .
               When you use forms, prompts are presented in standard video (light
               letters on a dark background) . Data items are normally presented in
               enhanced video or highlighted (dark letters on a light background) .
               The arrow keys can be used to place the cursor anywhere within
               the highlighted areas . Data is entered by typing within these identi-
               fied data areas .



                 NOTE
                 If you have a color card and monitor, you can change the col-
                 ors of the standard and enhanced displays on your screen . You
                 can choose colors via the SET menu and its Screen submenu or
                 by using the SET COLOR TO command . These colors are
                 present until you change them or QUIT dBASE III PLUS .
                 If you wish the colors to be present whenever you use
                 dBASE III PLUS, save them in the Config .db file (see Chapter 4
                 in this manual) .
                 For monochrome monitors, the Screen submenu has different
                 options . You cannot choose colors, but you can change the
                 intensity of the standard and enhanced areas of your screen and
                 include underlining and blinking .

Using           The following sections describe the commands you will use most
                often to manipulate your database and obtain the information you
Commands        need . Read the following sections for an overview of
for Your        dBASE III PLUS .
Database

Creating a      You create a database ( .dbf) file by typing CREATE < filename > at
                the dot prompt . If you do not include a filename, dBASE III PLUS
Database File   prompts for one . If you do not include an extension, .dbf is auto-
                matically appended . If you assign a different extension, you need to
                include it in the filename each time the file is USEd .
                After entering the command, a form appears through which you
                define the structure of the database file . At the top of the screen is a
                menu of cursor and editing keys . The file structure includes the
                field names, types, and widths . If the field is numeric, you also spec-
                ify decimal places . (See Chapter 1 for a description of fields .)
                After you have defined the structure, press Ctrl-End to save it .
                dBASE III PLUS asks if you wish to Input data records now?
                (Y/N) . Answer Y and the screen form for the APPEND command
                appears . Answer N and the dot prompt appears for your next
                command.
                To modify the structure of a database file, type MODIFY
                STRUCTURE . If you have not put a file into USE, dBASE III PLUS
                prompts you for a filename . The same screen form appears with the
                data you entered . You can change the name, type, and width of a
                field, or remove the decimal places in a numeric field, but you must
                only change one part a time .
                When you save the new structure, dBASE III PLUS creates two files,
                a backup of the original file and a new file with the new structure .
                Data from the backup file is automatically copied to the new file
                unless you have changed field names . In this case, you are asked
                first if you want the backup data copied to the new file . If you do,
                only fields with the same name are copied .

Adding New
Records

APPEND,           You can add new records to your database file through three com-
                  mands. APPEND adds records to the end of the file . It automatically
BROWSE, and       updates any open index files, putting them in order . INSERT puts a
INSERT            record in a specified physical location in the file . Generally, you use
                  INSERT only where it is important that the record number reflect
                  the record's true position in the file, which is often the case with
                  SORTed files . However, if you have index files open, INSERT works
                  like APPEND and adds records to the end of the file, one record at
                  a time . BROWSE has an option to add records to the end of the file .
                  APPEND and INSERT present the same screen form as EDIT . With
                  both, you can SET a format ( .fmt) file to custom design the screen .
                  SET CARRY ON copies the contents of the current record to the
                  newly APPENDed or INSERTed record .

APPEND            APPEND BLANK and INSERT BLANK add a blank record to a file,
                  but do not display a screen form for you to enter data . INSERT
BLANK and         BLANK lets you reserve a specific place anywhere in the file .
INSERT            APPEND BLANK puts the blank record at the end of the file . After
BLANK             issuing these commands, use APPEND, BROWSE, CHANGE, or
                  EDIT to enter data in the blank records . APPEND BLANK is often
                  used in application programs when it is necessary to verify the
                  accuracy of data . (See Chapter 11 in Programming with
                  dBASE III PLUS for more information on this procedure .)

APPEND            The APPEND FROM command lets you copy records from a named
                  database file to the end of the open database file . It copies only
FROM              those fields that are common to both files and only those records
                  that meet the criteria specified in the FOR statement of the com-
                  mand syntax .
                  You can use the APPEND FROM command to convert data from
                  Visicalc, Multiplan, Lotus 1-2-3, and other programs into a
                  dBASE III PLUS format and add it to the end of an open database
                  file . For more information on this procedure, see the alphabetical
                  entry for APPEND FROM in Chapter 5 .

Changing the contents of a database file is one of the fundamental
operations you'll perform in dBASE III PLUS . There are a variety of
ways to do this, and each has unique features .
The following table outlines the commands you use to alter records
in a database file.

 CHANGE        UPDATE              BROWSE          ZAP

Each command is described briefly in this section . See Chapter 5
for more information on any command .

If you make an error while entering data in the database file, or you
want to update the contents of a particular file, you can use either
the EDIT or BROWSE command . Both commands let you look only
at specific fields. Below are some general guidelines for using EDIT
and BROWSE .




                                                   USING dBASE III PLUS
USING COMMANDS

EDIT              You use EDIT or CHANGE when you want to view one record at a
                  time . (These commands are identical .) The record's appearance on
                  the screen depends on whether you have a format ( .fmt) file open .
                  If a format file is not open, the record appears in the default verti-
                  cal form . If a format file is in use, the record appears on the screen
                  in the manner specified by the format ( .fmt) file .

BROWSE            Use BROWSE when you want a table view of up to 17 records at
                  once. If the records are more than 80 characters long, you can't
                  view all of one record at a time . However, BROWSE does allow you
                  to select which fields appear on the screen and how many charac-
                  ters from each character type field will be displayed .
                  While using BROWSE you can also add records to the end of the
                  file and search for a key expression .

Changing a
Batch of
Records

REPLACE           If you want to make the same change to one field throughout the
                  file, dBASE III PLUS allows you to automate the process with the
                  REPLACE command . For more information, see the description of
                  REPLACE in Chapter 5 .

UPDATE            The UPDATE command lets you replace the content of one or more
                  fields in a database file using content from another database file .
                  This transfer is performed when key fields in both files are the
                  same . For more information, see the description in Chapter 5 .

Deleting          When you find that you no longer need a certain record, you can
                  remove it permanently from the file . Alternatively, you can just
Records           mark it for removal . It is then available to be reinstated if you
                  change your mind . DELETE marks records for deletion . Reinstate
                  records that are marked for deletion with the RECALL command .
                  The commands for permanently deleting records are PACK and
                  ZAP . PACK removes all records marked for deletion ; ZAP removes
                  all records in the database file . These are discussed in Chapter 5 .

In full-screen mode, such as EDIT and BROWSE, the word Del indi-
cates that a record is marked for deletion .
In other commands, such as LIST, an asterisk (*) before the record
indicates that a record is marked for deletion .
Use the Ctrl-U toggle when you are in full-screen mode to mark a
record for deletion or to reinstate a marked record .
If you want to work with a file that has records marked for deletion,
but do not want to include those records, type SET DELETED ON .
Then, all dBASE III PLUS commands treat the deleted records as if
they do not exist . The SET DELETED OFF command causes the
marked records to be visible to dBASE III PLUS again .

You can enter your data in a database file in any order and then
retrieve the data in a logical order: alphabetically, numerically, or
chronologically . For example, you enter names in the Clients
database file as you get them . However, to use the file most
efficiently, the names should be in alphabetical order . Not only does
this enable you to list the records in a logical order, but
dBASE III PLUS can search through the file more quickly .
dBASE III PLUS provides two commands that do this, INDEX and
SORT .

INDEX and SORT each have advantages . With INDEX, you specify a
key expression on which to order the file . A key expression can be a
field name or a complex expression . SORT uses a field list and has
options to establish ascending or descending order . Other differ-
ences between INDEX and SORT are summarized below .

                  For most purposes, you should use indexed files, because
                  dBASE III PLUS automatically updates open index files . With both
                  commands, your original file remains intact . INDEX creates an
                  associated index file that only contains pointers to the database file
                  from which it was created ; it does not contain the actual data
                  records . SORT, on the other hand, creates an entirely new file,
                  which can be used independently of the file from which it was cre-
                  ated. It is therefore up to you to maintain the order of a SORTed
                  file.
                  For more details on INDEX and SORT, see the individual listings in
                  Chapter 5 .

Indexing   A database ( .dbf) file can have as many associated .ndx files as you
           want. However, only seven .ndx files can be active at a time . Using
           the Tours database file, you can index the file on Seats_open by
           typing :

                • USE Tours
                • INDEX ON Seats_open TO Seats
                  100% indexed         30 records indexed

                • LIST Seats_open, Departure, Travelplan

           If you have several existing index ( .ndx) files that you want updated
           every time you change the contents of a record or add a new
           record, you must open them . There are two ways to do this :

                • USE Tours
                • SET INDEX TO <Index1 >, <Index2>, <Index3>

           or
                • USE Tours INDEX < Index 1>, < Index2 >, < Index3>




U2-28                                                             USING dBASE III PLUS
USING COMMANDS

SET ORDER TO      In both cases, Index 1 is the controlling or master index, because it
                  is the first in the list . This means that any operation, such as LIST,
                  acts as if the file is ordered according to the key expression of
                  Index 1 . If you want to change the controlling position to another
                  .ndx file, such as Index3, without closing and reopening the files,
                  type :
                         SET ORDER TO 3


                  The database file now acts in the order specified by Index3, the
                  third file in the list .

SET UNIQUE        There are times when you want to use a file but not include dupli-
                  cate records, or you only want to include the first record with a key
                  expression . For example, using Tours, you may want only a list of
                  tour dates .

                         USE Tours
                         INDEX ON Departure TO Udepdate UNIQUE
                         1001 indexed           25 records indexed
                         LIST Departure


                  Notice that there are 30 records in the database file, but only 25 are
                  indexed. That is because records 10, 18, 19, 20, and 27 duplicate a
                  date in a previous record .
                  An alternative way to create a unique index file is to issue SET
                  UNIQUE ON before INDEXing a file .
                  You can update UNIQUE and non-UNIQUE files at the same time,
                  however, duplicate records in a UNIQUE file are inaccessible .

REINDEX           Use the following commands to index files that were not open when
                  you altered your file contents :

                       • SET INDEX TO Index8, Index9, Index 10
                       • REINDEX

                In this SORT command /C ignores upper case and lower case dis-

                This is the same as /A, for ascending .

For Indexed    Both the FIND and SEEK commands require an indexed file . Use
               FIND to move the record pointer to a record containing a specified
Files : FIND   character string or number . Do not use FIND to search for an
and SEEK       expression or date . You must delimit the item you are looking for if
               it begins with leading spaces or any one of the delimiter characters :
                 , [, or ] .
               SEEK works only with expressions, therefore, character strings
               must be delimited.
               You also use SEEK rather than FIND in applications in which the
               user inputs a value to a memory variable . For instance, if a travel
               agent is looking for the record of a person named Michaels, the
               command file that accesses the database files may include an option
               to enter a name into a memory variable . The routine would be simi-
               lar to the following from the dot prompt .

                  • mname = 'Michaels'
                  • USE Travel INDEX Tnames
                  • SEEK mname
                  • DISPLAY Lastname
                 Record# Lastname
                      32 Michaels

               To use FIND for this example, you would have to use the & func-
               tion (macro function), which tells dBASE III PLUS to look for the
               contents of a memory variable . In the above example, you would
               replace the SEEK command with FIND &mname .

Using GOTO     You can use GOTO and SKIP to search either indexed or unindexed
               files . GOTO TOP and GOTO BOTTOM move the record pointer to
and SKIP       the first and last records in the file . In an unindexed file, the first
               and last records are the first and last records you entered . In an
               indexed file, the first and last records depend on the order of the
               index . GOTO <n> moves the record pointer to the specified
               record number .
               SKIP moves the record pointer forward or backward in a file . In an
               indexed file, SKIP follows the order of the index . In an unindexed
               file, SKIP moves through the records sequentially .




U2-32                                                           USING dBASE III PLUS
USING COMMANDS


Opening and       You must explicitly open and close many dBASE III PLUS file types .
                  These fall into two basic categories : those that make up a database
Closing Files     and can be stored in a catalog ( .cat) file, such as index and query
                  files, and those that are text-type files, such as program ( .prg) files .
                  Some file types are always used simultaneously . For instance, index
                  (.ndx) files and format ( .fmt) files require an open database ( .dbf)
                  file . Each file type has specific commands which open and close it .
                  Many files close automatically when you open another file of the
                  same type . All files close when you exit dBASE III PLUS with the
                  QUIT command . However, it is a good practice to close files your-
                  self when you are finished with them . This protects the data in case
                  of a power surge or other mishap to the computer .
                  Sometimes when you close files, you want all associated files closed
                  or memory variables released . With dBASE III PLUS commands,
                  you can close either one file at a time or several .

Number of         You can have a maximum of 15 dBASE III PLUS files open at one
                  time . This requires you to set the DOS Config.sys FILES parameter
Open Files        to 20 . DOS and dBASE III PLUS use five of the files, allowing you to
                  open 15 files while running dBASE III PLUS . (See Chapter 4 of this
                  manual for instructions on setting up and using a Config .sys file .)
                  If you get the message Too many files are open, you must close a
                  file before opening a new one . Remember that when you open a
                  view ( .vue) file, you may be opening several database ( .dbf) files and
                  possibly some index ( .ndx) files and a format ( .fmt) file as well . If in
                  doubt, use the DISPLAY STATUS command to see how many
                  database and related files are open .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                   U2-33

Using Files    A database is a collection of related files, including database ( .dbf)
               files and their associated index (.ndx), format (.fmt), and other files .
Simultaneously Because dBASE III PLUS is a database management system, it
                    allows you to use more than one file at a time .
                    You can work with up to ten database ( .dbf) files at once . Each file
                    must be stored in a separate work area numbered between 1 and
                    10 . If you open a catalog ( .cat) file, dBASE III PLUS automatically
                    puts it in work area 10 . This effectively lowers the number of possi-
                    ble open database files to nine .



                      WARNING
                      Do not move the catalog to a different work area . If you do,
                      dBASE III PLUS will not be able to locate it for updates and
                      catalog queries .



                    For each work area, dBASE III PLUS keeps track of :
                     • The database ( .dbf) filename
                     • Any open, associated index ( .ndx) files and their order
                     • File relations
                     • Any open, associated format ( .fmt) file
                     • The SET FILTER condition
                     • The record pointer position

                           command to move to another work area . When you move between

Aliases         Internally, dBASE III PLUS keeps track of a database file both by its
                filename and by its ALIAS . You can assign an ALIAS, or dBASE III
                PLUS can use the filename as an ALIAS by default . If you use an
                ALIAS name, you can SELECT a work area by its ALIAS name,
                rather than by its number. Choosing an alias name that is descrip-
                tive, or using the default filename, is easier to remember than a
                number .
                If you want to assign an ALIAS, do it when you open the file :

                  • USE Travel ALIAS Trip
                  • SELECT 2
                  • USE Clients

                  Beckman


                The alias symbol (->) is used to indicate that the field name
                belongs to the preceding ALIAS . The file must be in USE with the

                symbol is entered with two keystrokes, a hyphen (-) and a greater
                than symbol (>) .

                Often, there are fields with the same information, such as Lastname
                and Firstname in Clients .dbf and Travel .dbf.

        Having set up the index file based on Lastname + Firstname, the
        SET RELATION TO command causes the record pointer to move in
        both files, not just one . When the record pointer moves to a new
        name in the SELECTed file, Clients, it also finds the first occurrence
        of that name in the Trip file .
        To unlink files, you type SET RELATION TO +J.
        If you often correlate the same files in the same way, you can estab-
        lish the relation and store it in a file for repeated use . The file con-
        taining this information is called a view ( .vue) file which you create,
        modify, and use with these commands : CREATE VIEW FROM
        ENVIRONMENT, CREATE/MODIFY VIEW and SET VIEW TO .
        With this information stored in a view ( .vue) file, you can use the
        CREATE LABEL command to make mailing labels for all the people
        on selected trips ; summarize the data with CREATE REPORT ; or
        just LIST the names, telephone number, and departure dates for a
        particular trip .

View File
                  Another way to accomplish the same tasks is to use the CREATE
                  VIEW command . When you type CREATE VIEW < filename > at the
                  dot prompt, a menu appears from which you can select database
                  files and fields and set up a relation as if you were at the dot
                  prompt. You can also set up a filter condition and format file, and
                  then save the view .
                  Any view file created using CREATE VIEW FROM ENVIRONMENT
                  or CREATE VIEW can be modified using MODIFY VIEW .
                  To use a view file, you type SET VIEW TO < filename > at the dot

                  reappears . To deactivate a view file, open another view file, or type
                  CLOSE DATABASES to close all files in the view .

Reports and    In dBASE III PLUS, you can create reports and labels from your
               database files . The commands you use are CREATE/MODIFY
Labels         REPORT and CREATE/MODIFY LABEL . Each of these commands is
               menu-driven, using the standard menu interface for
               dBASE III PLUS .

CREATE/        With CREATE/MODIFY REPORT, you can design reports in a
               columnar layout, using selected fields from from either a database
MODIFY         ( .dbf) file or a view ( .vue) file. You can also include expressions,
REPORT         memory variables, and, if necessary, functions to convert data types .
               CREATE/MODIFY REPORT enables you to design a structure for
               the report. You do not see the actual data in a report until you print
               it out .
               There are several options for designing a page, including page titles,
               headings, and page numbers . You can divide your data into groups
               or subgroups, each with its own heading, or create a summary
               report only . Numeric fields can also be totalled .
               While you choose options to design the report, you will also see a
               diagram of your report showing the headings and column widths
               you've defined for the selected fields . This diagram can help you
               "see" what your report looks like as you design it . Finally, you can
               save the report structure in a report form ( .frm) file for future use .
               To print the report, you use the REPORT command and its options
               from the dot prompt. For more information, see the
               CREATE/MODIFY REPORT or REPORT commands in Chapter 5 of
               this manual . For a step-by-step example of creating a report, see
               Chapter 6 in Learning dBASE 111 PLUS .

          Format     ( .fmt) files consist of a series of @ commands that tell

          dBASE III PLUS where to position each of the fields and how to

          introduce     each   one . One advantage of using format files is that you

          don't have to use the field names to identify the fields . You can use

          more descriptive phrases to indicate what information to put in

          the field . For example, you can identify the Departure field with

          Departure      Date .


          Another advantage of using format ( .fmt) files is that you have more

          control over data . You can restrict what type of data is acceptable,

          such as characters only, or specify a range of dates or numbers like

          1 through 15 . To keep the data consistent, you can specify that data

          will be converted to upper case regardless of how it is entered . For

          more details on designing format ( .fmt) files, see the ~a command

          entry in Chapter 5 of this manual .


          Custom screens are also useful while working with several related

          files . Before creating the format ( .fmt) file, link the files with either

          SET    RELATION         TO   or   CREATE/MODIFY            VIEW . If you link the files

          with   CREATE/MODIFY           VIEW,   you    can   also   add    a   format        ( .fmt) file

          that contains fields from the linked files . In this case, whenever you

          SET VIEW TO < filename > , the associated format ( .fmt) file opens

          automatically .


          There are two ways to create a format ( .fmt) file :                  with      CREATE/

          MODIFY     SCREEN,    the      dBASE   III   PLUS   Screen       Painter,     or     with   a

          text   editor      such   as   MODIFY   COMMAND,      to   specify      the     @

          commands     yourself. Each is discussed in Chapter 5, "Commands ."



          When   you    type    CREATE         SCREEN   or    MODIFY       SCREEN   at        the   dot
CREATE/

          prompt, you are prompted for the screen filename, then the Screen
MODIFY
          Painter     menu   appears .
SCREEN
          If you have not already done so, your first step is to select a

          database file . Next you set up the fields to be included in the form .

          After that, you open the blackboard and start placing the fields . On

          the blackboard, you can also change the field names to make them

          more descriptive . If you are working with only one file (and not sev-

          eral related ones), you can permanently add, delete, or otherwise

          change fields in the file structure . To make menu selections, press

          F10   to   move   between      the   blackboard     and    the   menu   bar .

                  When you save the screen form, dBASE III PLUS stores the infor-
                  mation in a screen ( .scr) file and automatically creates a matching
                  format ( .fmt) file containing @ . . .SAY . . .GET statements . You can
                  modify the screen file via MODIFY SCREEN but you can't work
                  with it directly . The screen file is, in essence, only a tool for creat-
                  ing a format ( .fmt) file . Each time you alter and save the screen file,
                  the existing format ( .fmt) file is automatically updated .



                       NOTE
                       • Do not use double quotes in the field descriptions as they will
                         generate the error message Unrecognized phrase/keyword
                         in command when you use the format file.
                       • Do not ERASE the screen ( .scr) file if you want to modify the
                         format ( .fmt) file later. Once the screen file is gone, it can't be
                         re-created from the associated format file . If you ERASE the
                         screen, you can only make changes to the format file directly,
                         by changing the @ . . . SAY . . . GET command statements.
                       • Do not change the format file with MODIFY COMMAND or
                         another text editor if you intend to modify it again with
                         MODIFY SCREEN . The Screen Painter reads the screen file
                         only, which won't include the format file changes . When you
                         save the screen file, it overwrites the previous format file,
                         which eradicates any changes made to it by means other than
                         the Screen Painter .

        Catalogs keep track of which auxiliary files belong with which
        database file. You register a group of files into a catalog when the
        files have a connection with one another . For instance, suppose you
        have a set of files that relate to your accounts and another set for a
        project that includes bibliographies and research notes . All files
        relating to accounts can go in the catalog Accounts .cat and all
        research files in Research .cat.
        Then, whenever you open one of those catalogs, dBASE III PLUS
        acts as if only the files in that catalog exist . For example, when you
        issue the Catalog query clause with the command USE?, a menu of
        database ( .dbf) files in the open catalog appears .

Creating a        You create a new catalog to house a database by entering SET

Catalog           prompts you to add a title that defines the contents of the Catalog
                  by displaying Enter File title . This title can be up to 80 characters
                  long. dBASE III PLUS adds a .cat extension to the filename and
                  adds the filename to the master catalog, Catalog .cat.
                  dBASE III PLUS automatically creates Catalog .cat the first time you
                  create a catalog. Catalog .cat is stored in the default directory or
                  subdirectory. Its purpose is to help you keep track of the catalogs
                  you set up in the directory and to let you select one from a menu of
                  catalog names .



                       NOTE
                       Avoid naming your catalogs Catalog .cat since that name is
                       reserved for the master catalog .

Calculating   Using the TOTAL command, you can calculate totals from numeric
              fields in database files and store the information in a new database
Totals        file . For example, to summarize the work of the salespeople at a
              travel agency, you could create a new file as follows :

                 • USE Travel
                 • INDEX ON Agent TO Reps
                100% Indexed             49 recur s indexed
                  TOTAL ON Agent TO Cost
                •
                     49 Records (s) totalled
                      4 Records generated
                  USE Cost
                •
                • LIST Agent, Cost
                Record #    Agent         Cost
                       1   JT         24863 .00
                       2   LB          9650 .00
                       3   MM         19705 .00
                       4   RA         21808 .00


              The one-line TOTAL command :
              1 . Creates Cost .dbf with the same structure as Travel ; Cost .dbf will
                   not contain any memo fields .
              2. Examines each record to determine the agent .
              3 . Totals the cost of all trips the agent handled .
              4. Creates one record for each agent .
