ABOUT PROGRAM FILES

                  Running dBASE III PLUS from the dot prompt was discussed in
                  Chapter 2 . You can also run dBASE III PLUS by means of program
                  ( .prg) files in which the instructions you enter at the dot prompt are
                  combined. Any command or function you enter at the dot prompt
                  can be used in a program file . In fact, the command or function is
                  written exactly the same way in a program file . In addition, dBASE
                  has commands that you use only in program files and that give you
                  more control over your data.
                  This chapter tells you about the structure of a program file, and the
                  dBASE commands you need to create, alter, execute, close, and
                  debug it.
                  This chapter tells you :
                   • Why you should use program files
                       • About special commands for program files
                       • The structure of a program file
                       • How memvars are used in program files
                       • How to create, execute, close, and debug program files
                       • Some advanced features of using program files
                  This chapter does not teach you how to program or design and
                  write an applications program in dBASE ; these topics are covered
                  in Programming with dBASE III PLUS in Volume Two . If you need to
                  know the syntax or use of a specific command or function, refer to
                  Chapters 5 and 6 in this manual .

Why Do i          Using program files to run dBASE III PLUS can save you time . For
                  example, if you need to submit a report on overdue accounts every
Need              week, you could store the commands to create the report in a pro-
Program           gram file called Overacct .prg. Then when you need the report, you
Files?            only have to type DO OVERACCT at the dot prompt.
                  You can also use a program file to complete a more sophisticated
                  task like designing a menu . You can even write several program
                  files which do all your tasks, except typing in your own data . In this
                  case, the program files are usually referred to as a dBASE applica-
                  tions program .



USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                 U3-1
                                                                              CHAPTER 3


              Once you've written an applications program, you might want to
              market it. If you're interested in this, read RunTime + in Volume
              Two. This manual describes two programs, dBCODE and
              dBLINKER, which encrypt your program files and make them run
              faster.

Programming   dBASE III PLUS has commands that provide data handling methods
              similar to those in most programming languages . These commands
Commands      make programming in dBASE possible and enable program files to
              do more than store a set of commands you enter at the dot prompt .
              These commands are :
              •     DO WHILE . . . ENDDO
              •     IF . . . [ELSE] . . . ENDIF
              •     DO CASE . . . ENDCASE
               • the ON command
              These commands are described below . They have in common the
              ability to initiate a series of commands depending on the existence
              of a specified condition . Notice that the first three commands,
              unlike other dBASE commands, require an ending statement . It is
              important to remember the ending statement, since that's how
              dBASE III PLUS knows to execute the next command.



                  TIP
                  The IIF() function, a shortcut for the IF . . . [ELSE] . . . ENDIF con-
                  struction, and the ON command can also be used from the dot
                  prompt .



              DO WHILE . . . ENDDO enables you to execute a series of commands
              repeatedly as long as a specified condition is true . The program
              repeats the same commands until the condition is no longer true .




U3-2                                                              USING dBASE III PLUS
ABOUT PROGRAM FILES


                  You use IF . . . [ELSE] . . . ENDIF to specify a condition which may or
                  may not be present . dBASE III PLUS evaluates the condition and, if
                  it's present, executes the commands given . If the condition is not
                  present, dBASE III PLUS performs the commands following ELSE
                  (if included), or continues to the next command following the
                  ENDIF statement .
                  In either of these commands, you only specify one condition . How-
                  ever, in a DO WHILE construction, dBASE III PLUS checks the
                  condition repeatedly until it is false . In an IF . . . ENDIF construction,
                  dBASE III PLUS evaluates the condition only once .
                  Often, you may have several possible conditions you wish to evalu-
                  ate. DO CASE . . . ENDCASE allows you to list the different conditions
                  and what to do with each one .
                  For more complex processing, you may use any of the mathemati-
                  cal, relational, logical, and string operators to combine expressions
                  within a condition . (See Chapter 2 for a discussion of operators .)
                  You can also put any of the three commands within another, which
                  is called nesting . When nesting, the statements must fit entirely
                  within one another . If, for example, you nested an IF . . .ENDIF state-
                  ment within a DO WHILE construction, both the IF and its accom-
                  panying ENDIF must be contained between the DO WHILE and the
                  ENDO . Do not nest the commands too deeply, since that will make
                  it more difficult for you to document and keep track of the work
                  being done .
                  Normally, commands in a program file are executed line-by-line
                  in the order written . D O WHILE . . . ENDDO, IF . . . ENDIF, DO
                  CASE . . . ENDCASE also allow you to branch to another program file
                  and run it without returning to the dot prompt . The program file you
                  are branching from is the calling program ; the program file you are
                  branching to is the subprogram .
                  To execute a subprogram, you specify DO < program filename > ,
                  usually after a condition . When the condition exists, control is
                  transferred from the calling program to the subprogram . The sub-
                  program instructions are executed before returning control to the
                  calling program, where the remaining instructions are processed . It
                  is a good practice to include RETURN as the last command in a
                  subprogram .



USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                    U3-3
                                                                           CHAPTER 3


                 The ON command permits branching to a subprogram when a
                 dBASE III PLUS error occurs, or the Esc key or another key is
                 pressed . The command has three forms which test for these condi-
                 tions: ON ERROR, ON ESCAPE, and ON KEY . A sample use is
                 ON ERROR DO < program filename > . The ON command is
                 normally placed in the setup area of a program file (the setup area
                 is explained below) and stays active until a new ON command is
                 issued.
                 While learning these four commands is important, since they make
                 programming in dBASE possible, program design is equally impor-
                 tant. Good program design requires both practice and patience .
                 How one designs a program varies widely depending on the pro-
                 grammer and the application . For more information on using
                 these commands and program design, read Programming with
                 dBASE III PLUS .

Structure of a   In dBASE III PLUS a program file has four basic parts (also see
                 Chapter 2 in Programming with dBASE III PLUS) :
Program File
                  • A preamble
                  • A setup area
                  • The body of the program
                  • A closing section
                 The preamble includes the program filename, a description of what
                 it does, who wrote it, and dates indicating when it was started or
                 last edited. Each line with this information must be preceded by the
                 command NOTE or an asterisk (*), and followed by a i-1. Using
                 NOTE or the asterisk tells dBASE III PLUS to ignore the informa-
                 tion because it is not a dBASE command or program instruction .
                 This feature is especially useful when you have several program files
                 to keep track of, you are writing an applications program, or some-
                 one else needs to know how your program file works .




U3-4                                                            USING dBASE III PLUS
ABOUT PROGRAM FILES


                  The setup area contains commands which design the operating
                  environment for the program file . There are some aspects of the
                  dBASE III PLUS environment that you must change for a program
                  file ; these are established by the SET command and its options . For
                  example, you should use SET TALK OFF to turn off the interactive
                  mode, which is the default method for running dBASE III PLUS
                  from the dot prompt . That way, the response to certain dBASE com-
                  mands will not interfere with the program flow . If you are writing
                  an applications program, then you may want to program the func-
                  tion keys, SET ESCAPE OFF so your users cannot press Esc to stop
                  the processing of your program, or use SET COLOR TO for special
                  effects on the screen .
                  The body of the program file contains the commands which do the
                  work of the program . In this section, you open files, select work
                  areas, change or display database information, perform calculations,
                  produce reports and so on - using the same commands you would
                  enter at the dot prompt . See the Classes of Commands section in
                  Chapter 5 for an overview and brief description of all the dBASE
                  commands .
                  Also in this section are the dBASE commands used specifically for
                  program files, which give you more control over data . These com-
                  mands are summarized in the Programming Commands section
                  above, and discussed thoroughly in Programming with
                  dBASE III PLUS .
                  You should also document the tasks accomplished in the program .
                  You may add comments on separate lines, beginning each line with
                  NOTE or an asterisk (*) as described . You may also put a comment
                  on the same line as a command by preceding the comment with
                  two ampersands (&&) .
                  The closing section contains commands which tidy up the work
                  space used by your program file . For example, you would return the
                  environment to its default setup, remove memory variables, close
                  all files, and return to the dot prompt . (See Chapter 13 in Program-
                  ming with dBASE III PLUS .)




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                               U3-5
                                                                           CHAPTER 3


Memvars and     You can use any type of memory variable (character, numeric, date,
                or logical) in a program file . They are usually initialized with
Program Files   STORE < value > TO < memvar name > or < memvar name >
                 _ < value > ; however, you can also use the ACCEPT, AVERAGE,
                COUNT, PARAMETERS, INPUT, SUM, and WAIT commands to ini-
                tialize memory variables . You use memory variables to store (in
                memory) a value to be processed or evaluated in the program file .
                You can have up to 256 active memory variables with a combined
                size of up to 6,000 bytes . If your computer has more than 256K, you
                can increase the 6,000-byte capacity by setting the MVARSIZ option
                in Config .db . The contents of memory variables are only stored
                temporarily until you change them, release them, or QUIT
                dBASE III PLUS . However, you can SAVE memory variables to a
                memory (.mem) file, then RESTORE them later .
                Memory variables initialized or RESTOREd at the dot prompt
                always have a public status . Their values are available to any opera-
                tions you perform at the dot prompt, including the execution of a
                program file . However, memory variables initialized or RESTOREd
                within a program file have a private status by default . Their values
                are only accessible within the program file and to any subprograms .
                You can change or hide the status of a variable via the PUBLIC and
                PRIVATE commands .
                Memory variables are normally released in the closing section of a
                program file .

Functions and   You use functions in program files the same way you use them from
                the dot prompt (see the Using Functions section in Chapter 2) .
Program Files   Although all dBASE III PLUS functions can be used in program
                files, two particularly useful functions for program files are
                INKEY() and READKEY(), which evaluate data input . The INKEY()
                function allows you to execute certain commands or branch to
                another program when a certain key is pressed . For example, you
                could use INKEY() to indicate that when the letter E is pressed, the
                program branches to an Edit .prg subprogram .

Debugging               Mistakes are often made when creating or writing a program file .
                        You might have syntax errors such as a forgotten comma, space, or
Program Files           quotation mark, or misspelled commands and memvar names . The
                        expressions in the program may have mismatched data types . You
                        can also have run time errors which are not found until you actu-
                        ally run the program . Most run time errors are mistakes in logic .
                        You may think your instructions are correct, but the program does
                        not do what you expect .
                        There are several dBASE commands that enable you to test and
                        debug your program files . They are RESUME, SET DEBUG, SET
                        DOHISTORY, SET ECHO, SET HISTORY TO, SET STEP, and SUS-
                        PEND . The commands you use depend on how you like to work .
                        One popular method is to use SET STEP ON, SET ECHO ON, and
                        SET DEBUG ON . With SET STEP ON, program files are executed
                        one instruction at a time . Program execution is stopped after each
                        command and you receive a prompt to continue, suspend or cancel
                        execution . SET ECHO ON displays the program instructions on
                        your screen . SET DEBUG ON prints the output from SET ECHO .
                        Note that if you also SET TALK ON, you can see the results of some
                        of the commands you entered (such as STORE or SUM) .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                              U3-9
                                                                      CHAPTER 3


            Another method is to SET DOHISTORY ON to store the commands
            that were executed from your program file . The commands are
            stored in the history buffer . Only the last 20 executed commands
            are stored, unless you increase the size of the buffer with
            SET HISTORY TO .
            If dBASE III PLUS finds an error, it stops executing the program,
            displays an error message, and asks you if you wish to ignore the
            error or cancel or suspend the program . With this method,
            press S to suspend the program and display the dot prompt . Next
            you type DISPLAY HISTORY to find and edit the incorrect instruc-
            tion . Then you resume program execution by typing RESUME .
            Editing an instruction in the history buffer does not automatically
            update the program file . You must keep track of the changes you
            make and edit the program file yourself later .
            For a full discussion of debugging methods, read Chapter 15 in
            Programming with dBASE III PLUS . For more details on a specific
            debugging command, go to Chapter 5 in this manual .

Some        This section describes some programming techniques to make your
            program files more efficient .
Advanced
Features

Procedure   The program file you will probably create most often with
            MODIFY COMMAND is also called a command file . Command
Files       files do the bulk of the work in a program or an application .
            dBASE III PLUS has another type of program file called a
            procedure file . A procedure file contains utility programs (also
            known as procedures) that perform simple tasks you do very often
            in dBASE III PLUS . For example, if you need to print a lot of docu-
            ments and like to use different fonts, you could create procedures
            which send the different fonts to the printer .
            Unlike command files, a procedure file is stored in memory (if you
            have sufficient memory to store it) . This means that
            dBASE III PLUS does not need to access the disk drive to run pro-
            cedures as often . Instead, they are executed much more quickly
            from memory.




U3-10                                                      USING dBASE III PLUS
ABOUT PROGRAM FILES

                  Like command files, you create procedure files by entering
                  MODIFY COMMAND < filename > at the dot prompt . A procedure
                  file is also assigned a .prg extension, unless you assign a different
                  one
                  You can have up to 32 procedures in the procedure file . Each pro-
                  cedure must begin with PROCEDURE < procedure name > and as
                  a good programming practice, it should end with a RETURN state-
                  ment.
                  To execute a procedure file, you specify SET PROCEDURE TO
                   < filename > at the beginning of a command file to store the pro-
                  cedure file in memory . When you need a procedure in the file, you
                  use DO < procedure name > to run it . dBASE III PLUS branches
                  to the procedure and executes it . The RETURN statement at the end
                  of the procedure returns control to the calling command file or to
                  the dot prompt .
                  You close a procedure file by specifying CLOSE PROCEDURE or
                  SET PROCEDURE TO in the closing section of the calling command
                  file . Because you can only have one procedure file in memory,
                  SET PROCEDURE TO < filename > automatically closes the cur-
                  rent one and loads the named file into memory . Note that a proce-
                  dure file stays open until specifically closed, even after the calling
                  program has been executed .

Other             Another feature of program files is the ability to hide PUBLIC vari-
                  ables . For example, if you have a PUBLIC variable called Mprice
Features          with a value of 100, you can go to a subprogram, create a new
                  PRIVATE variable with the same name, and give it a different value .
                  dBASE III PLUS uses the new value only while running the subpro-
                  gram and its branching files . When dBASE III PLUS returns to the
                  controlling program, Mprice is reinstated as a PUBLIC variable with
                  a value of 100 .
                  Another advantage is that you can branch to binary ( .bin) files .
                  These are written in assembly language and give you more control
                  over the hardware of your computer, for example, aspects which
                  control cursor movement . LOAD stores a binary file in memory,
                  where it can be executed via the CALL command .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                               U3-11
                                                                   CHAPTER 3


        For details on procedure files, binary files, hiding PUBLIC variables,
        and techniques for creating more efficient program files, read
        Chapter 16 in Programming with dBASE III PLUS .

Chapter 4
dBASE III PLUS CONFIGURATION

                  dBASE III PLUS can be customized with two configuration files :
                  Config.sys and Config .db. These files contain commands that per-
                  form special functions and enhance your use of dBASE III PLUS .
                  When you receive your dBASE III PLUS package, the Config .sys and
                  Config.db files are included on System Disk #1 and are ready for
                  you to use . This chapter explains why these files are important and
                  how you can modify them to tailor dBASE III PLUS to meet your
                  needs.

Config.sys        Config .sys is a DOS file that may contain five DOS configuration
                  commands : BREAK, BUFFERS, DEVICE, FILES, and SHELL .
                  Only the BUFFERS and FILES commands are needed to run
                  dBASE III PLUS properly. Without them, dBASE III PLUS could not
                  perform some of its data handling tasks : opening several files at one
                  time, setting relations between database files, using view files or cat-
                  alogs . . . In short, you would not have the power and data handling
                  capabilities dBASE III PLUS gives you .
                  FILES refers to the number of files that can be open at any time .
                  BUFFERS designates the number of buffers allocated in memory to
                  read/write information to/from a disk .
                  The remaining commands are not needed for dBASE III PLUS,
                  however, if you have other software that require these commands,
                  their presence in Config .sys will not affect the performance of
                  dBASE III PLUS .
                  The Config .sys file on System Disk # 1 contains the following
                  information :
                  FILES = 20
                  BUFFERS = 15
                  You can have up to 15 dBASE III PLUS files open ; the remaining
                  files are reserved for DOS and dBASE III PLUS system files.
                  dBASE III PLUS uses 15 disk buffers . This value depends on the
                  amount of memory in your computer. For example, 256K comput-
                  ers can only have 4 disk buffers allocated to dBASE III PLUS .
                  The information in Config .sys is accessed by your computer when
                  you start it up . Therefore, Config .sys must reside in the disk or
                  directory from which your computer boots .



USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                  U4-1
                                                                              CHAPTER 4


Creating and   Config .sys is a standard ASCII text file that you create or modify
               with any word processor or line editor (such as EDLIN in DOS) .
Modifying      You can also use MODIFY COMMAND in dBASE III PLUS .
Config .sys
               Using MODIFY COMMAND, you would enter MODIFY COMMAND
               Config .sys at the dot prompt . The filename and menu of text editing
               commands appear at the top of the screen . Type the configuration
               commands and their values . Each command in the file must be on
               a separate line, as shown in the preceding section, and followed by
               a ~. To save the file, press Ctrl-W .
               Store Config .sys in the disk or directory from which your system
               boots . If you start your computer with a floppy disk, put Config .sys
               on this disk . If you boot from a hard disk, put Config .sys in the root
               directory.
               The information in Config .sys is accessed by your computer when
               you start it up . So, after creating the file for the first time, and each
               time you change the file, you must always reboot your computer to
               use the new values .



                 TIP
                 You can make System Disk # 1 a boot disk to start your com-
                 puter. See Getting Started for instructions .

               your workspace in dBASE III PLUS . The dBASE configuration com-
               mands are : BUCKET, COMMAND, GETS, MVARSIZ, PROMPT,
               TEDIT, and WP . The Config .db file can also contain new values for
               most of the SET commands and the function keys .
               When you receive dBASE III PLUS, all of these commands have
               default or preset values . You reset them by entering the commands
               and their new values in Config .db . For example, the Config .db file
               on System Disk # 1 contains values for two commands :
               STATUS = ON
               COMMAND = ASSIST

PROMPT
The PROMPT setting allows you to replace the dot prompt with a
string up to 19 characters long . You may use any character that you
can display on your screen, including graphics characters . Avoid
using characters which send commands to your printer .
TEDIT and WP
To use a word processor other than the dBASE III PLUS text editor
for either TEDIT or WP, you must have enough extra memory to
load the Command .com file and the word processor(s) . The word
processor specified with TEDIT is used with MODIFY COMMAND ;
the word processor specified with WP is used to enter memo fields .
By specifying another word processor for WP, you can have memo
fields larger than the default maximum of 5,000 bytes . The word
processor(s) should reside in the same directory as
dBASE III PLUS . Command .com can be in a separate directory, but
you must specify a path to find it using DOS SET COMSPEC . For
example, you would enter SET COMSPEC = C :\Command .com at
the DOS prompt.

You can include values for most of the SET commands in
Config .db. The SET commands control the dBASE III PLUS envi-
ronment . For example, you can SET BELL OFF so you don't hear
the beep . If you have a color monitor, you can use SET COLOR to
specify colors for your screen display . You can define specific
drives or directories using SET PATH TO . If dBASE III PLUS cannot
find a file in the current directory, it searches the designated drives
or directories .
Table 4-2 shows which SET commands you can implement in
Config .db . Chapter 5 describes them briefly in the Classes of Com-
mands section under Parameter Controls . For more information on
the default value, purpose, and use of a SET command, go to the
reference section, also in Chapter 5 .

COMMANDS


Symbols and        Symbols are used in a specific way throughout Chapter 5 as part of
                   the syntax of commands . Most of these symbols reflect common
Conventions        standards used with other programming languages . The symbols
                   used and their meaning are listed below :
   Symbol                       Use
   < >                          Angle brackets indicate that you must enter the
                                enclosed item . When you enter the requested item,
                                do not type the angle brackets .
   [   ]                        Square brackets indicate that the enclosed item is an
                                optional part of the syntax . If you enter the enclosed
                                item, do not type the brackets.
   /                            The slash indicates that there is more than one way
                                to use the command . The different options are
                                shown separated by a / . When you use a command,
                                you enter only one of the options .
   ?                            When you type a command followed by?, a
                                pull-down menu appears containing a list of appro-
                                priate files from which you can chose .This iscalled
                                the catalog query, and can only be used when a cata-
                                log is open .
   < expC >                     These notations are used to represent expressions of
   < expN >                     different types (character, numeric, or date), or a
   < expD >                     logical condition . When you enter the expression, do
   < condition >                not type the angle brackets.
   [ . . .]                     The ellipsis . . . indicates you may specify one or
                                more elements of the type listed. For example, when
                                multiple expressions can be entered, they may be
                                shown as [ < exp > , . . .] .
   ?,*                          These symbols are used to indicate wildcard charac-
                                ters which have the same meaning as they have in
                                DOS. A ? character in a filename or extension indi-
                                cates any valid character will match . A * character
                                indicates any acceptable number of valid characters
                                will match .
   &&                           Used to indicate a program code comment .

Limitations      The following limitations apply to using the commands in this
                 chapter :
       Item                   Limitations

   filenames                  Filenames may be up to eight characters long. They
                              must begin with a letter and cannot contain embed-
                              ded blank spaces. Letters, numbers, and underscore
                              characters are permitted .
   file                       You can specify a file extension of up to three char-
   extensions                 acters . Letters and numbers are permitted . You can
                              specify file extensions of your own choosing, or
                               BASE III PLUS will provide default file extensions
                              according to the file type used .
   field names                Field names may be up to ten characters long. They
                              must begin with a letter and cannot contain embed-
                              ded blank spaces. Letters, numbers, and underscore
                              characters are permitted.
   expression                 A valid expression may contain fields, variables,
                              functions, constants, and operators . Expressions may
                              be used in commands and functions, or used to
                              specify an index key expression . An index key
                              expression can be up to 220 characters long and
                              must evaluate to a single data type: character,
                              numeric, or date .
   index key                  When an index key expression is evaluated, it pro-
                              duces a result called the index key . The maximum
                              length of an index key is 100 charcters .

Classes of Commands
dBASE III PLUS commands can be categorized by the functions they perform . The com-
mands in each category are listed below .

User Assistance
The following commands give on-line information :
  ASSIST                       Menu-driven Assistant ; aids execution of dBASE III
                               PLUS commands .
  DIR                          Shows files present on the designated disk drive or
                               directory .
  DISPLAY MEMORY               Displays information about current memory variables .
  DISPLAY STATUS               Displays information about the files currently in USE
                               and system parameters .
  DISPLAY STRUCTURE            Displays structure of a database file in USE .
  HELP                         Menu-driven ; explains dBASE III PLUS commands
                               and provides other information .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                             U5-3
                                                                               CHAPTER 5


Creation of Files
The following commands create database and other associated files :
  COPY                          Copies database file in USE to a new file .
  COPY FILE                     Duplicates any closed file .
  CREATE                        Creates a new database file .
  IMPORT                        Creates database and format files from pfs :File forms
                                and creates a view file which includes both the
                                database file and the format file .
  INDEX                         Creates an index file .
  JOIN                          Combines specified records and fields from two
                                database files .
  CREATE LABEL                  Creates a label form file .
  CREATE QUERY                  Creates a query file .
  CREATE REPORT                 Creates a report form file .
  CREATE SCREEN                 Creates a screen file, a format file, and optionally a
                                database file .
  CREATE VIEW                   Creates a view file .
  EXPORT                        Creates pfs :File forms from a dBASE III PLUS
                                database file, using a dBASE III PLUS format file if
                                one is open .
  MODIFY COMMAND                dBASE III PLUS word processor; creates or modifies
                                a command, format, procedure, or text file .
  MODIFY STRUCTURE              Modifies a database file structure ; creates a backup of
                                the original database file .
  SAVE                          Copies current memory variables to a memory file .
  SET CATALOG TO                Creates a new catalog or selects an existing catalog.
  SORT                          Creates a sorted version of the current database file in
                                use
  TOTAL                         Sums numeric fields of the current database file,
                                creating a new database file with the resulting value
                                totals .
Addition of Data
The following commands allow the addition of new data records to databases :
  APPEND                        Allows addition of data at the end of a database file .
  BROWSE                        Allows addition of data at the end of a database file .
  INSERT                        Allows insertion of data in a database file .

COMMANDS

Editing of Data
The following commands allow editing of the data within a database :
  BROWSE                        Allows editing of data within a full-screen window dis-
                                play .
  CHANGE                        Allows editing of specified fields and records in
                                database files .
  EDIT                          Allows editing of specified fields and records in
                                database files (same as CHANGE) .
  READ                          Permits entry to fields or variables in a GET
                                command .
  REPLACE                       Replaces data fields with specified values .
  UPDATE                        Allows batch updates of a database file .


Deletion of Data
The following commands control deletion of data .
  DELETE                        Marks records for deletion .
  PACK                          Removes records marked for deletion .
  RECALL                        Unmarks records marked for deletion .
  ZAP                           Removes all records from the active database file .

Data Display
The following commands display selected data from database files .
   @ . . .SAY. . .GET           Displays user-formatted data on the screen or printer .
                                Displays an expression list .
   AVERAGE*                     Computes and displays the arithmetic mean of one or
                                more field expressions for the database records speci-
                                fied.
   BROWSE                       Displays up to 17 records per screen with as many
                                fields as will fit on the screen .
   COUNT*                       Counts and displays the number of records matching
                                a specified criteria .
   DISPLAY                      Displays records and fields in table form .
   LABEL                        Displays record data in label form .
   LIST                         Lists records and fields in table form .
   REPORT                       Displays data in report form .
   SUM*                         Computes and displays the sum of selected numeric
                                fields .
   * These commands do not display results if SET TALK is OFF .

Positioning the Record Pointer
The following commands position the record pointer within database files .
   CONTINUE                      Positions the record pointer to the next record meet-
                                 ing conditions specified by the LOCATE command .
   FIND                          Positions the record pointer to the record matching
                                 the specified character string or numeric value .
   GO/GOTO                       Positions the record pointer to a specific record,
                                 regardless of the record pointer's current position .
   LOCATE                        Positions the record pointer to a record matching a
                                 specified condition .
   SEEK                          Positions the record pointer to a record matching a
                                 specified expression .
   SKIP                          Positions the record pointer forward or backward a
                                 specified number of records relative to the current
                                 record pointer position .

Manipulating Database Files
The following commands affect entire database files :
  APPEND FROM                    Adds records from other files to the dBASE III PLUS
                                 file currently selected .
  CLOSE                          Closes all files of a specified type .
  COPY                           Copies the currently selected database file to another

                                                                                          . .

                  ?/?? evaluates and displays the value of dBASE III PLUS expression
                  lists . ?/?? roughly translates to : "What is . . . ?" or "What is the value
                  of . . .?"

Syntax :          ?/?? < expression list >

Usage             The single question mark issues a carriage return and line feed
                  before the expression list is displayed . The double question mark
                  does not. When used in a program, ?? displays the expression list
                  beginning with the current cursor or printer position . In the inter-
                  active mode (at the dot prompt), this overwrites the command on
                  the screen .

Tips              ? without a following expression displays a blank line and can be
                  used to skip a line in the output . ?/?? may be used with SET PRINT
                  ON and the CHR() function to send escape code sequences to your
                  printer, for example, to set bold or italic printing modes .

Examples          The Clients database file on the Sample Programs and Utilities disk
                  is used to illustrate the command . To display the contents of the
                  Lastname and City fields from the current record :

                       • USE Clients
                       • ? Lastname,City
                       Buckman               Oxnard


                  To determine if the current record belongs to Butler :

                       • ? Lastname = 'Butler'
                       • F.

                  dBASE III PLUS returns .F. for false, .T. for true .
                  To display the results of a calculation :

                         ? 2 * 4 + (9/3)
                       • 11 .00

                  To display the system date :

                       • ? DATE()
                       05/15/84

            is used to create custom forms for data input and output . It dis-
         plays information in a specified format at a given set of
         coordinates .

Syntax   @ < row, col > [[SAY < exp > [PICTURE < clause > ]]
         [GET < variable > [PICTURE < clause > ]
         [RANGE < low > , < high > ]]]/[CLEAR]

Usage    Row and col are numeric expressions . For a 24x80 terminal, the
         row coordinate can range from 0 to 23 and the column coordinate
         from 0 to 79 .
         With SET STATUS ON, line 22 is reserved for the status line . If you
         SET STATUS OFF and do not SET SCOREBOARD OFF, line 0 is
         used for status information display . To free these lines for other use,
         you must SET STATUS OFF and SET SCOREBOARD OFF.
         You can use SET DEVICE TO PRINT to route              . . . SAY commands
         to the printer . @ . . . GETS are not routed to the printer . Most print-
         ers have limitations on the row and column coordinates . When
         sending @ commands to a printer, decreasing the row number in
         consecutive @ commands causes a page eject . Similarly, if two
         commands have the same row coordinate, the second one must
         have a larger column coordinate .
         The @ . . . SAY command displays information that you do not want
         to change . The value of any valid dBASE III PLUS expression except
         memo fields can be displayed .
         The . . . GET command displays and allows editing of information
         from existing memory variables and fields . The READ command
         activates a full-screen editing mode which allows editing of GET
         fields.
         Besides using @ . . . SAY . . . GETS with the READ command, you can
         create a format ( .fmt) file containing @ . . . SAY . . . GETS . You can use
         a format file with the APPEND, EDIT, and READ commands . If you
         create a format file, you can also specify memo fields with the GET
         command .




U5-16                                                        USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS

                  @ row,col CLEAR erases the screen below and to the right of the
                  coordinates.
                  @a row,col erases a line beginning at the column position specified .

Options           The RANGE option is used with numeric and date variables to spec-
                  ify lower and upper bounds . < low > and < high > are expressions
                  which define the minimum and maximum values that may be
                  entered in response to the GET .
                  Since there is no literal representation for dates, you must use the
                  CTOD() function to use constant dates in a RANGE . For example,
                  RANGE CTOD('01 /01 /85'), CTOD(' 12/31 /85') excludes all dates
                  with a year other than 1985 . Enter one expression if you want to
                  specify only a lower or upper limit . You must include the comma
                  (,) as in RANGE ,30 or RANGE 10, . If an invalid number or
                  date is then entered, dBASE III PLUS prompts for a new value until
                  a valid number or date is entered .
                  If you specify a RANGE and press +1 in response to a GET, no range
                  checking is done . Therefore, if a field or variable is set to a value
                  outside the specified range, pressing      leaves the value unchanged .
                  The PICTURE option allows formatted output capability and
                  restricts the type of data that may be entered into a variable . The
                  clause may consist of a function and/or a template, and must be
                  delimited.

Functions         If a PICTURE function is used, the @ symbol must appear as the
                  first character in the clause . If a function is used in conjunction
                  with a template, a space must separate the two .

                                                                 CHAPTER 5


        dBASE III PLUS provides the following functions :
         Symbol       Description
         C           Displays CR (credit) after a positive number .
         X           Displays DB (debit) after a negative number .
         (           Encloses negative numbers in parentheses .
         B           Leftjustifies numeric data.
         Z           Displays zero numeric value as a blank string .
         D           American date format .
         E           European date format.
         A           Alphabetic characters only.
                     Allows any character and converts letters to
                     upper case.
         R           Literal characters displayed in the template, but not
                     entered in the field .
         S <n>       Limits field width display to <n> characters and
                     horizontally scrolls the characters within it in <n>
                     columns . <n> must be a literal positive
                     integer.

        Some functions are restricted according to the data types to which
        they apply. The functions C, X, (' B, and Z can be used with
        numeric data only . Furthermore, C, X, and ( can only be used with
        the SAY clause. D and E apply to date, character, and numeric data .
        A, !, R, and S are only relevant to character data .
        New functions may be defined by logically combining the functions
        in the table . For example, the function XC displays DB after nega-
        tive numbers and CR after positive numbers . However, some func-
        tions cannot be used together, such as D and E or X and ( .
        S <n> is used to display and edit a character GET variable in a
        number of columns that is less than the actual length of the charac-
        ter string . The number of columns is defined by a literal integer
         <n>, and no spaces are allowed between the 'S' and the
        integer .




U5-18                                                 USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS

                  The string scrolls within the specified width, allowing you to view
                  and edit the entire character string . Use ->, F-, Ctrl-F, and Ctrl-A to
                  bring hidden characters into view . When entering data, the string
                  scrolls automatically .

Templates         A template is formed by using a single symbol for each character to
                  be displayed or input . Any character may be used, but characters
                  other than the template symbols have no special meaning .
                  If the R picture function is used with a template containing charac-
                  ters other than template symbols, those characters are inserted into
                  the display and not stored as part of the GET variable . If R is not
                  used, those characters are displayed rather than the corresponding
                  string character and are stored in the GET variable . R applies only
                  to character type variables . For numeric variables, non-template
                  symbols are always inserted into the display and never stored as
                  part of the number . Avoid using non-template symbols for date and
                  logical variables .
                  dBASE III PLUS provides the following template symbols :

                       Symbol    Description
                       9        Allows only digits for character data . Allows digits
                                and signs for numeric data .
                   #            Allows only digits, blanks, and signs.
                   A            Allows only letters .
                   L            Allows only logical data .
                   Y            Allows only logical Y, y, N, n . Converts y and n to
                                upper case letters .
                       N        Allows letters and digits .
                       X        Allows any character.
                                Converts letters to upper case and has no affect on
                                other characters .
                       $        Displays dollar signs in place of leading zeroes .
                       *        Displays asterisks in place of leading zeroes .
                                Specifies decimal position .
                                Displays if there are digits to left of the comma .

COMMANDS                                                                        ACCEPT

ACCEPT            ACCEPT is used primarily in command files to prompt a user for
                  keyboard entry. It creates a character memory variable in which it
                  stores the keyboard entry . Terminate data entry with ~,

Syntax            ACCEPT [ < prompt > ] TO < memvar >

Usage             The prompt may be a character type memory variable or a charac-
                  ter string . If a character string, it must be delimited by `single
                  quotes', "double quotes", or [brackets] .
                  The keyboard entry does not require delimiters : ACCEPT treats all
                  user input as character-type data .
                  If    is entered in response to the ACCEPT command, the content
                  of the memory variable is null (without any contents, or ASCII 0) .
                  A maximum of 254 characters can be entered into a variable with
                  ACCEPT .

Example           To prompt the user to "Enter your social security number :" and
                  store the keyboard entry in the Ssno memory variable :

                         ACCEPT "Enter your social security number :" TO Ssno
                       Enter your social security number :



See Also          INPUT, WAIT




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                               U5-25
APPEND                                                                 CHAPTER 5


APPEND    APPEND allows you to add new records to the end of the active
          database file. It is the primary command for full-screen data entry .

Syntax    APPEND [BLANK]

Usage     APPEND places you in the full-screen data entry mode . One new
          record at a time is presented as a screen "form" for data entry .
          Terminate the process by pressing       when a new record is
          presented, or by pressing Ctrl-End . If you move to a new record and
          press Ctrl-End, a blank record is added to the file .
          The PgUp key moves the cursor to previous records, enabling you
          to edit them . They will be in record order, not indexed order . The
          PgDn key moves forward through the records, and returns to the
          APPEND mode after the last record is indexed .
          To enter data into a memo field, press Ctrl-PgDn when the cursor is
          positioned at the beginning of the field . A blank screen appears and
          text can be entered . The control keys are the same as for MODIFY
          COMMAND . A cursor control menu can also be toggled on and off
          with F1 . To exit a memo field, press Ctrl-End (or Ctrl-W) to save
          your entry in the memo field or press Esc to abandon the entry .
          APPEND allows you to add records to a single database file only .
          Using a format file, it is possible to do @ . . .GETS for fields from sev-
          eral related files . Using APPEND with a format file like this does not
          add records to unselected files .

Options   The BLANK option adds a blank record to the end of the database
          file, but the full-screen mode is not entered. The BLANK record
          becomes the current record .

Tips      If index files are active during APPEND, any new record will be
          added to the index file in the appropriate location .
          The directory entry for the active database file may not reflect all
          new records until the file is closed .

APPEND FROM                                                               CHAPTER 5


APPEND     APPEND FROM copies records from an existing file to the end of
           the active database file . The FROM file does not have to be a
FROM       dBASE III PLUS file .

Syntax     APPEND FROM < filename/? > [FOR < condition > ]
           [[TYPE] < file type > ]

Defaults   The filename must include the drive designator if the file is not on
           the default drive unless a path is set to that drive.
           If a file extension is not entered as part of the filename, and the file
           type is not specified, dBASE III PLUS assumes the .dbf
           extension .
           If a file extension is not entered as part of the filename and the SDF
           or DELIMITED option is specified, dBASE III PLUS assumes a .txt
           extension . Other file types are assumed to have the default exten-
           sions supplied by their respective software packages .

Usage      If the FROM file is a dBASE III PLUS database ( .dbf) file :
            • Records marked for deletion are appended and are not marked
              for deletion in the active database if SET DELETED is OFF . If
              SET DELETED is ON, only records not marked for deletion are
              appended .
            • Only field names found in both files are appended. They do not
              have to be in the same order .
            • Do not specify a file type .
           If a field in the FROM file is larger than the same field in the active
           database, excess character data is lost, and excess numeric data is
           replaced by asterisks .
           The FOR expression refers only to field names that are common to
           both files .




U5-28                                                       USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                        APPEND FROM

Options           The options for < file type > are :
                   • DELIMITED [WITH BLANK/ < delimiter > ]              Delimited For-
                      mat ASCII file . Data is appended character by character starting
                      on the left. Each record must end with a carriage return and
                      line feed . A comma separates each field and, in addition, double
                      quotation marks surround character data unless you specify
                      another delimiter. This is the same as DELIMITED WITH" .
                      DELIMITED WITH BLANK works with files containing fields
                      separated by one space .
                      DELIMITED WITH < delimiter > works with files containing
                      fields separated by commas and character strings also enclosed
                      in specified delimiters . The default delimiter is the double quote
                      character.
                   • SDF - System Data Format ASCII file . Data is appended char-
                     acter by character starting on the left . Each record is the same
                     length and ends with a carriage return and line feed .
                   • DIF - VisiCalc file format . The VisiCalc rows convert to
                     records, and the columns convert to fields .
                   • SYLK - Multiplan spreadsheet format in row major order. The
                     Multiplan rows convert to records, and the columns convert to
                     fields . dBASE III PLUS will not APPEND FROM a SYLK file
                     saved in column major order.
                   • WKS - Lotus 1-2-3 spreadsheet format, release 1A . The Lotus
                     1-2-3 rows convert to records, and the columns convert to
                     fields . The file begins with the cell in the upper left-hand corner
                     of the spreadsheet . This is usually cell Al unless you have
                     renamed it .
                  Blank rows in any spreadsheet type are converted to blank records
                  in the database file.




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-29
APPEND     FROM                                                             CHAPTER 5


                When using APPEND FROM to read any of the three supported
                spreadsheet formats, keep in mind that this command expects the
                incoming data in a format that matches the database file structure .
                This means that the spreadsheet should be stored in row major (as
                opposed to column major) order, and that column headers should
                be removed before attempting to read the data into
                dBASE III PLUS . However, APPEND FROM will store row names as
                long as the database file structure is designed with them in mind .
                WKS files should not have leading blank rows or columns . With this
                type of file, you should justify data in the upper left-hand corner
                before using APPEND FROM .

Tips            If you are APPENDing FROM a file for which dBASE III PLUS
                assumes a particular extension and your file does not have an exten-
                sion, include a period after the filename .

Special Cases   Use the IMPORT command to convert pfs :File formats to
                dBASE III PLUS format.
                dBASE III PLUS date fields can APPEND FROM character data in
                date format . Conversely, character fields in the proper format and
                size can be APPENDed FROM date fields . From text files, dates can
                only be APPENDed FROM in the form YYYYMMDD, not delimited
                (where YYYY is the year, MM is the month, and DD is the day) .

Examples        You can append records from the Travel database file to the end of
                the Clients database file . (Use a copy of the Clients database file so
                you can keep the original file intact to use with other examples .)

                  • USE Clients
                    APPEND FROM Travel
                  •
                       49 records added

                To see the number of records now in the Clients database file, type

                  • ? RECCOUNT()
                          98

THE         The Assistant is a full-screen, menu-driven command that prompts
            you through many dBASE III PLUS commands .
ASSISTANT
Syntax      ASSIST

Usage       The Assistant helps you create new database ( .dbf) files and ancil-
            lary files : index ( .ndx), format (.fmt), label ( .lbl), query ( .qry), report
            (.frm), and view ( .vue) files . It also allows you to modify these files
            and perform basic editing, search, and display operations .
            Whenever you need help on how to use dBASE III PLUS while in
            The Assistant, press F1 for more information on any active main
            menu option . Press any key to erase the information from the
            screen and continue .
            Each menu option activates a specific dBASE III PLUS command .
            For more information on a specific command, see the individual
            entry in the alphabetical listing of commands .
            As you choose options from The Assistant, the actual command as
            you would type it from the dot prompt is built on the action line . In
            this way, you can learn the dBASE III PLUS command syntax .

Options     The Assistant menu bar offers eight action choices : Set Up,
            Create, Update, Position, Retrieve, Organize, Modify, and Tools .

Set Up      The Set Up Menu lets you open files . An option on this menu also
            lets you exit from the dBASE III PLUS program .
            When you choose an option, a list of available drives appears, with
            the current one as the default . Choose the drive containing your
            files before choosing a file .
            The Database file option lets you open a .dbf file . After you choose
            a drive and database file from the pull-down menu, the next prompt
            asks if the file is indexed . If it is indexed, and you want to open one
            or more indexes, enter Y . A list of index files appears . The first one
            that you select, regardless of its position in the index list, becomes
            the controlling index. The word Master appears next to it. If you
            select additional index files, they also are opened, and the numbers
            02, 03, and so on, appear next to them . You can select up to seven
            index files .

BROWSE         BROWSE is a full-screen, menu-assisted command for editing and
               appending records in database ( .dbf) files . It presents up to 17
               records at once and as many fields as fit across the screen.

Syntax         BROWSE [FIELDS < field list > ] [LOCK < expN > ]
               [FREEZE < field > ] [NOFOLLOW] [NOMENU] [WIDTH
               < expN > ] [NOAPPEND]

Usage          The BROWSE menu bar is activated when you press FlO . Once you
               choose an option, the menu bar disappears . You can set many of
               the same options provided on the menu bar by entering them at the
               dot prompt (see the Command Line Options below) .
               To turn the navigation key menu on and off, press F1 .

Command
Line Options

FIELDS         You specify a fields list to indicate the fields you want to display,
               and the order in which you want them to appear :

LOCK           This specifies the number of fields that you want to keep displayed
               on the screen, starting from the first field in the fields list . When
               you press Ctrl--- or Ctrl-4-- to scroll fields left or right, the number
               of fields you locked will remain displayed in the same position on
               the screen .

FREEZE         Freezing a field prevents you from editing any of the other fields in
               the field list until you reissue the BROWSE command . Although you
               can edit only one field, all the other fields are still displayed .




U5-40                                                             USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                  BROWSE

NOFOLLOW          The NOFOLLOW option only has an effect on indexed files . Ordi-
                  narily, if you alter the contents of the key field of a record, the
                  record pointer is repositioned immediately according to the new
                  contents of the field . The edited record remains the current record .
                  If you issue NOFOLLOW before changing the field's contents, the
                  record is repositioned, but the record that took its original place in
                  the file order becomes the current record .

NOMENU            The NOMENU option suppresses display of the menu bar .

WIDTH             The WIDTH option limits the number of character positions
                  (between 4 and 99) that BROWSE may display for any character
                  field . You can move (scroll) within fields using the E- and -* keys,
                  and move from field to field using the Home and End keys.

NOAPPEND          The NOAPPEND option prevents you from adding records to the
                  current file when in BROWSE .

Menu Bar          The Browse Menu bar offers up to six selections : Top, Bottom,
Options           Record No ., Lock, Freeze, and Find .

Bottom            The Bottom option moves the record pointer to the last record in
                  the file, making it the current record .

Top               The Top option moves the record pointer to the first record in the
                  file, making it the current record . The first record may not be
                  record number 1 if the file is in an indexed order .

Lock              The Lock option allows you to specify a number of columns (fields)
                  that you want to remain in the same position on the screen, while
                  other fields scroll horizontally across the display . You are prompted
                  to enter the number of columns (fields) currently displayed on your
                  screen that you want to remain .

Record No.        The Record No . option allows you to go to a specific record num-
                  ber. You are prompted to enter a record number, after which the
                  record pointer moves to highlight the record you selected.

           want to edit. All other fields will remain displayed, but cannot be
           edited . See the explanation under Command Line Options .

Find       The Find option appears on the menu bar only if the database file

COMMANDS                                                                       CALL


CALL              The CALL command allows you to call binary file program
                  modules loaded in memory from within a dBASE program file . You
                  must have first loaded the binary program files in memory using the
                  LOAD command.

Syntax             CALL < module name > [WITH < expC > / < memvar > ]

Usage             The CALL command executes a binary program file that has been
                  loaded in memory with the LOAD command . dBASE III PLUS treats
                  each loaded file as a subroutine or module rather than as an exter-
                  nal program (which could be executed with the RUN command) . As
                  a result, each time you want to execute the program, it can simply
                  run from memory without having to be reloaded from a disk . Up to
                  16 binary program files can be loaded in memory at one time, and
                  each can be up to 32,000 bytes in length .
                  When you CALL the binary program file, you specify the name of
                  the file without the .bin extension . The program module name is
                  the same as the file loaded in memory . When you call the file, you
                  can pass either a character expression or a memory variable of any
                  data type to the binary program file . All character type memory
                  variables and expressions end with a null (ASCII value of zero) .
                  When the program module is called, the Code Segment (CS) points
                  in memory to the beginning of the module . The Data Segment (DS)
                  and BX registers contain the address of the first byte of the memory
                  variable or character expression .

Options           The WITH option is a character expression or a memory variable .
                  Memory variables can be of any type .

Example           Refer to the LOAD command for an example of the CALL command
                  calling a LOADed binary program file . The CALL passes a character
                  string, which is used to change the shape and size of the cursor .

See AISO          LOAD, RELEASE




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                             U5-43
CANCEL                                                                 CHAPTER 5


CANCEL     CANCEL stops the execution of a command file, closes all open
           command files, and returns dBASE III PLUS to the dot prompt.
           CANCEL does not close procedure files .

Syntax     CANCEL

Usage      dBASE III PLUS ignores any text on lines in a dBASE program
           ( .prg) file following CANCEL .

Example    To stop command processing when an error is found, include
           CANCEL within an IF . . . ENDIF or DO CASE . . . ENDCASE structure .
           In the following example, the Error memory variable was
           previously established ;

             IF Error            && If error is true,
                 CANCEL          && command file execution
             ENDIF               && i s cancelled .



See Also   RETURN




U5-44                                                        USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                   CHANGE

CHANGE            The CHANGE command provides full-screen editing of specified
                  fields and records in the active database file .

Syntax            CHANGE [ < scope > ] [FIELDS < field list > ]
                  [WHILE < condition > ] [FOR < condition > ]

Defaults          If CHANGE is used without parameters, the current record is
                  displayed.

Usage             The CHANGE command is identical to the EDIT command .
                  CHANGE uses the same full-screen cursor control keys as both
                  EDIT and MODIFY COMMAND . (Refer to Appendix B .) The arrow
                  keys move the cursor within a record. PgUp backs up to the previ-
                  ous record, or to previous fields of the same record if not all the
                  fields fit on one screen . Similarly, PgDn advances to the next
                  record, or to additional fields of the same record if all the fields do
                  not fit on one screen . Ctrl-End exits CHANGE and saves changes to
                  the current record. Esc exits and saves all changes except those
                  made to the current record .
                  To edit a memo field, place the cursor on the word memo and
                  press Ctrl-PgDn . To finish editing the memo field, press Ctri-End to

                  If you use the CHANGE command at the dot prompt, control auto-

Options           All records are edited sequentially unless otherwise specified by the

CONTINUE                                                                  CHAPTER 5


CONTINUE   CONTINUE searches for the next record in the active database file
           that meets the condition specified by the most recent LOCATE
           command.

Syntax     CONTINUE

Usage      A CONTINUE search ends when it finds a record that meets the
           specified LOCATE condition or when it reaches the end of the
           LOCATE scope .
           LOCATE and CONTINUE are specific to the work area in which you
           issue them . You can issue different LOCATE/CONTINUE commands
           in each work area . If you leave a work area, the LOCATE/
           CONTINUE condition will still be in effect when you return .

Record     When a CONTINUE is successful, the record number is displayed .
           Otherwise dBASE III PLUS displays the message End of LOCATE
Pointer    scope . If the search is unsuccessful, the record pointer is positioned
           at the last record of the LOCATE scope . If this is the last record in
           the database, EOF() will return a True value .

Example    To locate records containing CN7 or AV 10 in the Travelcode field
           in the Travel database file :

             • USE Travel
             • LOCATE FOR Travel code = 'CN7 .OR. Travel code = 'AV 90'
             Record =        2
             • CONTINUE
             Record =       15
             • CONTINUE
             Record =       47
             • CONTINUE
             End of LOCATE scope

           The message End of LOCATE scope indicates that no more
           records fit the FOR condition .

See Also   EOF(), FOUND(), LOCATE




U5-54                                                            USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                         COPY

COPY              COPY duplicates all or part of an active database file to a new file .
                  COPY is the primary command used to export data to non-
                  dBASE III PLUS programs.

Syntax            COPY TO < new file > [ < scope > ] [FIELDS < fields list > ] [FOR
                  < condition > ] [WHILE < condition > [[TYPE] < file type > ]

Defaults          All records are copied, including records marked for deletion,
                  unless SET DELETED is ON, or you specify otherwise with a scope,
                  FOR, or WHILE clause . All fields are copied unless you specify a
                  FIELDS list or use the SET FIELDS TO command . Memo fields are
                  copied only if the new file is another dBASE III PLUS database file .
                  The directory listing of new files created by the COPY command
         N        shows the dates on which the new files were created .
                  If a file type is not entered with the command, the file is copied to
                  another dBASE III PLUS database ( .dbf) file .

Usage             If the TO file is another dBASE III PLUS database ( .dbf) file, do not
                  specify TYPE or [ < file type > ] . Otherwise you need to specify one
                  of the file type options supported, to transfer the dBASE III PLUS
                  database file to another software program or create a delimited text
                  file .



                       NOTE
                       dBASE III PLUS may allow you to build files with more fields,
                       more characters per field, or more records than certain other
                       software programs allow . In such cases, when you copy a
                       dBASE III PLUS file, original data may be lost . Note the limita-
                       tions of the software program to which you're exporting a file
                       before creating the files with COPY .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                 U5-55
COPY                                                                  CHAPTER 5


Options   The options for < file type > are :
           • DELIMITED [WITH BLANK/ < delimiter > ]               Delimited for-
             mat ASCII text ( .txt) file . Data from fields is copied character by
             character beginning with the first character on the left . Each
             record ends with a carriage return and line feed . All fields are
             separated by commas unless you specify DELIMITED WITH
             BLANK. In addition, character fields are enclosed by double
             quotes ("), unless you specify a different delimiter character
             using DELIMITED WITH < delimiter > or you specify
             DELIMITED WITH BLANK .
             DELIMITED WITH BLANK separates each field with a single
             space character instead of a comma . Character fields are
             treated like any other field and are not enclosed by delimiter
             characters .                                               f


             DELIMITED WITH < delimiter > allows you to enclose charac-
             ter fields with a delimiter character of your choice .
           • SDF - System Data Format ASCII file . Data in fields is copied
             character by character beginning with the first character on the
             left. Each record has the same length and ends with a carriage
             return and line feed .
           • DIF - VisiCalc file format . Database records are converted
             to VisiCalc rows, and database fields are converted to VisiCalc
             columns .
           • SYLK - Multiplan spreadsheet formula . Database records are
             converted to Multiplan rows, and database fields are converted
             to Multiplan columns .
           • WKS - Lotus 1-2-3 spreadsheet format, release 1A . Database
             records are converted to Lotus 1-2-3 rows, and database fields
             are converted to Lotus 1-2-3 columns .
             When using COPY to write any of the three supported spread-
             sheet formats, the field names are written as column headers in
             the resulting file . The file is created in row major order .




U5-56                                                      USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                                            COPY

                  pfs:File format .

Tips              Do not use the single letters A through J or M as a database
                  filename if you COPY TO a dBASE III PLUS database file . However,
                  you can, for example, specify AA as a database filename .
