U5-148                                                    USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                        LOAD

LOAD              LOAD allows you to load binary program files in memory and run
                  them directly from memory with the CALL command .

Syntax            LOAD < binary filename >

Usage             LOAD places a binary ( .bin) file in memory where it can be
                  executed with the CALL command .

Programming       dBASE III PLUS treats each loaded file as a subroutine or program
                  module, not as an external dBASE program file .
Notes
                  A maximum of sixteen files may be resident in memory at one time .
                  Each can be up to 32,000 bytes and must be a binary type file .
                  Each LOADed module must have a unique name . The default exten-
                  sion is .bin . When you CALL a file, omit the extension ; the filename
                  itself becomes the module name .
                  If you LOAD a file that has the same filename but a different exten-
                  sion than one already LOADed, the new one replaces the first one in
                  memory .
                  To see the names of LOADed modules, issue the DISPLAY/LIST
                  STATUS command.
                  dBASE III PLUS does not check the integrity of the files you LOAD .
                  Make sure the programs are in binary form and each program
                  executes properly.




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                             U5-149
LOAD                                                                    CHAPTER 5


         You must conform to the following specifications while designing
         the assembly language program from which the binary file is made :
          •   It must originate (ORG) the first executable instruction at an
              offset of zero .
          • The program must not allocate or use memory over and above
            its actual size, because LOAD uses the file size to determine how
            much memory to allocate .
          • The assembly language program must not lengthen or shorten
            memory variables passed as arguments from CALL . . . WITH in
            DS :BX .
          • Before returning control to dBASE III PLUS, the program must
            restore both the Code Segment (CS) and the Stack Segment (SS)
            Registers .
          • Return control to dBASE III PLUS using a far return (RET
            FAR) . Most commercial programs end with an exit call rather
            than a far return ; execute these with the RUN/! command, not
            with LOAD and CALL.
         To prepare an assembly language program written in 8086/8088
         assembler for LOADing by dBASE III PLUS, use the DOS macro
         assembler and the following DOS program commands :
          • To assemble programs and create an object ( .obj) file :
            MASM < filename > < filename > NULL NULL
          • To link OBJ files and create an executable ( .exe) file :
            LINK < filename > NULL NULL
          • To create a binary ( .bin) file from an executable file :
            EXE2BIN < filename >

U5-152                                                        USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                          LOCATE

LOCATE            LOCATE searches the active database file for a record that satisfies
                  specified criteria .

Syntax            LOCATE [ < scope > ] [WHILE < condition > ]
                  [FOR < condition > ]

Defaults          Unless otherwise restricted by the scope or a WHILE clause,
                  LOCATE searches the entire database beginning with the first
                  record.

Usage             The NEXT <n> option for the scope limits the search to the spec-
                  ified number of records and begins the search at the current
                  record.
                  To find the next occurrences of the specified condition, use the
                  CONTINUE command .

Record            If a match is found, the record pointer moves to that record and
                  displays the record number. FOUND() returns .T.
Pointer
                  If no match is found, the record pointer moves to the end of the file
                  (EOF() is .T.), or the end of the scope if one was specified .
                  dBASE III PLUS displays the message End of locate scope .
                  FOUND() returns .F.

Special Cases     Unless the scope is NEXT < n>, REST, or WHILE, LOCATE starts
                  searching at the beginning of the file . If there are multiple
                  LOCATES, the most recent overrides any other .
                  LOCATE and CONTINUE are specific to the work area in which
                  they are issued . You can have a different LOCATE/CONTINUE for
                  each work area . If you leave the work area, they will still be in
                  effect when you return .

Examples          To locate the first record in Travel .dbf that contains the Travelcode
                  H114 or CN7 :
                       • USE Travel
                       • LOCATE FOR Travelcode = 'HI 14' .OR. Travelcode = 'CNT
                       Record =        5

           To LOCATE the first of the next five records that contains XX in the
           Travelcode field :

                  GO TOP

             End of LOCATE scope

MODIFY            MODIFY COMMAND is the dBASE III PLUS full-screen text editor .
                  Its main function is to create and edit dBASE program and format
COMMAND           files, but it can also be used to create or edit any standard ASCII
                  text file .

Syntax            MODIFY COMMAND/FILE < filename >

Defaults          If the drive, directory, or extension are not explicitly specified as
                  part of the filename with MODIFY COMMAND, the default drive
                  and directory and the .prg extension are used . MODIFY FILE is an
                  alternative syntax for the dBASE text editor which does not provide
                  a default extension . If no extension is specified when you create a
                  file, none is provided .
                  The maximum file size that MODIFY COMMAND/FILE can handle
                  is 5,000 bytes, unless an external word processor is specified in
                  a dBASE III PLUS Config .db file . (Refer to Chapter 4 for instruc-
                  tions on setting up an external word processor as the default
                  dBASE III PLUS text editor .) A warning message is issued if an
                  attempt is made to exceed the 5,000-byte limit, and the text in the
                  file may not be reliable after it is saved .

Usage             When you issue the MODIFY COMMAND/FILE command,
                  dBASE III PLUS searches for the specified file . If the file exists, it is
                  called up for editing . Each time a file is edited, the previous version
                  is saved as a backup file with the .bak extension . If the file is not
                  found, a new file is created .
                  When you first begin MODIFY COMMAND/FILE, the keys you can
                  use appear in a menu at the top of the screen . Pressing F1 toggles
                  this menu on or off.

USING dBASE III PLUS                                                             U5-159
ON                                                                  CHAPTER 5


ON       ON branches the execution of a program if one of three specified
         conditions occurs .

Syntax   ON ERROR/ESCAPE/KEY < command >

Usage    You can specify a command to be executed for each of three ON
         conditions . The ON conditions remain in effect until you explicitly
         remove them, or until you leave dBASE III PLUS .
         To remove an ON, enter ON ERROR, ON ESCAPE, or ON KEY
         without specifying a command.
         Note that ON ESCAPE does not . work when SET ESCAPE is OFF .
         dBASE III PLUS responds to the ON options in the following order
         of precedence :
             ON ERROR        = A dBASE III PLUS error occurred
             ON ESCAPE       = The Esc key is pressed
             ON KEY          = Any key is pressed
         If, for example, ON KEY and ON ESCAPE are in effect at the same
         time, pressing the Esc key executes the ON ESCAPE command . It
         does not branch to the ON KEY command line .
         If only ON KEY is in effect and SET ESCAPE is OFF, pressing the
         Esc key activates the command specified in the ON KEY command
         line .
         If the ON KEY command is in effect, and any key other than Esc is
         pressed, the ON KEY command is executed after the current com-
         mand is completed . For instance, pressing a key while INDEXing a
         file will not interrupt the index procedure . However, it is important
         to note that unless the program uses the stored key, the command
         specified on the ON KEY command line will execute repeatedly .
         Proper use of ON KEY requires that the key pressed and stored in
         the buffer is removed from the buffer with commands such as
         INKEY() or READ . If you use ON KEY WAIT TO < memvar > , the
         key that was pressed to cause the program to branch to the ON
         KEY command is put into the memory variable ; you do not have to
         press a key for this to occur .




U5-160                                                   USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                          ON
                  ON ERROR does not respond to errors at the operating system
                  level, such as a drive or printer not being accessible . It responds
                  only to dBASE III PLUS errors, such as a syntax error or a nonexist-
                  ent file . Also, returning from an ON ERROR < DO program > will
                  not re-evaluate an IF or DO WHILE condition in the program in
                  which the error occurred .

Examples          The ON examples below assume that the procedure file containing
                  the two procedures IF_err and Stop is already open (see the SET
                  PROCEDURE TO command) .

                   < program > command when a dBASE III PLUS error occurs, type
                  the following :

                       ON ERROR DO If_err


                  Then, if dBASE III PLUS encounters an error, it branches to :

                       PROCEDURE If_err
                       < commands >



                         Turn off the on error flag if you
                         don't want to trap additional errors .
                       ON ERROR
                       RETURN


                  The next example shows you how to set up the ON KEY option to
                  execute a DO < program > command . To halt printing and branch
                  to a procedure named Stop, enter :

                       ON KEY DO Stop


                  Afterward, if you press any key, the program branches to the Stop
                  procedure . The Stop procedure prompts you to press the letter A if
                  you want to stop printing ; pressing any other key would cause print-
                  ing to resume .

             PROCEDURE Stop
             * First clear the key that triggered ON KEY
             * from the type-ahead buffer with INKEY() .
             i = INKEY()
             WAIT "Press A to Abort printing, " + ;
                  "any other key to continue" TO choice
             IF choice $ "Aa"
                RETURN TO MASTER
             ENDIF
             RETURN


           In this example, the substring operator $ evaluates the key pressed
           in response to the WAIT command to see if it is either an upper-
           case or lower-case letter A .

PARAMETERS                                                             CHAPTER 5



PARAMETERS   PARAMETERS assigns local variable names to data items passed
             from a calling program . This command receives variables passed
             using the DO < filename > WITH < parameter list > command .

Syntax       PARAMETERS < parameter list >

Usage        When included in a dBASE program file, PARAMETERS must be
             the first executable command . In a procedure file, the PROCEDURE
             name is the first command, followed by the PARAMETERS com-
             mand . The parameters you pass can be any legitimate expressions .
             The parameter list assigns local variable names to receive parame-
             ters from the sending program's parameter list . The local variables
             created by specifying PARAMETERS are discarded when control is
             returned to the calling program . The parameter list must contain
             the same number of items as in the calling program .
             If the parameter being passed is a memory variable, its value may
             be changed . The change is transferred to the variable in the calling
             program . If the parameter being passed is an expression, the value
             of that expression is stored to a memory variable in the receiving
             program .

Examples     The following command file calculates the area for a given length
             and width .

               *The command file Areacalc . g
               PARAMETERS Length,Width,A
               *A corresponds to area
               A=Length * Width
               RETURN
               *EOF ; Areacalc .prg


             To execute this command file :
               • area=0
               0
                   DO Areacaic WITH 6,4, area
               •
                                    24

               • ?area
                       24



See Also     DO, PRIVATE, PROCEDURE, PUBLIC, SET PROCEDURE

COMMANDS                                                              PRIVATE

PRIVATE           PRIVATE allows you to create new memory variables in a lower-
                  level program with the same names as memory variables that were
                  created in a calling program or were previously declared as
                  PUBLIC .

Syntax            PRIVATE < memvar list > /[ ALL [LIKE/EXCEPT < skeleton > ]]

Usage             Changes made to a PRIVATE memory variable do not overwrite the
                  values in memory variables with the same name in other programs .
                  Previous values of PRIVATE memory variables are retained in mem-
                  ory with the name of the programs that created them .
                  When the program containing PRIVATE memory variables ends, the
                  values that were hidden by PRIVATE are reinstated . The PRIVATE
                  values are no longer in effect .

See Also          DO, PARAMETERS, PUBLIC

COMMANDS                                                                     PUBLIC

PUBLIC            PUBLIC makes memory variables global by enabling them to be
                  used and altered by any dBASE program or subprogram . Unlike
                  other memory variables, they are not released when the program
                  ends .

Syntax            PUBLIC < memory variable list >

Usage             Memory variables which you want to be PUBLIC must be declared
                  PUBLIC before they are given values . The values of PUBLIC mem-
                  ory variables may be changed by any program that uses them .
                  The value of a PUBLIC memory variable may be hidden temporarily
                  when a program or procedure file is called, by declaring memory
                  variables with the same name PRIVATE, or passing a parameter
                  with the DO WITH < parameter list > command .
                  Variables saved in a memory file are always RESTOREd as PUBLIC
                  variables, if they're restored at the dot prompt . Variables restored
                  from a memory file in a dBASE program are RESTOREd as
                  PRIVATE variables unless you specify otherwise . To RESTORE
                  PUBLIC variables in a dBASE program file, you first need to
                  redeclare the variables you intend to be PUBLIC as PUBLIC vari-
                  ables . Then RESTORE FROM < filename > ADDITIVE restores the
                  variables as PUBLIC, overwriting any variables of the same name .



                       NOTE
                       Variables you declare PUBLIC are stored as logical type
                       variables until you initialize them .

READ          READ activates all @ . . . GETS issued since the last CLEAR, CLEAR
              ALL, CLEAR GETS, or READ . It is most commonly used in dBASE
              program files for full-screen entry or editing of data .

Syntax        READ [SAVE]

Usage         The READ command uses the same full-screen editing keys as the
              APPEND and EDIT commands . You need to use the READ com-
              mand to edit memory variables with the @ command .
              READ clears all GETS after you finish editing .

Options       READ SAVE does not clear GETS . This means that the next time you
              issue READ, the same set of GETS appears for editing . If you use the
              READ SAVE option, make sure to issue CLEAR GETS before you

              to Chapter 4 for more information .

              ~ . . . SAY . . . GETS continue on from 2 to 32 screen pages, include a
Notes         READ wherever you want a page break .

              variable :

                STORE SPACE(25) TO mname

              SPACE(25) function initializes a blank character string that is 25
              characters long.

REPLACE                                                                   CHAPTER 5


REPLACE    REPLACE alters the contents of specified fields in the active
           database file .

Syntax     REPLACE [ < scope > ] < field > WITH < exp > [, < field > WITH
           < exp > . . . ] [WHILE < condition > ] [FOR < condition > ]

Defaults   Unless otherwise specified by the scope or the WHILE or FOR
           clause, only the current record is replaced .

Usage      The field and the WITH expression must have the same data type .
           With numeric fields, the WITH expression may not be larger than
           the field width . If it is, asterisks replace the field contents, and some
           data may be lost .



             NOTE
             Replacements on a key field of an indexed database file also
             update the index file if it's in use . When the replacement is
             made, the record moves to a new position in the index file . If
             you specify a scope, WHILE, or FOR when making replace-
             ments on an indexed field, not all of the records you intended
             will be replaced . For example, if you REPLACE ALL, only the
             first record and those that follow the new key field value will be
             replaced . That's because each record is reindexed as the
             REPLACE is done, and the record pointer is moved to follow
             the replaced record . To REPLACE all the records, you should
             use the database file without an index, and then REINDEX
             afterwards .




Record     The REPLACE command does not reposition the record pointer
           unless a scope, FOR, or WHILE is specified . If the record pointer is
Pointer    at the end of the file (EOF() is .T.), no replacements are made
           unless a SCOPE or FOR condition is specified in the command . Be
           sure to position the pointer with a command such as GO TOP
           before beginning a REPLACE option .

REPORT                                                               CHAPTER 5


REPORT     REPORT prints information from the active database using the
           report form file created by CREATE or MODIFY REPORT . A report
           may be directed to the screen, the printer, or an ASCII text file .

Syntax     REPORT FORM < filename > /? [ < scope > ]
           [WHILE < condition > ] [FOR < condition > ] [PLAIN]
           [HEADING < expC > ] [NOEJECT]
           [TO PRINT/TO FILE < filename > ] [SUMMARY]

Defaults   The default extension is .frm for the FORM filename .
           Unless otherwise specified by the scope, a FOR clause, or an active
           filter condition or query file, all records in the database are
           included in the report .

Usage      If group subtotals are defined in the report form file, the active
           database should be INDEXed or SORTed on the same fields as in
           the group expression .

Options    Use the catalog query clause to activate a menu of all report forms
           for the active database file .
           PLAIN causes the report to print without page numbers or a system
           date . The page heading defined in the report form file appears on
           the first page only .
           HEADING, followed by a character expression, defines an extra
           heading that is printed on the first line of each page . If the
           heading is a character string, you must delimit it . PLAIN and
           HEADING are mutually exclusive, with PLAIN taking precedence .
           NOEJECT, with TO PRINT, suppresses the usual initial form feed,
           causing the report to print on the first page that comes up in the
           printer .
           The semicolon (;) character in a character or memo field causes a
           carriage return and line feed in a report form . This semicolon does
           not print .




U5-178                                                    USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                      REPORT

                  TO FILE sends the report to a text ( .txt) file on the default drive
                  (and displays it on the screen), unless otherwise directed .
                  SUMMARY suppresses display of detail lines, showing only subtotals
                  and totals on the report.

           file.

Syntax     RESTORE FROM < filename > [ADDITIVE]

Defaults   A .mem file extension is assumed unless otherwise specified .

           of the currently active memory variables are deleted unless
           ADDITIVE is specified . Unless you redeclare memory variables as

           PRIVATE . Memory variables you restore from the dot prompt, how-

           No more than 256 memory variables may be active at any time .
           dBASE III PLUS allocates 6,000 bytes for active memory variables
           (unless you specify a different amount MVARSIZ in the dBASE

Options    To retain the current memory variables, include the ADDITIVE
           option, which causes the RESTOREd memory variables to be added
           to the current ones . Any current memory variables with the same
           name are overwritten . To restore variables in a memory file as
           PUBLIC, you must redeclare them as PUBLIC before you RESTORE
           the memory file and use the ADDITIVE option .

U5-182                                                 USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                    RETRY

RETRY             RETRY is used mainly in error recovery . RETRY returns control
                  from a program in progress to the prior program from which it was
                  called. The command in the first program that called the second
                  program is then re-executed . This is in contrast to the RETURN
                  command, which executes the next line .

Syntax            RETRY

Usage             The primary use of RETRY is in error recovery situations where it
                  can repeat a command until it is successfully executed . Note, how-
                  ever, that RETRY will not re-evaluate an IF or DO WHILE condi-
                  tion
                  When executing a program called with ON ERROR, RETRY returns
                  control to the program where the error originated, and re-executes
                  the command in which the error occurred .
                  RETRY can be used in procedures as well as dBASE program files .
                  When RETRY is used in a program file, it closes the file . RETRY
                  clears out the value returned by the ERROR() function .

Examples          The following command files illustrate how to recover from the
                  File is already open message with an ERROR() number of 3 :

                         Main .prg
                       ON ERROR DO RECOVER WITH ERROR()
                       USE My_fi le
                       * EOF :Main .prg

                       * Recover .prg
                       PARAMETERS Error
                       IF Error=3
                          CLOSE DATABASES
                       ENDIF
                       RETRY
                       * EOF : Recover .prg


See Also          ERROR(), RETURN




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                           U5-183
RETURN                                                              CHAPTER 5


RETURN     RETURN is used in programs to restore control to calling
           programs, or to the dot prompt . When control is restored, the
           command following the calling command is executed .

Syntax     RETURN [TO MASTER]

Usage      If the TO MASTER option is used in a program, control returns to
           the highest-level calling program .
           RETURN can be used in procedures as well as command files . If
           used in a command file, RETURN closes the file .
           If the RETURN command is not included in a program,
           dBASE III PLUS exits and closes the program after it executes the
           last command in the file, or when it reaches a CANCEL or QUIT
           command . It returns to the program that called it or, if it is
           executed in the highest-level program, to the dot prompt .
           RETURN releases all PRIVATE memory variables but does not
           affect PUBLIC variables . RETURN also clears out any value
           returned by the ERROR() function .

See Also   ERROR(), PRIVATE, PUBLIC




U5-184                                                   USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                       RUN/!
RUN/!        RUN executes a specified DOS command, or any program which
 < command > can be executed by DOS, from within dBASE III PLUS .
Syntax       RUN/! < command >

Usage        RUN executes the specified DOS command or program . When
                  execution is finished, control returns to dBASE III PLUS .
                  RUN requires more memory than the 256K needed to run
                  dBASE III PLUS . It requires enough additional memory for the DOS
                  Command .com file, plus the amount required for the command or
                  program file itself . If your computer does not have sufficient mem-
                  ory for the RUN command, dBASE III PLUS returns the message
                  Insufficient memory .
                  The operating system file Command .com must be in the current
                  directory, or specified by the DOS COMSPEC parameter .
                  Use the DOS SET COMSPEC command to tell the operating system
                  where to find Command .com . For example, SET COMSPEC =
                  A:\Command .com . Refer to your DOS manual for more information
                  on SET and COMSPEC .



                       WARNING
                       Some DOS commands, such as ASSIGN and PRINT, remain in
                       memory after being RUN, occupying memory that should be
                       restored to dBASE III PLUS . You should run these commands
                       before loading dBASE III PLUS . If you are not able to load
                       dBASE III PLUS or get an Insufficient memory error message,
                       clear any memory-resident programs or restart your computer
                       and try again . Also, do not run commands which may not leave
                       enough memory for dBASE III PLUS to operate .

USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                  U5-187
SEEK                                                                 CHAPTER 5


SEEK       SEEK searches for the first record in an indexed database file with a
           key that matches the result of a specified expression . SEEK
           conducts a very rapid record search .

Syntax     SEEK < expression >

Usage      The specified expression must be a valid dBASE III PLUS
           expression and must have the same data type as the index key
           expression .
           Substring or partial key searches work only if the search expression
           matches the index key, starting with the leftmost character . The cri-
           teria for the search also depend on the setting of SET EXACT .
           For example, if the index key is 'Smith, John' with SET EXACT
           OFF, 'Smi' will find the index key . However, if SET EXACT is ON,
           the search expression would have to match the full length of the
           index key, which in this example would be 'Smith, John' .

Record     If the search is unsuccessful, the message No find, is displayed, and
           the record pointer moves to the end of the file (EOF() is .T .) . Use
Pointer    SET TALK OFF to suppress the message .
           The FOUND() function is set to True (.T .) when the SEEK is
           successful .

Example    The Tours database file and its index Tour date on the Sample Pro-
           grams and Utilities disk are used to demonstrate the command .
           To SEEK a date < expression >

             • USE Tours INDEX Tourdate
                 SEEK CTOD('11/03/85')
             •   ? Sea ts_open, Departure
                  32    11/43/85



See Also   EOF(), FIND, FOUND( ), INDEX, SET DELETED, SET EXACT, SET

U5-188                                                    USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                       SELECT

SELECT            SELECT chooses a work area from the ten which are available to
                  open a database file or selects a a work area in which a database file
                  is already open .

Syntax            SELECT < work area/alias >

Usage             When you enter dBASE III PLUS, the active work area is work area
                  one . The valid work areas are 1 through 10, or A through J or M .
                  You can open a database file in each work area you select . Work
                  area 10 is reserved for an open catalog . You cannot open a database
                  file in this area if a catalog is open . If you have a database file open
                  in work area 10 and then open a catalog, your database file will be
                  closed automatically since the catalog has precedence .
                  Each work area is also used for opening other files associated with
                  the database file, for example, index, query, and format files. How-
                  ever, the same associated files cannot be open in more than one
                  work area at the same time .
                  You can use SELECT to change work areas so that the database file
                  open in the selected work area becomes the active database file .
                  You can change the current work area by specifying the alias of the
                  database file open in another work area . If you do not specify an
                  alias when you open the file, the filename (without the extension) is
                  the default alias name .
                  To use a variable to select a work area or its alias, the variable must
                  be used as a macro (&) function . For example, if the alias name is
                  stored in a character memory variable, type SELECT
                  & < memvar > .
                  Normally, commands display or change the contents of fields in the
                  active database file . However, you can specify fields in other work
                  areas containing related files using the syntax :
                  alias- > field name
                  If you have issued the SET FIELDS TO command, and SET FIELDS
                  is ON, you can also display or change data for the fields in the spec-
                  ified FIELDS list in other work areas .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-189
SELECT                                                                    CHAPTER 5


Record     Each work area maintains a separate record pointer . Moving
           between work areas does not affect the position of any record
Pointer    pointer . Commands that change the position of a record pointer
           affect only the active database file, unless you set a relation with
           SET RELATION TO, or you open a view file in which a relation
           is set .

Tips       A maximum of 15 open files of all types is allowed . If you get the
           error message Too many files are open and the number of open
           files is less than 15, verify that the Config .sys file on your startup
           disk or hard disk root directory specifies FILES =20 and
           BUFFERS =15 (refer to your computer's operating system manual) .
           Work area 10 is reserved for a catalog file if one is open .

Examples   In this example, the Clients database file is opened in work area l,
           and the Travel database file is opened in work area 3 .

               SELECT 1
             •
             • USE Clients ALIAS Names
               SELECT 3
             •
               USE Travel
             •
           To change the work area, SELECT the alias of the file or the num-
           ber or letter of the work area .

              • SELECT Names
           In these examples, work areas were selected by using a work area
           number, and the alias name of a database file open in a work area .
           You could also select a work area by a letter, for example, selecting
           work area 1 by entering SELECT A .

SET               SET is a full-screen, menu-driven command for displaying and
                  changing the values of many SET commands .

Syntax            SET

Usage             To exit the SET menu, press Esc. This retains any changes made to
                  a SET command, but only for the duration of your current session
                  in dBASE III PLUS . You can alter the default value of SET
                  commands by changing the value in the dBASE Config .db file. Refer
                  to Chapter 4 for more information .
                  For details on any SET command, see the individual entry of the
                  same name in this chapter, for example, SET CONSOLE .

Options           SET provides seven choices : Options, Screen, Keys, Disk, Files,
                  Margin, and Decimals .

Options           The Options Menu contains SET commands with two possible val-
                  ues, such as Help, which can be ON or OFF, and Device, which can
                  be TO SCREEN or TO PRINT .

Screen            The Screen Menu allows you to change the color and screen
                  attributes .

Keys              The Keys Menu lets you reprogram the function keys on your key-
                  board . F1 is reserved for use as a Help key and is not program-
                  mable . From the Keys Menu, you can define the F2 through F10
                  keys for commands of up to 33 characters . (You can set a command
                  of up to 238 characters with the SET FUNCTION command .)

Disk              The Disk Menu lets you specify a default disk drive and a drive
                  search path .

Files             The Files Menu opens Alternate, Format, and Index files . When you
                  choose Alternate, you enter the name of the Alternate file . Choosing
                  any of the others activates a menu list of possible files, such as all
                  .fmt files in the open catalog, or on the default disk drive if no cata-
                  log is open .

Decimals   The Decimals Menu specifies the maximum number of decimal

           calculation .

SET               SET ALTERNATE records all output other than that of full-screen
                  commands to a text file .
ALTERNATE

Syntax            SET ALTERNATE ON/OFF
                  SET ALTERNATE TO [ < filename > ]

Defaults          SET ALTERNATE is normally OFF.
                  The filename must include the drive designator if the file is not on
                  the default drive . The file extension .txt is assumed unless otherwise
                  specified .
                  SET ALTERNATE TO iJ closes an open ALTERNATE file . CLOSE
                  ALTERNATE is an alternative syntax .

Usage             This command consists of two parts :
                  SET ALTERNATE TO < filename > creates a text file and opens the
                  file. It overwrites any file with the same name .
                  SET ALTERNATE ON starts recording of keyboard entries and
                  screen displays in the alternate file . Full-screen operations such as
                     . . . SAY, EDIT, and APPEND are not recorded .
                  You can use SET ALTERNATE OFF to suspend writing to the text
                  file without closing the text file . You can then start recording again
                  with SET ALTERNATE ON . The text file will not be closed until you
                  issue the CLOSE ALTERNATE command . Be sure you issue the
                  CLOSE ALTERNATE command before using the text file (for exam-
                  ple, with your word processor) . The file created by SET
                  ALTERNATE is a standard ASCII text file and may be edited with
                  most word processing programs .

SET CARRY   SET CARRY copies data from the prior record to a new record
            when using APPEND or INSERT .

Syntax      SET CARRY ON/OFF

Defaults    SET CARRY is normally OFF .
            The command does not affect INSERT BLANK or APPEND BLANK;
            a blank record is still added.

Usage       Used with the APPEND command, the last record is carried over
            into the appended record. Pressing PgDn will carry over the same
            record contents into each appended record . Pressing Ctrl-W will
            save the record and exit the APPEND command . Simply pressing
            will not save the record.
            With INSERT BEFORE, the preceding record's contents are carried
            over into the inserted record . For example, if you type GO 4
            followed by INSERT BEFORE, the new record has the same con-
            tents as record 3 .

U5-196                                                   USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                           SET CATALOG

SET               The SET CATALOG command is used to create or open a catalog
CATALOG           file . When a catalog is open and SET CATALOG is ON, new files
                  which are used are added to the catalog .

Syntax            SET CATALOG ON/OFF
                  SET CATALOG TO [ < filename > ]/?

Defaults          SET CATALOG is normally OFF, and no catalogs are selected . How-
                  ever, selecting a catalog with SET CATALOG TO automatically SETS
                  CATALOG ON .

Usage             SET CATALOG TO < filename > is used to open an existing catalog
                  or, if one doesn't exist, to create a new catalog . New catalog
                  filenames are limited to eight characters . Catalog filenames are
                  always given the .cat file extension .
                  When you create a new catalog, you are prompted to enter a one-
                  line text description of the catalog file (provided SET TITLE is ON) .
                  This file description will be displayed later, if you use the SET
                  CATALOG TO ? command to select from a list of available catalogs .
                  The description for each catalog entry is displayed when the catalog
                  name is highlighted .
                  A master catalog file, Catalog .cat, is created the first time you create
                  a catalog . dBASE III PLUS always checks to see if this main catalog
                  exists . If it doesn't, dBASE III PLUS creates one . The master catalog
                  is stored in the current directory and keeps track of other catalogs .
                  You can create different master catalogs in other drives or
                  directories .
                  The master catalog allows you to use the SET CATALOG TO ? com-
                  mand . It stores catalog filenames along with the catalog title
                  descriptions .
                  Catalogs are database files which have a predefined file structure .
                  When you create or select a catalog file, it is automatically opened
                  in work area 10 . When a catalog is open, work area 10 is reserved
                  for the system to update the catalog file, so you cannot select and
                  use that work area for another database file .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-197
SET CATALOG                                                           CHAPTER 5


         When you open or create a new catalog, SET CATALOG is automati-
         cally set ON . From then on, all database files (and associated files
         such as index, query, report, and label files) you use, or new files
         you create, are added to the catalog . With SET CATALOG ON, the
         open catalog records entries for files associated with open database
         files, and it is updated automatically by certain commands such as
         CREATE, INDEX, and CREATE/MODIFY REPORT . You will be
         prompted to enter a file title description for any file you create or
         add while SET CATALOG is ON (if SET TITLE is ON) .
         Whenever you open a catalog, dBASE III PLUS checks the catalog
         contents against the disk . If you've previously deleted any files with
         SET CATALOG OFF, dBASE III PLUS updates the catalog by delet-
         ing the appropriate filename to match the disk .
         If you decide you want to close a catalog, you use the command,
         SET CATALOG TO i-' . If you just want to stop adding files to an
         open catalog, you can SET CATALOG OFF . Then, when you want to
         resume adding files to the catalog, SET CATALOG ON again .
         SET CATALOG OFF, unlike turning off the catalog with SET
         CATALOG TO i-i, keeps the catalog open and allows you to use the
         query clause (?) with other dBASE commands . For example, with
         SET CATALOG OFF, you can type MODIFY REPORT?, and
         dBASE III PLUS activates a menu list of .frm files in the open cata-
         log . Because the files in the catalog are linked with the database file
         they were created or used with, only the files relevant to the active
         database file are listed .

COMMANDS                                                            SET CATALOG

                       displays the message File not cataloged, since SET CATALOG
                       was OFF when the active database file was USEd .

U5-202                                                      USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                           SET CENTURY

SET CENTURY       SET CENTURY allows the input and display of century prefixes in
                  the year portion of dates .

Syntax            SET CENTURY ON/OFF

Defaults          SET CENTURY is normally OFF, meaning that the century is not
                  displayed and can't be input .
                  The default date entry and display is six digits, allowing only two
                  digits for a year entry (current twentieth century only) . However, if
                  a date calculation results in a non-twentieth century date, this value
                  can be placed into a date field, and it will retain the correct cen-
                  tury . If the field is edited with a full-screen editing command and
                  SET CENTURY is OFF, the year is changed to a twentieth-century
                  date .
                  Although the four-digit year displayed with SET CENTURY ON
                  makes the date display ten characters, the database field size is
                  always eight bytes . This is because dates are stored internally as
                  numbers . Also, the format in which a date is displayed does not
                  affect its internal storage .

Usage             With SET CENTURY ON, the date display contains a four-digit year .
                  When SET CENTURY is OFF, the year is displayed in two digits,
                  with the twentieth century assumed .
                  SET CENTURY affects all full-screen editing commands and date
                  displays . When SET CENTURY is OFF, you can input only twentieth
                  century dates .

Examples
                       • ? DATE()
                       02/14/85

                       • SET CENTURY ON
                       • ? DATE()
                       0211411985
                       • SET CENTURY OFF

See Also          CTODO, DATE(), DTOCO, YEAR()

            You may also specify an asterisk ('L) following a selected color to
            indicate blinking, or specify a plus sign ( + ) to indicate high inten-
            sity (except for brown, yellow, and grey colors) . When high inten-
            sity is displayed in color, the color is generally brighter and lighter.
            For machines that allow you to set different colors for standard and
            enhanced text areas, set the standard and enhanced colors in pairs
            as foreground/background colors, and then specify the border . For
            example, SET COLOR TO G/B, RB/N, BG, sets standard colors to
            green on a blue background, enhanced colors to magenta on a
            black background, and provides a cyan border .
            For machines that require the same background for standard and
            enhanced areas, you specify the foreground colors individually, and
            then set the [, < background > ] color . For example, SET COLOR
            TO B, G, RB, R, displays standard text as blue over red standard dis-
            play areas, enhanced (highlighted) text as green on red, with a
            magenta border .

            position of commas indicates the setting you want to change . For
            example, to set the border to green without affecting the other
            options, you would type SET COLOR TO „G. In specifying
            foreground/background pairs, you can omit the foreground or back-
            ground color . When you do not specify a color, either before or
            after the slash [/] in the foreground/background pair, the color
            black is selected .
            If you do not want characters in a specific area to appear on your
            screen (for instance, for a password entry), specify Blank (X) for
            either a foreground or background color in those areas .
            You can store a color setup in a dBASE Config .db file, however, the
            syntax is then :

SET DEBUG                                                            CHAPTER 5


SET DEBUG   SET DEBUG is a tool for locating errors in a program . It determines
            whether output from SET ECHO is sent to the screen or printer .

Syntax      SET DEBUG ON/OFF

Defaults    SET DEBUG is normally OFF .

Usage       When SET DEBUG is ON, the output of SET ECHO is routed to the
            printer . This prevents interference between the program's screen
            operations and the screen displays that are normally generated by
            the debugging process .
            With both SET DEBUG ON and SET ECHO ON, the output for the
            TALK (for example, the number of records indexed), LIST, and
            DISPLAY commands, and error messages are not sent to the printer
            unless SET PRINT is ON .

See Also    SET ECHO, SET TALK

SET DEFAULT   SET DEFAULT TO allows the user to select the drive where all oper-

Syntax        SET DEFAULT TO < drive >

Defaults      The default drive is initially the drive from which you started
              dBASE III PLUS .
              When you change drives with SET DEFAULT TO, the default direc-

              drive A was left in subdirecory \DATA when you left it for a differ-

              SET DEFAULT does not check whether or not the named drive

              Refer to Chapter 4 to find out how to set the default drive in the
              dBASE III PLUS Config .db file .

                    USE Clients
                •

                •

                •

SET DELETED       SET DELETED determines whether records that are marked for
                  deletion are included or ignored by other dBASE III PLUS
                  commands .

Syntax            SET DELETED ON/OFF

Defaults          SET DELETED is normally OFF .

Usage             INDEX and REINDEX always include all records regardless of the
                  status of SET DELETED .
                  With SET DELETED ON, most commands do not consider deleted
                  records part of the file . For example, dBASE III PLUS will not
                  LOCATE or LIST deleted records . However, commands in which
                  the RECORD or NEXT <n> scope is specified, and DISPLAY
                  (operating on current record), DISPLAY RECORD <n>, and
                  GO/GOTO <n>, include deleted records .
                  If SET DELETED is ON, RECALL ALL does not recall any records,
                  because the deleted records are ignored .

DELIMITERS
             full-screen mode .

Syntax       SET DELIMITERS ON/OFF
             SET DELIMITERS TO [ < expC > /DEFAULT]

Defaults     SET DELIMITERS is normally OFF so that entry fields are not
             enclosed by specified delimiter characters . While SET INTENSITY
             is ON, entry fields are displayed in reverse video .
             SET DELIMITERS ON uses colons ( :) to set off the field areas,
             unless another delimiter is chosen with the SET DELIMITERS TO

             SET DELIMITERS must be ON for the symbols defined by SET
             DELIMITERS TO to be in effect .

               • SET DELIMITERS ON

             To reset the delimiters to colons :

               • SET DELIMITERS TO DEFAULT

COMMANDS                                                     SET DOHISTORY

SET               SET DOHISTORY determines whether or not commands from com-
                  mand files are recorded in a memory buffer as they're executed .
DOHISTORY         This buffer is referred to as the history buffer .

Syntax            SET DOHISTORY ON/OFF

Defaults          SET DOHISTORY is normally OFF .

Usage             When SET DOHISTORY is ON, commands from command files are
                  stored in the history buffer in the order of their execution . You can
                  then edit these commands in full-screen edit mode .
                  Note that SET DOHISTORY has no effect on commands you issue
                  directly from the dot prompt. dBASE III PLUS always stores these
                  in the history buffer unless you SET HISTORY OFF . If SET
                  HISTORY is OFF, commands executed from dBASE program files
                  will not be stored in the history buffer .



                       NOTE
                       Editing a command in the history buffer does not change
                       the command in the dBASE program file . You need to edit
                       the commands in the dBASE program file using MODIFY
                       COMMAND .




Tips              In conjunction with SUSPEND and DISPLAY HISTORY, SET
                  DOHISTORY is useful for debugging programs . However, because
                  SET DOHISTORY slows down command file execution, use it only
                  when debugging .

See Also          DISPLAY HISTORY, LIST HISTORY, RESUME, SET DEBUG, SET
                  ECHO, SET HISTORY, SET STEP, SUSPEND

COMMANDS                                                              SET ESCAPE

SET ESCAPE        SET ESCAPE determines whether pressing Esc halts the processing
                  of a program or pressing - or Ctrl-S halts scrolling . It also affects
                  whether INKEY() is able to record the Esc key (and E- and Ctrl-S) .

Syntax            SET ESCAPE ON/OFF

Defaults          SET ESCAPE is normally ON .

Usage             With SET ESCAPE ON, if you press Esc while a command is being
                  processed (for example, during a LIST operation), the processing
                  stops . If running the command from the dot prompt,
                  dBASE III PLUS displays the message *** INTERRUPTED ***, and
                  returns to the dot prompt.
                  If you press Esc while a dBASE program is running, the program
                  halts and dBASE III PLUS displays the message :
                  Called from < filename .prg >
                  Cancel, Ignore, Suspend? (C, I, or S)
                  With SET ESCAPE OFF, the Esc key is disabled and command pro-
                  cessing cannot be interrupted . SET ESCAPE OFF also disables the
                  operation of Ctrl-S or - when they are used to temporarily suspend
                  scrolling .



                       NOTE
                       With SET ESCAPE OFF, program execution cannot be termi-
                       nated without rebooting your computer . SET ESCAPE OFF
                       should only be used in programs that terminate naturally .
                       Rebooting your computer with files open may cause data loss .




See Also          INKEY(), ON ERROR/ESCAPE/KEY, READKEY()




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                               U5-221
SET EXACT                                                               CHAPTER 5


SET EXACT   SET EXACT determines whether a comparison between two charac-
            ter strings requires the strings to be the same length .

Syntax      SET EXACT ON/OFF

Defaults    SET EXACT is normally OFF.

Usage       If SET EXACT is OFF, comparisons between character strings begin
            with the leftmost character in each string and continue character-
            by-character to the end of the string on the right of the relational
            operator . If the two strings compare favorably up to that point, the
            result of the comparison is true .
            If SET EXACT is ON, the comparison of characters in each string is
            the same, except that both character strings must be the same
            length for the comparison to be evaluated as true .

Examples    Consider the two character strings 'abc' and 'abcdef . First, com-
            pare the two character strings with SET EXACT OFF .

              • ? 'abc'= 'abcdef'
              • F.

            If the character string on the right is longer than the character
            string on the left, the two strings do not match, and the result of the
            comparison is False .

              ? 'abcdef'= 'abc'
              .T .

            Since the character string on the right is identical to the starting
            characters of the longer character string on the left, the two strings
            are considered equal .
            With SET EXACT ON, the same character strings are no longer con-
            sidered equal because they do not match exactly :

              • SET EXACT ON
              • ? 'abcde f' _ 'abc'
               F.

COMMANDS                                                                SET FIELDS

SET FIELDS        SET FIELDS defines a list of fields that may be accessed in one or
                  more files . It also determines whether that list is used as the default
                  fields or expression list for several dBASE commands .

Syntax            SET FIELDS ON/OFF
                  SET FIELDS TO [ G fields list > /ALL]

Defaults          SET FIELDS is normally OFF . It is automatically set ON when you
                  specify a fields list with SET FIELDS TO .
                  When SET FIELDS OFF (the default), all the fields of the active
                  database are available . Fields in files open in other work areas are
                  available for display only if you specify their alias names .
                  When SET FIELDS is ON, only those fields listed with the SET
                  FIELDS TO command can be displayed or altered . The fields list
                  can contain fields of the active database file and any other files in
                  use .



                       WARNING
                       If you SET FIELDS ON without first using SET FIELDS TO, no
                       fields may be accessed.




                  SET FIELDS TO defines a list of fields that may be accessed in one
                  or more files . It also redefines the default field or expression list
                  used with dBASE commands which use or display fields . The list of
                  fields specified by SET FIELDS TO is not active unless SET FIELDS
                  is ON . Using the SET FIELDS TO command automatically turns the
                  SET FIELDS command ON .
                  SET FIELDS TO iJ removes those fields from the list that belong to
                  the active database file . SET FIELDS TO ALL includes all the fields
                  of the active database file in the fields list .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-223
SET FIELDS                                                                  CHAPTER 5


                 SET FIELDS TO does not impose any order on the fields listed . It
                 only limits the fields that are accessible . This command is also used
                 with CREATE VIEW FROM ENVIRONMENT to define the fields
                 provided in the view .
                 After a fields list is set, additional or consecutive SET FIELDS TO
                 commands add fields to the current fields list . To include fields
                 from files in other work areas, SELECT the work area of the file and
                 use the SET FIELDS TO command, or specify the file's alias with
                 the field name .
                 When SET FIELDS is ON, the LIST STRUCTURE and DISPLAY
                 STRUCTURE commands indicate the fields which are in the cur-
                 rently defined fields list with the > symbol .



                   NOTE
                   SET FIELDS TO can define a list of fields from multiple files,
                   but it does not relate those files . You must use SET RELATION
                   to establish a connection between files in different work areas .




Other Commands   SET FIELDS TO affects the potential of several other commands.
Affected         Among these commands are the ones allowing you to specify
                 FIELDS as part of their syntax . SET FIELDS TO allows these com-
                 mands to support multiple fields from multiple files . The commands
                 affected are :
                    AVERAGE
                  • BROWSE
                    C HANGE
                  • COPY TO
                  • COPY STRUCTURE
                  • DISPLAY
                  • EDIT
                  • JOIN
                  • LIST
                  • SUM
                  • TOTAL



U5-224                                                           USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                SET FIELDS

                  Prior to using SET FIELDS TO, the default field or expression list
                  for these commands is defined as all the fields in the active database
                  file structure . SET FIELDS TO, however, redefines the list as fields
                  that are either part of the active database file structure or part of
                  the structure of a related file .
                  There are two commands that operate only on fields and can also
                  access work areas beyond the area currently selected . These com-
                  mands are . . . GET and REPLACE . These commands are only able
                  to access those fields included in the SET FIELDS list, regardless of
                  whether an alias is specified .
                  APPEND and INSERT are also affected by the SET FIELDS TO com-
                  mands. View files and relations established between files with SET
                  RELATION should be used in conjunction with SET FIELDS TO
                  only when the following information is understood :
                   • APPEND and INSERT add records to the active database file
                     only, not to all database files in the view files .
                   • APPEND and INSERT use all fields in the active database file
                     unless a format file is used with APPEND to exclude certain
                     fields .
                   • Even though a view may be in effect, and its fields list contains
                     fields from related files, APPEND and INSERT do not add data
                     to fields in these files .
                  It is possible to perform an APPEND BLANK or INSERT BLANK in
                  several work areas, open a format file with multiple fields from
                  multiple files, and then use READ to append to these files simulta-
                  neously. However, this can cause problems if the files are related,
                  and the files related to the active database file contain records with
                  blank key fields .
                  Using SET RELATION, if more than one record in the related file
                  has a key matching that of the record in the parent file, the record
                  pointer is moved to the first matched record it finds . Therefore, if
                  you're appending or inserting a blank record, SET RELATION posi-
                  tions the record pointer of the related file to the first record with a
                  blank key .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                               U5-225
SET FIELDS                                                               CHAPTER 5


             When editing records in a view, dBASE commands such as EDIT,
             BROWSE, @ . . . GET, and READ don't update related key fields
             when the parent key fields are changed . As a result, changing key
             fields is not recommended when a relation is set .
             The SET FIELDS TO command does not check to make sure that
             files are related . You must make sure of this yourself .
             The commands INDEX, LOCATE, SET FILTER, and SET RELATION
             ignore the SET FIELDS TO fields list entirely, regardless of the SET
             FIELDS ON/OFF status . Therefore, these commands can access
             fields in the active database file structure that are not in the fields
             list . To access fields in files from an unselected work area, you must
             specify the file alias with each of these fields .
             The normal and recommended way to use INDEX, LOCATE, and
             SET RELATION is with fields in the active database file structure .
             However, SET FILTER commonly requires the use of fields in
             unselected work areas . Since a separate filter condition is
             maintained for each work area, take care when closing a database
             file . Filters which specify fields of database files closed in other
             work areas should also be removed .
             This same precaution about closing files also applies in applications
             where INDEX, LOCATE, or SET RELATION is used with fields
             other than those belonging to the active database file .
             dBASE III PLUS does not check these conditions automatically
             because to do so would slow down processing time .




U5-226                                                       USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                    SET FIELDS




                       NOTE
                       To insure data integrity when using view files, or the SET
                       FIELDS and SET RELATION commands, you should add
                       records to one database file at a time, with all fields of the
                       database file accessible .
                       Changes to key information should be done knowing that if you
                       change parent key information without also changing
                       corresponding key information in related files, you will lose the
                       relation between those records .
                       Do not construct field lists from multiple unrelated files unless
                       you have a sound reason for doing so .




Accessibility     Using multiple related files can bring up questions of ambiguity and
                  the accessibility of certain fields . The rules governing accessibility
                  are :
                   • Files unaffected by a SET FIELDS TO command retain their
                     default fields lists .
                   • Fields from files unaffected by a SET FIELDS TO command are
                     accessible if an alias is specified provided you opened the file
                     (with USE) after issuing the SET FIELDS TO command .
                   • Fields of the active database file are accessible only if they are
                     included in the fields list .
                   • Fields in related files are accessible if they appear on the fields
                     list and an alias is specified .
                   • Within files that do have fields on the fields list, files not on the
                     fields list are not accessible .
                   • Unless a file has related descendants, fields beyond its own
                     listed fields are not displayed .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                    U5-227
SET FIELDS                                                                                    CHAPTER 5


             When referring to fields without the use of an alias, dBASE resolves
             ambiguities on these guidelines :
              • The active database file is searched first .
              • If the field is not in the active database file, the fields list is
                searched .
              • If a field isn't found on the fields list for the active database file,
                then fields list entries for related files are searched .

COMMANDS                                                                  SET FILTER

SET FILTER        SET FILTER allows display of only those records of a database file
                  that meet a specified condition .

Syntax            SET FILTER TO [FILE < filename > /?] [ < condition > ]

Defaults          SET FILTER TO a' without a condition turns off the filter for the
                  active database file . SET FILTER TO adds a filter (query) file to a
                  catalog if one is open and SET CATALOG is ON .

Usage             SET FILTER applies only to the database file open in the work area
                  where the command is issued . Therefore, a different filter condition
                  may be set for each open database file .
                  All commands that require a database file to be in USE, such as
                  AVERAGE, BROWSE, EDIT, and REPORT, can use conditions spec-
                  ified by SET FILTER.
                  SET FILTER TO FILE reads the filter condition from a query ( .qry)
                  file created by CREATE/MODIFY QUERY . If a catalog is open, you
                  can use the catalog query clause (?) to display a menu of all query
                  files for the active database file .
                  SET FILTER TO < condition > sets up a filter based on a valid
                  dBASE expression . The condition can filter records in the active
                  database file based on any of the allowed data types, for example,
                  on a character field, SET FILTER TO Lastname = 'Jones' ; or on a
                  date field, SET FILTER TO Departure = CTOD('01 /01 /86') .
                  Filters aren't activated until after the record pointer is moved
                  within a file . This means that your filter condition isn't in effect
                  unless something has caused the pointer to change position since
                  the condition was set . The best way to assure that a filter is in effect
                  is to execute a GOTO TOP command after setting the filter .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                 U5-229
SET FILTER                                                               CHAPTER 5


Examples     You can set a filter for the Clients database file to limit the records
             to those in which the state is NV (Nevada) :

               • USE Clients
               • SET FILTER TO State = 'NV'
               • GO TOP
               • LIST Las tname, State
               Record#     Lastname             State
                       4   Garnett              NV
                    31     Rizzo                NV

               • GO TOP

SET FORMAT    SET FORMAT allows the user to select custom forms stored as for-
              mat ( .fmt) files .

Syntax        SET FORMAT TO [ < filename > /?]

Defaults      If you do not specify a file extension with a format filename, the
              .fmt extension is assumed .
              Each work area with an open database file can have an open format
              file . Both SET FORMAT TO       and CLOSE FORMAT close the open
              format file in the currently selected work area .
              The SET FORMAT TO command updates a catalog if one is open,
              and SET CATALOG is ON .

Usage         If SET FORMAT TO is not used, APPEND, CHANGE, EDIT, and
              INSERT use the standard display and entry form dBASE III PLUS
              provides .
              If a catalog is open, SET FORMAT TO? displays a menu of all for-
              mat files for the active database file .
              Remember that you can use CREATE/MODIFY SCREEN, a menu-
              driven screen painter, to create format files . CREATE/MODIFY
              SCREEN first creates a screen ( .scr) file, and then when you save
              that file, it creates a format ( .fmt) file . You can use the Screen
              Painter to create a format file which you can use with SET
              FORMAT TO to APPEND or EDIT records in the associated database
              file
              When you want to make changes to the format file, you can make
              them with MODIFY SCREEN, through which both the .scr and .fmt
              files are updated . However, if you make changes to the format file
              using the MODIFY COMMAND text editor, the changes will not be
              made to the screen file and future use of MODIFY SCREEN will not
              reflect changes to the format file .

Programming   If you want to use a multi-page format ( .fmt) file in which the
                 . . . SAY . . . GETS continue on from 2 to 32 screen pages, include a
Notes         READ wherever you want a page break . The PgDn and PgUp keys
              flip the pages . Multi-page format files only work when the format
              file is opened with SET FORMAT TO .

SET FUNCTION                                                                  CHAPTER 5


SET        SET FUNCTION reprograms a function key . You may specify a char-
           acter string expression of up to 238 characters for each function
FUNCTION   key . The sequence of characters you specify will then be transmitted
           to the computer each time you then press that function key .

Syntax     SET FUNCTION < exp > TO < expC >

Usage      The standard function key assignments are :

            Key            Value                      Key           Value
            F1             help ;                     F6            display status ;
            F2             assist;                    F7            display memory ;
            F3             list ;                     F8            display ;
            F4             dir;                       F9            append ;
            F5             display structure ;        F10           edit ;

           Function key F1 cannot be reprogrammed .
           The expression designating a function key can be numeric or char-
           acter . You can use either type of expression if your terminal has
           numbered function keys . If not, you can use a character expression
           to enter the name of the programmable function keys .
           A semicolon included in the string of characters specified for a
           function key assignment generates a carriage return .

Examples   To assign the SET command to function key F10, so that pressing
           F10 executes the command:

                 SET FUNCTION 10 TO 'SET;'


           To assign multiple commands to function key F9, so that
           the sequence of commands CLEAR, USE Clients, and LIST
           STRUCTURE is executed:

             . SET FUNCTION 9 TO 'CLEAR; USE C( Tents; LIST STRUCTURE;'

U5-236                                                USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                         SET HISTORY

SET HISTORY       SET HISTORY ON/off determines whether previously executed
                  commands are stored in a history buffer . SET HISTORY TO speci-
                  fies the desired number of executed commands to be stored in the
                  history buffer.

Syntax            SET HISTORY ON/OFF
                  SET HISTORY TO < expN >

Defaults          SET HISTORY is normally ON . The default number of stored com-
                  mands is 20 . The allowable range of commands is an integer
                  between zero and 16,000 .

Usage             SET HISTORY allows you to redisplay, edit, or re-execute com-
                  mands (including those issued from The Assistant) . You use T and y
                  to redisplay commands you previously executed from the dot
                  prompt. Commands are displayed from most recent to least recent
                  as you step through the history buffer using the f key. (Refer to
                  Chapter 2 for more information on the operation of the history
                  buffer .)
                  The maximum number of commands the history buffer stores is
                  determined by SET HISTORY TO . When this number is reached,
                  the earliest commands executed are cleared from the buffer . If you
                  SET HISTORY to a number that is less than the number of com-
                  mands currently stored in the history buffer, all stored commands
                  are erased. Otherwise, they are retained .
                  Commands stored in the history buffer reside in memory. You can
                  LIST HISTORY or DISPLAY HISTORY to view the entire contents
                  of the history buffer at one time . The command SET HISTORY OFF
                  clears the history buffer .
                  You can also store commands executed from dBASE programs if
                  you SET DOHISTORY ON . You can redisplay, edit, and re-execute
                  commands from dBASE programs . Edits you make to commands
                  will not be saved in the program file, however .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                            U5-237
SET HISTORY                                                        CHAPTER 5


           The maximum size of the history buffer is limited by the amount of
           memory you have available, and by the memory occupied by other
           programs already resident in memory, including dBASE III PLUS .
           To calculate the amount of memory that the history buffer uses, add
           nine bytes to the number of bytes in each command .

See Also   DISPLAY HISTORY, LIST HISTORY, SET DOHISTORY
