COMMANDS                                                                 SET INDEX

SET INDEX         SET INDEX opens the specified index files .

Syntax            SET INDEX TO [ < list of index filenames > /?]

Defaults          The file extension .ndx is assumed unless otherwise specified .
                  SET INDEX TO iJ closes all open index files in the current work
                  area . It is an alternative syntax for CLOSE INDEX .

Usage             If a catalog is open, use SET INDEX TO ? to display a list of all
                  index files for the active database file if a catalog is open .
                  Up to seven index files may be opened with SET INDEX if they all
                  have been created from the database file in USE . Note that SET
                  INDEX doesn't create the index files ; it only opens them .
                  The first index file in the list is the master index, which controls the
                  order of the database file . The master index file also specifies the
                  index key expression for which you can specify a search value with
                  FIND and SEEK . You can switch the index file designated as the
                  master index with the SET ORDER command . You specify a num-
                  ber from 1 to 7, which corresponds to the order of the open index
                  files in the file list of the currently selected work area .
                  Not just the master but all open index files are automatically
                  updated whenever a change is made to the associated database file .
                  You can restore the natural order of the database file with SET
                  ORDER TO 0 ; however, if you make any changes to the index keys
                  or add records, you'll need to reindex the file .
                  If you APPEND records to a database file which uses an index file,
                  new records are appended to the end of the database file . After you
                  complete field entries in an appended record, the record will be
                  repositioned according to its position determined by the index key
                  expression of the master index file . The INSERT command is equiv-
                  alent to APPEND when an index file is in use .

Record            When you issue SET INDEX TO, the database record pointer is posi-
                  tioned at the beginning of the file as determined by the master
Pointer           index file .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-239

SET ORDER         SET ORDER sets up any open index file as the master (controlling)
                  index, or removes control from all open index files, without closing
                  and reopening the files .

Syntax            SET ORDER TO [ < expN > ]



                       NOTE
                       After a SET ORDER command, you must position the record
                       pointer in a database file with a GOTO, FIND, or SEEK record-
                       positioning command . This activates the index file so that
                       records appear in the indexed order.




Usage             The numeric expression must be an integer between 0 and 7,

                  data.

Tip               SET ORDER saves time when you want to reassign a controlling

                  move the record pointer .

U5-248                                                      USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                  SET PATH

SET PATH          SET PATH TO specifies the route that dBASE III PLUS follows to
                  find files that are not found in the current directory .

Syntax            SET PATH TO [ < path list > ]

Defaults          SET PATH TO       without additional parameters releases any dBASE
                  search path set previously with SET PATH TO . By default,
                  dBASE III PLUS will only search the current directory .

Usage             SET PATH enables you to access your files in a tree-structured
                  directory system . It specifies the sequence of directories that
                  dBASE III PLUS can search to find specified files that are not found
                  in the current directory.
                  The current disk directory is the one from which you started
                  dBASE III PLUS, unless it was changed using the DOS CHDIR (CD)
                  command or you changed drives with the SET DEFAULT command .
                  Only the current directory is searched, unless you use the SET
                  PATH command to specify an alternate search path .
                  dBASE III PLUS does not use the paths established by the DOS
                  PATH command, nor does DOS use the path that dBASE III PLUS
                  establishes with SET PATH .
                  A path is a list of directories separated by backslashes and listed in
                  order from the top level directory to the level where the file is
                  located, for example A :\DBASE\DATA .
                  A path list is a series of paths separated by commas or semicolons,
                  up to 60 characters in length, which specifies more than one direc-
                  tory search path .

Tips              SET PATH does not affect the DIR command listing . The DIR com-
                  mand lists files in the current or specified directory, not in the
                  directory set through a path .
                  SET PATH applies only to commands that search for existing files .
                  If you create a file and the file is to be placed in a directory other
                  than the current directory, you must explicitly specify the path
                  name with the filename .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                               U5-249
SET PATH                                                               CHAPTER 5


Example    The following SET PATH command specifies two additional directo-
           ries to be searched if a file (in this case, Program.prg) is not found
           in the current default drive directory . The next search directory is
           the \Baseline directory on drive A . If the Program .prg file is not
           found there, dBASE III PLUS will search for the file in the
           \Dbase\Newpgms directory on drive B .

               SET PATH TO A : \BASELINE,B : \DBASE`NEWPGMS
               DO Program



See Also   DIR, SET DEFAULT

U5-254                                                   USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                           SET RELATION

SET               SET RELATION links two open database files according to a key
                  expression that is common to both files .
RELATION
Syntax            SET RELATION TO [ < key expression > / < expN > INTO
                  < alias >

Defaults          SET RELATION TO i--', without any additional parameters, removes
                  the relation from the currently selected work area .

Usage             SET RELATION links the active database file to an open database
                  file in another work area . The INTO file is identified by its alias .
                  Only one relation can be set from each work area . The active
                  database file that controls the relation is referred to as the parent
                  file. The file which is linked to the parent file by a relating expres-
                  sion is referred to as the child .

Options           With the key expression option, the key must be contained in the
                  parent database file, and the child file must be indexed on that key .
                  Whenever the parent file is repositioned, the child file is searched
                  for the first record matching the key expression from the active file .
                  With the numeric expression option, the active database is always
                  linked to the record number in the file specified by the numeric
                  expression . The linked file must not be indexed . Typically, the
                  numeric expression will be the RECNO() function . This causes
                  record 1 in the parent file to be linked to record 1 in the child,
                  record 2 in the parent to record 2 in the child, and so on .

Record            If a matching record cannot be found in the linked file, the linked
                  file is positioned at the end of the file (a blank record), and EOF() is
Pointer           True .

Tips              You can save a working environment, including relations, with
                  CREATE VIEW < .vue filename > FROM ENVIRONMENT .
                  Remember that CREATE/MODIFY VIEW is available to you as a
                  menu-driven command for linking files . It also allows you to save
                  relations to a .vue file .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-255
SET RELATION                                                          CHAPTER 5


Examples   Following the steps in this example, you can use data from two
           database files simultaneously .

                 SELECT 1
               •
               • USE Travel
               • SELECT 1
               • USE Clients INDEX Cnames
               • Select 1
                                  Las tname INTO B
               • SET RELA TION TO
               • LIST NEXT l Lastname, B-> Zipcode
               Record#   Lastname              B-> Zipcode
                     1   Buckman               93034

                     3   Bicksby               86001
                     4   Garnett               89504

                     6   Johnson               92504
                     7 Collins                 97219

           In this example, the Travel database file is opened in work area one .
           The Clients database file is opened in work area two, indexed on
           Lastname plus Firstname by the Cnames index file . The Lastname
           field is used as the link between the two files . Lastname is also a
           part of the index key expression of Cnames . From work area one,
           the example lists the Lastname field from the parent file, Travel,
           and the related Zipcode field in the child, the Clients file,
           referenced in work area two by alias B .
           To relate the two files used in the previous example but change the
           relations to a numeric expression (by using RECNO()), you could
           enter the following :

               • SELECT B
               •• SET INDEX TO
                  SELECT A

TYPEAHEAD
TO

Syntax            SET TYPEAHEAD TO < expN >

Defaults          The default number of characters that the type-ahead buffer holds is
                  20. The allowable range is an integer between 0 (zero) and 32,000 .

Usage             SET TYPEAHEAD only works when SET ESCAPE is ON .
                  To completely disable the type-ahead buffer, SET TYPEAHEAD TO
                  0. This deactivates both the ON KEY command and the INKEY()
                  function .
                  In full-screen EDIT or APPEND operations, the type-ahead buffer
                  will only hold 20 characters regardless of a previous setting with
                  SET TYPEAHEAD TO .

                  If you execute an error-handling program using ON ERROR DO
                   < program > , it is a good idea to include SET TYPEAHEAD TO 0
                  as the first line of the error-handling program . Because an error is
                  an unanticipated condition, disabling the type-ahead buffer is a
                  safety precaution .

                  If you try to enter more than the specified number of characters
                  into the type-ahead buffer, all of the extra characters are lost . If SET
                  BELL is ON, the bell will sound . If this happens repeatedly, you
                  should increase the size of the type-ahead buffer .

                  INKEY(), ON, SET BELL, SET ESCAPE




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-263
SET UNIQUE                                                                CHAPTER 5


SET UNIQUE   SET UNIQUE determines whether all records with the same key
             value are included in the index ( .ndx) file .

Syntax       SET UNIQUE ON/OFF

Defaults     SET UNIQUE is normally OFF .

Usage        If you create a new index file while SET UNIQUE is ON, and several
             records have the same key value, only the first record that
             dBASE III PLUS encounters with that value is included in the new
             index file .
             SET UNIQUE is the same as issuing INDEX ON < key expression >
             TO < filename > UNIQUE . When several records have the same
             key value, only the first record that dBASE III PLUS encounters
             with that value is included in the index file .
             Whenever you REINDEX an index file that was created with
             UNIQUE, the file retains its UNIQUE status, regardless of whether
             SET UNIQUE is ON or OFF.
             Adding new records or editing existing records in the database file
             with a unique index engaged retains the UNIQUE status of the index
             file . This means that if you APPEND a record with an index key that
             is already in the index file, that record does not become a part of
             the index file, although it gets added to the database file . Similarly,
             EDITing a record and changing its key to one which is already in
             the index file removes that record from the index file, even though
             the record is still in the database file .

Examples     This example shows how you can get an alphabetical list of all the
             states in which your clients live . The index file consists of only the
             first record that contains each state .
               • USE Clients
               • SET UNIQUE ON
               • INDEX ON State TO State
               100% indexed            5 records indexed




U5-264                                                         USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                              SET UNIQUE



                       NOTE
                       You could also have created the unique index file by typing :
                       INDEX ON State TO State UNIQUE .




                  To display the five unique records, each containing a different state,
                  you would type :

                         LIST State, Las tname

                             3   At       Bi cksby
                                          Buckman

                                          Garnett
                                          Collies


                         SET UNIQUE Off
                         REINPEX

                            15 NM         Adams

                             7 OR         Collies



Programming       To restore an index file to a non-unique status, rebuild the index
                  with SET UNIQUE OFF and the INDEX ON command.

               • The active filter
               • The open format ( .fmt) file, if any

SKIP                                                                   CHAPTER 5



SKIP       SKIP moves the record pointer forward or backward in the active
           database file .

Syntax     SKIP [ < expN > ]

Record     If an index file is in use with the database file, SKIP follows the
           order of the index . If the file in use is not indexed, the record
Pointer    pointer moves sequentially by record number .
           The record pointer moves forward unless the result of the numeric
           expression is negative . If the expression is not included, dBASE III
           PLUS moves forward one record .
           If SKIP is issued when the record pointer is on the last record in a
           file, the value of RECNO() is one greater than the last record num-
           ber in the file, and EOF() is True .
           If SKIP -1 is issued when the record pointer is on the first record,
           RECNO() remains at 1, but BOF() (beginning-of-file) is True .

Examples   The database file Tours on the Sample Programs and Utilities disk is
           used for the following examples .
           To move forward one record in the database :

             • USE Tours
             • SKIP
             Record No .     2


           To move forward five records :

             • STORE 5 TO mskip
             5
                SKIP mskip
             •Record No .    7


           To move backward three records :

             • SKIP -3
             Record No .     4


See Also   BOF(), EOF(), RECNO()



U5-268                                                      USING dBASE III PLUS
COMMANDS                                                                          SORT

SORT              SORT creates a new database file in which the records of the active
                  database file are reordered alphabetically, chronologically, or
                  numerically by the specified key fields .

Syntax            SORT < scope > TO < newfile > ON < field > [/ A] [/C] [/D]
                  [, < field2 > [/ A] [/C] [/D] . . .] [WHILE < condition > ] [FOR
                   < condition > ]

Defaults          The TO file has the .dbf extension unless otherwise specified .
                  SORTS are in ascending order (/A) unless otherwise specified .
                  Ascending order is the same as ASCII order (refer to Appendix D) .
                  SORT updates a catalog if one is in use .

Usage             You may not SORT logical or memo fields .
                  SORT does not work with substrings or other expressions . Use
                  INDEX to use these as a key and then COPY to create a sorted file .
                  You can SORT on a maximum of ten fields .
                  A file cannot be SORTed to itself or to any other open file .

Options           The keywords ASCENDING and DESCENDING are alternatives to
                  specifying /A for ascending order and /D for descending order .
                  /C causes the SORT not to differentiate between upper and lower
                  case .

Tips              Do not use the letters A through J or M as database filenames,
                  because they are reserved for default ALIAS names . However, AA is
                  a valid database filename .
                  You may combine /C with either /A or /D . When using two options,
                  only include one slash (for example, /DC) .
                  When SORTing on multiple fields, the most important key is placed
                  first . Separate field names with commas .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                U5-269
SORT                                                                              CHAPTER 5



Examples   The Travel database is to be SORTed on the initials of the selling
           agent. The field name is Agent :

             • USE Travel
             • SORT ON Agent TO Agent

             • SORT ON Agen t, Cos t/D TO Csa (es
               100% Sorted          49 Records sorted . . . Copying text file

STORE             STORE creates and initializes one or more memory variables .

Syntax            STORE < expression > TO < memory variable list >
                  An alternative syntax for STORE is :
                   • memory variable > _ < expression >
                  If a memory variable of the same name already exists, it is overwrit-
                  ten.

Usage             A single expression may be stored to several memory variables with
                  a single STORE command. With the alternative syntax,
                   • memvar > _ < expression > , you may only store an expression
                  to one memory variable at a time .
                  If you create a memory variable using the syntax < memvar > _
                  • expression > , the memory variable name cannot be the same as
                  a dBASE III PLUS command .
                  A numeric variable may be added to itself ; a character variable may
                  be concatenated to itself.
                  The maximum number of active memory variables is 256 . A maxi-
                  mum of 6,000 bytes is allocated to memory variables unless
                  changed in the Config .db file .

Special Cases     A field with the same name as a memory variable takes precedence
                  in all operations except with macro substitution (&) . To explicitly
                  specify that the memory variable has precedence, use the following
                  representation with m->, the symbol used to specify a memory
                  variable:
                  m-> < memvar >

Examples          To store the logical False condition (.F.) to the memory variable
                  Truth :
                       • STORE •F . TO truth
                        F.

SUSPEND                                                           CHAPTER 5


SUSPEND    SUSPEND is primarily a debugging tool that lets you stop a program
           while it is executing . You can then enter commands from the key-
           board or the history buffer, and RESUME the program .

Syntax     SUSPEND

Usage      If you press the Esc key while a program is running,
           dBASE III PLUS prompts Cancel, Ignore, or Suspend? (C, I, or S) .
           If you respond with S, you can either change a command line
           stored in the history buffer or execute new commands . You cannot
           modify the SUSPENDed dBASE program file or other open dBASE
           program or procedure files . If you try, dBASE III PLUS responds
           with File is Already Open .
           When you are ready to continue the execution of the program, type
           RESUME.
           You can also SUSPEND execution by placing the SUSPEND com-
           mand within a program .
           If you create any memory variables while the file is SUSPENDed,
           they are PRIVATE at the level of the suspension .
           CANCEL cancels all DO files, including ones that are SUSPENDed .
           You must close any procedure file with CLOSE PROCEDURE .

See Also   CANCEL, RESUME, RETURN, SET ECHO, SET STEP

TOTAL                                                                       CHAPTER 5


TOTAL      TOTAL sums the numeric fields of the active database file TO a sec-
           ond database file . The numeric fields in the TO database file contain
           the totals for all records that have the same key value in the original
           database .

Syntax     TOTAL ON < key field > TO < filename > [ < scope > ] [FIELDS
            < fields list > ] [WHILE < condition > ] [FOR < condition > ]

Defaults   The TO filename must include the drive designator if it is not on the
           default drive . A .dbf extension will be assumed unless otherwise
           specified .
           Unless otherwise specified by the scope, or the WHILE or FOR
           clause, all records are TOTALed . All numeric fields are totalled
           unless limited by the FIELDS list .
           If a catalog is in use, the TO file is added to it .

Usage      The active database file must be either INDEXED or SORTed on the
           key field . If the TO filename exists, TOTAL does not overwrite the
           existing file without a warning prompt, unless SET SAFETY is
           turned OFF.
           All records with the same value in the specified key field become a
           single record in the TO database . All numeric fields appearing in
           the FIELDS list contain totals . All other fields contain the data from
           the first record in the key field set .
           The structure of the TO file is identical to that of the active database
           file, except that memo fields are not copied to the new file .

Tips       Do not use the single letters A through J or M as database filenames
           because they are reserved for ALIAS names . However, AA is a valid
           database filename .
           If a field size in the TO file is not large enough to accommodate the
           total, dBASE III PLUS places asterisks in the field indicating an
           overflow . To avoid this, use MODIFY STRUCTURE to increase the
           size of the fields in the active database file to a size that can handle
           the largest total .

TYPE       TYPE displays the contents of a text file containing only ASCII-value
           characters .

Syntax     TYPE < filename > [TO PRINT]

Defaults   The filename must include the file extension . If the file is not on the
           default drive, and a SET PATH is not set to the file's location, you
           must precede the filename with its drive and directory location .
           Files with extended ASCII characters will be displayed as graphic
           characters .

Usage      TYPE will display standard ASCII files only . dBASE III PLUS
           database files, index files, and database text files cannot be read .
           TYPE cannot specify an open file . In other words, a program may
           not include a command to TYPE itself or any other open file .

COMMANDS                                                                  UPDATE

UPDATE            UPDATE uses data from an existing file to replace fields in the
                  active database file . The changes are made by matching records in
                  the two database files based on a single key field .

Syntax            UPDATE ON < key field > FROM < Alias > REPLACE < field >
                  WITH < exp > [, < field2 > WITH < exp > . . . ] [RANDOM]


Usage             The database being UPDATEd must be the active database file ; the
                  FROM database file is an open database file in another work area,
                  specified by its alias .
                  The key field must have the same field name in both database files .
                  If the key field in the UPDATEd file is not unique for each database
                  record, only the first record that matches the key field value is
                  updated.

Options           Both files must be either sorted or indexed on the key field unless
                  RANDOM is used . RANDOM requires the UPDATEd database to be
                  indexed on the key field, however, the FROM file may be in any
                  order.
                  If the REPLACE expression involves a field in the FROM database
                  (which is usually the case), the WITH field must be identified as
                  alias- > field .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                             U5-279
UPDATE                                                                                CHAPTER 5

                      has 17) .

USE               USE opens an existing database file and up to seven index files in
                  the selected work area . If the database contains memo fields, the
                  associated .dbt file is opened automatically .

Syntax            USE [ < filename > /?] [ INDEX < index file list > ] [ALIAS < alias
                  name > ]

Defaults          The USE command without any additional parameters closes the
                  active database and any associated index files in the currently
                  selected work area .
                  Unless otherwise specified, dBASE III PLUS assumes the .dbf exten-
                  sion for the filename and the .ndx extension for the files specified in
                  an index file list .
                  If the filename isn't already recorded, USE < filename > updates a
                  catalog if one is open and SET CATALOG is ON .

Usage             USE? displays a menu of cataloged .dbf files when a catalog is
                  open . The index file list can consist of up to seven files, all associ-
                  ated with the database file in USE .
                  If no alias name is included, the name given to the alias is the same
                  as the database filename . You can also use the letters A through J to
                  select work areas 1 through 10 . When you select a new work area,
                  the database file in that work area becomes the active database file .

Record            When you USE a database file without any index files, the record
                  pointer is positioned at the first record in the file .
Pointer
                  When you USE a database file with one or more index files, the
                  record pointer is positioned at the first logical record of the first
                  index file listed. The record pointer follows the order of that index
                  file.

Examples          To open the Clients database file in the currently selected work area
                  without index files and without specifying an alias, you would type
                  the following :

Syntax            WAIT [ < prompt > ] [TO < memvar > ]

Usage             The prompt may be a character variable or a literal character
                  string . If no prompt is specified, Press any key to continue . .   0

                  displays .

Options           If the TO < memvar > option is included, a character type memory

                       ENDIF

U6-6                                                    USING dBASE III PLUS
FUNCTIONS                                                                              &


                  & is the macro substitution function . It substitutes the contents of a
                  memory variable for its name in those cases where dBASE III PLUS
                  would otherwise take the variable name literally . This function can
                  be used only for character variables .

Syntax            & < character variable > [ . < cstring > ]

Usage             The macro substitution function is used to obtain the contents of a
                  character memory variable when dBASE III PLUS expects a literal
                  value rather than a character expression . It can also be used to con-
                  vert a character memory variable to a number . Some examples of
                  when dBASE III PLUS expects a literal value are FIND, USE, and
                  other commands that use a filename . Of course, the commands and
                  their keywords are also literal values .

Special Cases     Field names normally take precedence over memory variables when
                  their names are the same . Therefore, the syntax m-> < memvar >
                  is used when a memory variable with the same name should take
                  precedence over a field name . Since the & function always expects
                  a memory variable as its argument, this syntax is unnecessary and
                  redundant .

Examples          To use the FIND command with a memory variable :

                       . STORE 'Lo f tus' TO mname
                       Loft us
                         USE Clients INDEX Cnames
                       •
                         FIND &mname
                       •
                       • DISPLAY Las tname
                       Record# Lastname
                            34  Loftus




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                 U6-7
&                                                               CHAPTER 6


       dBASE III PLUS normally takes the character sequence following
       FIND literally. Without the &, dBASE III PLUS searches the data-
       base for the character sequence mname instead of Loftus . With the
       &, dBASE III PLUS searches for the contents of Mname .
       To substitute the contents of a memory variable name in a charac-
       ter string :

         • STORE 'Loftus' TO name
         Loftus
             STORE 'Hello &name' TO greeting
         •
         Hello Loftus
           ? greeting
         •
         Hello Loftus


       To insert the contents of a memory variable into a character
       sequence that contains no blanks :

         • STORE 'Cash' TO Income I
         Cash
         • STORE 'Savings' TO Income2
         Savings

         • STORE 'Checking' TO Income3
         Checking
         • STORE 'Income' TO Account
         Income
         • ? &Account .2
         Savings


       When nonblank characters are to be appended to the contents of a
       memory variable, as in the third example, use a period to indicate
       the end of the memory variable name .
       To USE a database the name of which is in a memory variable
       called Dname :

         • dname = 'Cl Tents'
         Clients

         • USE &dname
         • ? DBF()
         B :Clients .dbf

FUNCTIONS                                                                       CHR()

CHRO              The CHRO function converts a number to a character . It enables
                  you to produce special effects on a printer and/or monitor by send-
                  ing a value in the IBM Extended Character Set for any keyboard
                  character or graphics character . Note that ASCII code values (deci-
                  mal 0 through 127) are a subset of this set (decimal 0 through 255) .

Syntax            CHR( < expN > )

Usage              < expN > must be an integer from 1 to 255 .
                  CHR(0), which is a null character, cannot be sent to the printer or
                  any device . However, some printers allow CHR(128) to be
                  interpreted as CHR(0) . If the printer supports 8-bit characters, use
                  printer escape commands or DIP switches to set the eighth bit off
                  before sending CHR(128) .
                  In comparisons, CHR(0) must be on the left side of the equation .
                  When dBASE III PLUS performs character string comparisons, it
                  reads what is on the right side first . Because CHR(0) is a null string,
                  if it is on the right side, dBASE III PLUS reads no further and
                  returns a .T.

Examples          To display the ASCII character with a code (decimal value) of 65 :

                           ? CHR(65)
                       •
                       A

                  On most systems, the bell is sounded by means of ASCII code 7 .
                  Note that there is no keyboard equivalent for CHR(7) . To ring the
                  bell :

                       • ? CHR(7)

                  To ring the bell and write descriptive text on the screen :

                            CHR(7) +'Be more careful'
                       •Be ?more careful




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                 U6-15
CHR()                                                               CHAPTER 6

           no keyboard equivalent . For example, CHR(24) displays an up
           arrow .

                 ? CHR(14)

COL()                                                                 CHAPTER 6


C01()      The COL() function returns the current column position of the cur-
           sor . COL() makes it easier to control cursor positioning from within
           a program .

Syntax     COL()

Usage      You may store the value of COL() to a memory variable .
           COL() may be used for relative addressing . For instance,
           @ 1, COL() + 5 is the same as       1, $ + 5 . Both position the cur-
           sor five columns to the right of the current position .



             NOTE
             $ is a special operator that can also be used with
             @ . . . SAY . . . GET commands to indicate the current row or col-
             umn position on the display, or the coordinates on a printed
             page .




Examples   Use COL() within a program to find the current cursor position on
           the screen . For example, if you want to end a loop when the cursor
           is at column 70, part of the program might include :

             DO WHILE COL() < 70
                @ S,COLO + 5 SAY 'X'
             ENDDO


           To print the sentence "This is relative addressing" starting on row
           7, column 10 :

             @ 7, 10 SAY 'This is
             @ 7, COL() SAY 'relative addressing'


See Also   ~, PCOL(), PROW(), ROW()

                  CTOD() is the only way to create a date variable from a literal

ERROR()                                                                     CHAPTER 6


ERROR()    The ERROR() function returns the number corresponding to the
           error that caused an ON ERROR condition .

Syntax     ERROR()

Usage      ERROR() traps errors so corrective action may be taken if recovery
           is possible . Corrective actions may include closing files, changing
           disks, deleting files to make space, or redisplaying menus to choose
           other options .
           Some errors, of course, are not recoverable . Normal termination is
           done with the CANCEL command . Termination in debugging mode
           is done with the SUSPEND command . See Chapter 7 for the num-
           ber that is returned by ERROR() for a particular error message .



             NOTE
             For this function to return a number, an ON ERROR command
             must be active . RETURN and RETRY clear the error number
             and message that dBASE III PLUS recorded .




Examples   Here is a sample error procedure that illustrates how to use the ON
           ERROR command to recover from the error indicated by the mes-
           sage File is already open :

             *MAIN . PRG
             ON ERROR DO Err_prog WITH ERROR()



             MODIFY COMMAND Screen .fmt &&If Screen .fmt is in use, close it .



             *EOF :MAIN . PRG

                       *Err_prog .prg

                          CLOSE FORMAT
                          RETRY
                       ENDIF

FOUND()                                                              CHAPTER 6



FOUND()    The FOUND() function returns a logical True ( .T.) if the previous
           FIND, SEEK, LOCATE, or CONTINUE command was successful .

Syntax     FOUND()

NOTES      FOUND() is usually used in programming to determine which
           branch to take, depending upon whether or not a search command
           finds the requested data . There is one FOUND() per work area.
           If files are linked by SET RELATION, dBASE III PLUS sets
           FOUND() to True (.T.) or False (.F.) in the related work area when
           the record pointer moves in the current database file . When you
           move the record pointer in the current database file,
           dBASE III PLUS does an implicit search in any RELATEd
           database files .
           If you move the record pointer with any command other than
           FIND, LOCATE, SEEK, or CONTINUE, the result of FOUND() is .F .

Examples   The following examples use the Travel database .
           To check the results of a search on an unINDEXed file, a program
           might contain :

             LOCATE FOR agent ='JT'
             DO WHILE FOUND()
                 ? Agent
                 CONTINUE
             END DO


           To check the results of a search on a file INDEXed on Agent, a pro-
           gram might contain :

             SEEK 'JT'
             IF FOUND()
                DO WHILE Agent = 'JT'
                    ? Agent
                    SKIP
                ENDDO
             ENDIF


See Also   CONTINUE, EOF(), FIND, LOCATE, SEEK, SET RELATION

                                                                                           CHAPTER 6


           IIF() stands for "Immediate IF" and is a shortcut to the IF . . .ENDIF
           construction . It works both interactively from the dot prompt and
           within programs .

Syntax     IIF(< expL > , < exp 1 > , < exp2 > )

Usage      If the logical expression is True, IIF() returns the result of the first
           expression, otherwise it returns the result of the second expression,
            < exp 1 > and < exp2 > can be character, numeric, or date expres-
           sions . However, both must be the same type . The result is the same
           data type as the two expressions .
           You can use the IIF() function from the dot prompt, or with com-
           mands such as CREATE/MODIFY REPORT and CREATE/MODIFY
           LABEL . The IIF() function allows you to replace a field or a value
           in an expression with one of two values, based on the evaluation of
           a condition .

Tips       Replacing IF . . . ENDIF structures in programs with IIF() improves
           execution time .

Examples   In the following program, you can replace the first set of commands
           with the one IIF() command line that immediately follows them.
           This example uses the IF . . . ENDIF structure :

             IF Sex   = 'F'
                mname   =     'Ms . ' +   Last_name
             ELSE
                mname   = 'Mr . ' +       Last_name
             ENDIF


           This is the one-line replacement using IIF() :
             mname = IIF(Sex = 'F',          'Ms . ', 'Mr . ')   +   Last_name


           You could use this IIF() construction to print labels with the appro-
           priate salutation .
           If you have a database file with the date fields Start_date and
           End_date, you can extend the End_date by 30 days if that date has
           already passed .



U6-38                                                                            USING dBASE III PLUS
FUNCTIONS

                       In the interactive mode :

   REPLACE ALL   End_date WITH IIF(End_date > DATED, End_date, End_date + 30)


                       If you have already assigned a value to the logical memory variable
                       Is_error, the following routine converts the variable to a number,
                       then saves it in the numeric memory variable Error_code . If
                       Is_error is True, the new memory variable is 1, otherwise it is 0 .

                          error_code = IIF(is_error, 1, 0)

INKEY(    The INKEY() function returns an integer representing the most
          recent key pressed by the operator . It does not halt program
          execution .

Syntax    INKEY()

Notes     The INKEY() function returns an integer between 0 (zero) and 255,
          corresponding to a value in the IBM Extended Character Set
          entered from the keyboard .
          If there are several characters in the type-ahead buffer, INKEY()
          returns an integer representing the first of the characters entered .
          This clears the character from the type-ahead buffer.
          INKEY() returns a zero if no key is pressed .
          INKEY() returns the control-key equivalent of special keys, such
          as arrow keys and Ctrl-Home .
          This function is often used in programs as a condition for
          branching .
          It lets you use arrow and other nonprintable keys within a
          dBASE III PLUS program .

                  display for monochrome .

LEFT()     The LEFT() function returns a specified number of characters from
           the specified character string, starting with the first character on the
           left.

Syntax     LEFT( < expC > , < expN > )

Usage      The LEFT() function lets you retrieve the first part of a character
           string. This is the same as defining the SUBSTR function with a
           starting position of one, and the number of characters to extract
           with < expN >
           The numeric expression defines the number of characters to extract
           from the character string . If the numeric expression is zero or nega-
           tive, dBASE III PLUS returns a null string .
           If the numeric expression is greater than the length of the character
           string, dBASE III PLUS returns the entire string .

Examples   To extract the first three characters from a character string :

               ? LEFT('abcdef',3)
             abc


See Also   AT(), LTRIM(), RIGHT(), RTRIM(), STUFF(), SUBSTR(), TRIM()

MOD()             The MOD() function returns the remainder from a division of two
                  numbers . MOD() is particularly useful for base number
                  conversions, such as inches to yards .

Syntax            MOD(< expN 1 > , < expN2 > )

Usage             The MOD() function returns a whole number, the modulus, which
                  is the remainder of < expN 1 > divided by < expN2 > .
                   • expN 1 > is the numeric expression which is being limited
                   • expN2 > -1 is the upper limit of MOD() if < expN2 > is a positive
                  integer.
                  MOD() returns a positive number if < expN2 > is positive and a
                  negative number if < expN2 > is negative .
                  The modulus formula is :
                   • expN 1 > - floor( < expN 1 > / < expN2 >) * < expN2 >
                  where floor is a mathematical function that returns the greatest
                  integer less than or equal to its argument . The INT( ) function dif-
                  fers from floor in that INT( ) simply truncates any decimals . Floor is
                  not a dBASE III PLUS function .

Examples          To determine the MOD() of two numbers :

PCOL()     The PCOL() function returns the current column position on the
           printer, and helps keep track of printer column positions within
           programs .

Syntax     PCOL()

Usage      You may store the value of PCOL() to a memory variable .
           PCOL() may be used for relative addressing . The symbol $ is used
           to represent the current row or column position . For example,
           @ 1,PCOL() + 5 is the same as l, $ + 5 . Both position the printer
           five columns beyond the current column . Use PCOL() when you
           want to use a value stored in a memory variable .
           When used interactively with SET PRINT ON, the result is
           always 0 .

Examples   To start printing a specified number of columns from the last
           printer column position :

                  SET DEVICE TO PRINT
             •
                     9,PCOLU   + S SAY 'An example of relative addressing'
                  SET DEVICE TO SCREEN
             •

           To determine the current printer position :

             • ? PCOL O
             10

             • X = PCOL O
             14

FUNCTIONS                                                          RECCOUNT()

RECCOUNT()        RECCOUNT() returns the number of records in the currently
                  selected database file .

Syntax            RECCOUNT()

Usage             Using the RECCOUNT() function is a faster equivalent to issuing a
                  GO BOTTOM followed by RECNO() on an unindexed file .
                  If no file is in use, RECCOUNT() returns a zero .
                  RECCOUNT() includes all records, even if SET DELETED is ON or
                  SET FILTER is in effect .

Tips              Use RECCOUNT() with RECSIZE() and DISKSPACE() in applica-
                  tion programs that automatically back up database files . This
                  enables you to check if there is sufficient space on the disk for the
                  backup file . See the example in the RECSIZE() entry .

Examples          To find the number of records in the Travel file :

                       • USE Travel
                       • ?
                           RECCOUNT O
                               49
                       • USE

See Also          DBFO, DISKSPACEO, FIELDO, NDXO, RECSIZE()

RECSIZE()         The RECSIZE() function returns the size of a record in the
                  currently selected database file .

Syntax            RECSIZE()

Usage             If no file is in use, RECSIZE() returns a zero .
                  The RECSIZE() function enables a program to manipulate files
                  which are larger than available disk space .

Programming       Use RECSIZE() with RECCOUNT() and DISKSPACE() in applica-
                  tion programs that automatically back up database files . This
Notes             enables you to check if there is sufficient space on the disk for the
                  backup file . You also must know the header size, which is calcu-
                  lated as follows :
                        32 * < number of fields > + 35 .

Examples          To copy a large file named File from a hard disk to several floppy
                  disks on drive B, you can use the following routine in a program
                  file :

                       USE File
                       SET DEFAULT TO B
                       DO WHILE .NOT . EOF()
                            WAIT 'Insert new disk in drive B, and press a key . . .'
                            COPY NEXT (DISKSPACE() - <header size>)IRECSIZE() ;
                              TO Backup
                            SKIP
                       END DO
                       USE

REPLICATE()   REPLICATE() repeats a character expression a specified number of
              times .

Syntax        REPLICATE( < expC > , < expN > )

Usage         The character expression defines what character string to repeat .
              The numeric expression tells REPLICATE() how many times to
              repeat the character . REPLICATE() will only use the integer portion
              of the evaluated numeric expression .
              The resulting character expression must not exceed 254 characters .
              Therefore, the numeric expression must be a number less than 254
              divided by the number of characters in < expC > .
              The REPLICATE() function lets you produce a horizontal bar graph
              and is useful whenever you want to repeat a character .

Examples      To create a bar graph that enables you to see the commission rate
              in the Percent numeric field ;

                 • USE Tours
                 • LIST NEXT 5 Percent, REPLICA TE('*',Percent)
                 Record#    Percent REPLICATE('*',Percent)
                        1   10 .000   **********
                        2    7 .500   *******
                        3    5 .000   *****
                        4   10 .000   **********
                        5    7 .500   *******

RIGHT()           The RIGHT() function returns a specified number of characters
                  from a character string, counting from the last character in the
                  string .

Syntax            RIGHT( < expC > , < expN > )

Usage             The RIGHT() function allows you to extract a substring of charac-
                  ters from a character string . The numeric expression defines the
                  number of characters to extract from the character string, starting
                  from the last character on the right in the character string . If the
                  numeric expression is zero or negative, RIGHT() returns a null
                  string .
                  If the numeric expression is greater than the length of the character
                  string, RIGHT() returns the entire string .

Examples          To extract the last three characters from a character expression ;

                       def

STR()             The STR() function converts a number to a character string .

Syntax            STR( < expN > [,< length > ] [, < decimal > ])

Defaults          If the length is not specified, the string length is 10 characters . If no
                  decimal places are specified, the number is rounded to an integer .

Usage             The length you specify is the total number of characters in the
                  string created by STR(), including, if applicable, the decimal point,
                  minus sign, and the number of decimal places .
                  The number you specify for Decimal is the total number of decimal
                  places to output .
                  If you specify a smaller length than there are digits to the left of the
                  decimal in the numeric expression, dBASE III PLUS returns aster-
                  isks in place of the number .
                  If you specify fewer decimals than are in the numeric expression,
                  dBASE III PLUS truncates the result to the specified number of
                  decimal places .

Examples          To display the number 11 .14 as a character string :

                       . ? STR(11 . 14,5,2)
                       11 .14

FUNCTIONS                                                                    STUFF()

STUFF()           The STUFF() function replaces a portion of a character string with
                  another specified character string .

Syntax            STUFF( < expC 1 > , < start position > , < number of
                  characters > , < expC2 > )

Usage             Character expression < expC 1 > is the character string you want to
                  alter.
                  Character expression < expC2 > is the character string you want to
                  substitute for a specified number of characters in < expC 1> .
                  The start position is a numeric expression that indicates where you
                  want to begin the replacement in < expC 1 > .
                  The number of characters is a numeric expression that indicates
                  how many characters you want to remove from the original string .
                  If the number of characters is zero, the second character expression
                  is inserted, and no characters are removed from < expC 1> .
                  If character expression < expC2 > is a null string, dBASE III PLUS
                  removes the specified number of characters from character expres-
                  sion < expC 1 > without adding characters .
                  The new string will not be the same size as the original string if the
                  specified number of characters is different than the actual number
                  of characters in < expC2 > .

Examples          To replace a string :

                       • ? STUFF ('abc,2,1,'xyz')
                       ax yzc

                       • ? STUFF('abc,2, 1,")
                       ac

                       • ? STUFF ('abc,2,0,'xyz')
                       axyzbc

TRIM()                                                                   CHAPTER 6


TRIM()     The TRIM() function removes all trailing blanks from a character
           string .

Syntax     TRIM( < expC > )

Usage      TRIM() is followed either by a comma (,) or a plus sign (+) when
           used in a list of more than one field . A comma following TRIM()
           inserts one blank space before the listing of the next field in the list .
           A plus sign following TRIM() does not add any spaces before the
           next field in the list is displayed .
           If you use TRIM( < field name >) with either LIST or DISPLAY, the
           trailing blanks are not removed . Instead, the field contents are
           trimmed, but the field widths remain the same .

Examples   The Clients database file contains the fields Lastname and Address
           used in this example .

             • USE Clients
             •   ?
                 Las tname, Address
             Buckman                 830? Santa Anita Blvd


           The address is separated from the name by the number of trailing
           blanks in the Lastname field . To eliminate the blank spaces between
           the name and the address :

             •   ? TRIM(tas tname), Address
             Buckman 8307 Santa Anita Blvd


           The single space now separating the name from the address is
           caused by the comma in the command . If you used a plus (+) sign,
           there would be no spaces between the name and address .
             •   ? TRIM(Lastname) +Address
             Buckman8307 Santa Anita Blvd

TYPE()     The TYPE() function evaluates an expression and returns a single
           upper case character that indicates whether the expression is char-
           acter, numeric, logical, memo, or undefined . It is a test for the
           existence of a variable and/or the validity of an expression .

Syntax     TYPE( < expC > )

Usage      The TYPE() function always returns an upper case letter .
           The possible TYPE() values are :
           Character = C
           Numeric = N
           Logical = L
           Memo = M
           Undefined = U

Examples   To determine if the memory variable Test exists (note that the
           variable name is delimited by quotes unless it refers to another
           variable) :

                 ? TYPE('test')
             U

           U indicates that the memory variable does not exist . To test for a
           memory variable which does exist :

             • STORE 'testing 12 3' TO test
             testing 1 2 3
             •
               ? T YPE ('tes t')
             C

           C indicates that the memory variable does exist and that it is a char-
           acter type memory variable .
           To evaluate the expression "test/loo" and determine if the expres-
           sion is valid (this test can be used to avoid syntax errors) :

             • STORE 'hello' TO test
             hello
             • ? TYPE('test/100')
             U




U6-86                                                      USING dBASE III PLUS
FUNCTIONS                                                                    TYPE()

                  TYPE() returns a U since a character string cannot be divided by a
                  number.

                       • STORE 5 TO x
                       S
                       • STORE T To y
                       7
                       • ? TYPE('x*y/4')
                       N


                  TYPE() returns N since the operation evaluated creates a valid
                  expression .
                  To test an expression for validity, compare the result of the TYPE()
                  function to the upper case letter representing the expression type :

                       • ? TYPE('(1 + 2) = 5') _ 'L'
                       •T .

                  When the delimiters are omitted, TYPE() evaluates a variable that is
                  the content of the named variable . In the following instance, the
                  expression 'Sample' does not need to be delimited :

                       • STORE 5 TO cat
                       S
                       • STORE 'cat' TO sample
                       cat
                       • ? TYPE (sample)
                       N


                  TYPE() returns an N since 'cat', a numeric variable, is referred to
                  in Sample .

FUNCTIONS                                                                             VAL()

VAL()             The VAL() function converts numbers that are defined as characters
                  into a numeric expression .

Syntax            VAL( < expC > )

Usage             If the expression consists of leading non-numeric characters other
                  than blanks, dBASE III PLUS returns a value of zero .
                  VAL() displays the decimal portion of a number as designated by
                  SET DECIMALS .
                  The VAL() function operates from left to right, converting charac-
                  ters to numeric values until a text character is encountered . Lead-
                  ing blanks are ignored if the argument contains both numeric and
                  non-numeric characters . The leading numeric characters will be
                  converted to a numeric value . Trailing blanks are treated as text
                  characters and, when encountered, terminate the conversion
                  process .

Examples          The value of a non-numeric character sequence in VAL() is zero :

                            ? VAL ('ABC')
                       •
                            0 .00

Chapter 7
ERROR MESSAGES AND THEIR EXPLANATIONS

Below is a list of error messages for dBASE III PLUS .
The messages are arranged alphabetically . To the right of the error messages are num-
bers in square brackets . These are the numbers returned by the ERROR() function for
the corresponding error . If no error message number is listed, the ERROR() function
does not return a number .
Error messages that are specific to dBASE III PLUS on a local area network can be

Index expression is too big (220 char maximum) .                                      [112]
     The key expression you INDEXed ON exceeds the maximum length of 220 charac-
     ters . This limitation refers to the number of characters in the key expression,
     rather than the actual length of the resulting key. For example, the following key
     expression is 22 characters long :
         INDEX ON First_name + Last_name TO Alpha
         That is, 10 characters for First_name, 3 characters for the plus sign and spaces on
         either side, and 9 characters for Last_name . The actual key length may be larger or
         smaller, depending on the length of the First_name and Last_name fields in the
         database file structure .

The Structure   Following the header is the actual data in the database file . The end
                of the file is marked by a single byte . The rules for structuring data
of Database     records are :
( .dbf) File
                l.        Data records are preceded by one byte, a space (20H) if the
Records                   record is not deleted, an asterisk (2AH) if the record is deleted .
                2.        Data fields are packed into records and have no field separators
                          or record terminators .




UC-2                                                                      USING dBASE III PLUS
THE STRUCTURE OF DATABASE ( .DBF) AND MEMO ( .DBT) FILES

                  3 . Data types are stored in ASCII format as follows :

                       Data Type       Data Record Storage
                       Character       ASCII characters
                       Numeric         - .0123456789
                       Logical         ? Y y N n T t F f (? when not initialized)
                       Memo             10 digits representing a .dbt block number
                       Date            8 digits in YYYYMMDD format, such as
                                       19840704 for July 4, 1984


                                     Table C-3 ASCII codes for data types

                  4. The end-of-file marker is an ASCII 26 (1AH) character .

The Structure     Memo ( .dbt) files consist of 512-byte blocks numbered sequentially
                  (0, 1, 2, and so on) . Each time you write to the memo field in a
of Database       record of your database file, another block is added to the memo
Memo (.dbt)       file .
Files             The first block in the memo file, block 0, is the memo file header .
                  Only the first four bytes in the header block are used. That's where
                  dBASE III PLUS indicates the next available block number . The
                  number is hexadecimal, byte one containing the least significant
                  portion . For example, if the next available block is number 200, the
                  first four bytes of the .dbt file are C8 00 00 00 (hexadecimal) . If the
                  next available block is number 4321, the bytes are El 10 00 00, and
                  so on . The following table provides an example of how memo file
                  blocks are used .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                  UC-3
                                                                     APPENDIX C


           Block Number          .dbt Datafile

                  0              05000000 . . .
                  1              first memo field saved
                  2              second memo field saved
                                 (exceeds 512 bytes)
                  3              still second memo field
                  4              third memo field saved
                  5              next available block (not yet in file)

                           Table C-4 The structure of .dbt files

       Each memo field of each record in the .dbf file contains the number
       of the block (in ASCII) where the memo field data is located . If the
       memo field contains no data, there is no number in the .dbf file .
       When you write to the memo field, the next available block is used,
       and its number is stored invisibly in ASCII in the memo field of that
       record, behind the word memo .
       When data is changed in a memo field, the old contents remain in
       the .dbt file, and the entire changed contents are rewritten to the
       next available block . The number in the .dbf is changed to reflect
       the new location . This leaves the old block unused, with no pointer
       to it in the .dbf, and explains why .dbt files grow so large when
       edited repeatedly . When the file is copied from within
       dBASE III PLUS with USE < filename > and COPY TO
        < filename > , only the blocks that are pointed to get copied, thus
       discarding blocks no longer used and recovering the disk space .
       If the data written to a memo field uses more than one 512-byte
       block, the next available block number is incremented by the num-
       ber of blocks added . In other words, if the next available block is
       number 15, after 1200 bytes (which take up 3 blocks) are entered,
       the next available block is 18 .
       Each memo field terminates with two hex lA bytes . If 520 charac-
       ters are entered into a memo field, the ninth and tenth bytes of the
       next block will hold these terminators . The remaining 502 bytes of
       this block will be unused.

Glossary
                  This section defines terms used with dBASE III PLUS which may
                  also have special meaning when used to describe dBASE commands
                  and functions .

                  Catalog query clause . Activates a pull-down menu list in the open
                  catalog that displays files of a special type, such as .frm files with
                  the command CREATE REPORT? .
                  Command used to display immediate results of expressions or the
                  contents of fields, for example, ? SQRT(16) or? Lastname,firstname.

Abandon           An option which terminates a dBASE III PLUS command operation .
                  Any changes which have been made are not saved .

Action Line       A line near the bottom of a menu that is used to display information
                  about the application in progress .

Active File       The database file in USE in the currently selected work area .

Alias             An alternative database filename by which its work area can be ref-
                  erenced . An alias may be up to 10 characters in length and can con-
                  tain letters, numbers, and underscore characters . It must begin with
                  a letter and may not contain embedded blank spaces . Do not use
                  the single letters A through J or M as file or alias names, because
                  these are the default alias names for the 10 work areas and memory
                  variables .

Application       A customized program written in the dBASE programming language
                  that performs tasks required by a specific situation . The checkbook
                  management system used in Programming with dBASE III PLUS is
                  an application .

Applications      A special program on the Applications Generator disk that helps
Generator         users quickly create or modify database files or simple program-
                  ming applications .

Ascending Order   An order from the lowest to the highest value (for example, A to Z
                  and 0 to 9) . In dBASE III PLUS, ascending order for character data
                  is determined by the ASCII value . See Appendix D for a list of ASCII
                  character codes .



USING dBASE Ill PLUS                                                                  UG- 1
                                                                                  GLOSSARY

ASCII               An acronym for American Standard Code for Information
                    Interchange . It is a seven-bit code that defines 128 standard charac-
                    ters, including control characters, letters, numbers, and symbols .
                    An extra 128 characters are part of the extended ASCII set . The
                    seven-bit ASCII character codes are listed in Appendix D .

Assembly            A programming language that directly controls the machine code of
Language            a specific computer's microprocessor .

Attribute           A descriptive characteristic . In this manual, attributes refer to the
                    characteristics of the video display, including intensity, inverse
                    video, and underline .

Background          The area on the monitor upon which characters appear .

Back up             The process of copying all or some of the files on a disk to another
                    disk as insurance against the possible failure or loss of the first disk .

Backup File         A duplicate file copied on a separate disk and kept in a safe location
                    as insurance against loss of the original file .

Batch               A sequence of commands that perform a particular task and can
                    be executed with a single overall command . Also, a group of
                    records that may be considered as a single unit for the purposes of
                    processing .

Blackboard          The screen area used to design screen entry forms in the Screen
                    Painter.

Beginning-of-File   A location before the first physical record of a file .
(BOF)

Block               A unit of data as recorded on a disk . In MS-DOS, disks are divided
                    into sectors, each of which contains a block of 512 bytes . The COPY
                    FILE command transfers data in blocks only, meaning that the size
                    of the file created is rounded up to the next 512-byte unit .




Uc- 2                                                                  USING dBASE III PLUS
GLOSSARY

Branching          An unconditional change in program flow whereby commands in
                   another program, usually a subprogram, are performed . When the
                   subprogram commands are finished, program control returns to the
                   calling program .

Calling Program    A program module which contains instructions to branch to other
                   programs, known as subroutines .

Catalog            A special class of database file used to track dBASE III PLUS files
                   that are associated with a database file. Each associated file
                   becomes one record in the catalog . A catalog keeps records on all
                   files except command, text, and memory files . A catalog also allows
                   selection of files from pull-down menus, rather than by specifying a
                   filename .

Character          A keyboard symbol . Characters include letters, numbers, blank
                   spaces, and special symbols .

Character String   A sequence of letters, numbers, or symbols . The sequence 1234
                   Main Street, Anytown, is a character string. In this example, blanks
                   are included as part of the character string . Character strings are
                   normally enclosed in quotation marks or some other type of
                   delimiter.

Chronological      In date order . Dates do not appear in chronological order when
                   converted to character strings, unless put in the format of
                   `YYYYMMDD' .

Column             A number indicating the horizontal position on either the video
                   monitor or the printer. Column values increase from the left, with
                   the smallest value being zero . Also used to explain a field as a col-
                   umn in a rectangular table of rows and columns . Column is also
                   used to refer to a REPORT FORM column, that is, the content that
                   falls under a heading .

Command            An instruction to the computer to carry out a specific operation . A
                   verb that begins an instruction to dBASE III PLUS and appears as
                   the first word in a command line .




USING dBASE III PLUS                                                                  UG- 3
                                                                                GLOSSARY


Command File        A computer program containing dBASE III PLUS commands and
                    saved as a disk file with a .prg extension .

Concatenation       The joining of two or more character strings to form a single char-
                    acter string . In dBASE III PLUS, character strings may be concate-
                    nated with the plus (+) or minus (-) sign.

Condition           An expression that evaluates to a logical value of .T. or .F.

Conditional         A technique for changing the contents of records in a database file
Replacement         where the replacement of data depends on a specified condition
                    being met.

Constant            A data item that does not change during an operation . A constant is
                    also referred to as a literal.

Control Key         A key that assigns another function to certain keys on the computer
                    keyboard . Like the shift key, the control key is held down while
                    another key is pressed .

Control Structure   A way to alter the normal step-by-step flow of a program . In dBASE,
                    control structures are DO (branching), DO WHILE . . . ENDDO (loop-
                    ing), and IF . . . ENDIF and DO CASE . . . ENDCASE (conditions) .

Coordinate          A number, referring to a specific screen row and column position,
                    used as a reference point for displaying information .

Counter             A display that shows the number of items currently processed by a
                    command .

Cstring             An abbreviation for character string .

Current Option      The highlighted menu option .

Current Record      The record at which the record pointer is positioned . The record in
                    use.

Cursor              The visible marker used to indicate the current position on the
                    screen .
